pages.title: Introduction
pages.text:
Module 1: Basic understanding of traffic.

The instruction in Module 1 is designed to give you a basic understanding of traffic, including the handling characteristics of vehicles, the significance of road conditions, and the impact of human factors on road safety.

You will also gain knowledge of the most important legal provisions regarding driving instruction and the basic rules of the road.

The course will also familiarise you with the applicable legal provisions regarding your driving ability and health, and the duty to show particular consideration towards certain road users.

pages.title: Drivers education's purpose and content M
pages.text: In their driving lessons, driving instructors must follow the Danish Road Safety and Transport Agency’s curriculum for Category B. The curriculum sets out the knowledge, skills and behaviour you must possess in order to obtain a Driver's license.

pages.title: Drivers education's purpose and content
pages.text: The teaching plans and accompanying teacher’s guide can be viewed on the Danish Road Safety and Transport Agency’s website www.fstyr.dk and at www.retsinfo.dk

pages.title: Drivers education's purpose and content
pages.text: The overall aim of the driving course is to provide you with the skills that will enable you to drive a motor vehicle safely and to pass the driving test.

pages.title: Drivers education's purpose and content
pages.text: The purpose of the driving course is to give you insight into and an understanding of the dangers and difficulties you will encounter as a driver on the road, as well as to provide you with knowledge of the traffic rules and other Legal provisions relevant in this context.

pages.title: Drivers education's purpose and content
pages.text: You must also be familiar with the vehicle and its operation so that you can identify any faults that may arise and affect safety.

pages.title: Drivers education's purpose and content
pages.text: The training must give you an understanding of the fundamental human conditions that influence driving ability, so that you can make full use of your abilities and, to the extent necessary, counteract common human limitations.

pages.title: Drivers education's purpose and content
pages.text: You must learn to assess traffic critically and drive the vehicle without endangering yourself or others, and the training must help you become a considerate and responsible driver.

pages.title: Drivers education's purpose and content
pages.text:
You must also acquire knowledge of and understanding for the situation of vulnerable road users, particularly under conditions that involve motorised traffic.

It is therefore not enough that, during your training, you learn about the ideals and requirements of the Highway Code regarding how one ought to, must and may behave on the road.

The course also places particular emphasis on the risks and dangers that, despite the rules of the Road Traffic Act, arise daily in traffic.

children.title: The connection between theory and practical education

pages.title: B Not001 M
pages.text:
The course is divided into theoretical instruction in the classroom and practical driving lessons in the training vehicle.

As a general rule, a lesson must last at least 45 consecutive minutes.

pages.title: Not002 M
pages.text:
The theoretical and practical instruction must follow the curriculum. The order and content of the individual lessons are set out so that you must have covered the theory for a practical exercise in the theory classroom immediately before you undertake the practical exercise in the driving school car.

In the module plan, which the driving school must provide to you, you can see how the course is structured, comprising theory lessons in the classroom and practical lessons in the training vehicle.

The driving instructor must go through the module plan with you during the first theory lesson.

pages.title: Not003 M
pages.text:
The Driver's License Regulations stipulate that an applicant for a standard car driver's license must have at least 30 theory lessons of at least 45 minutes each and at least 24 lessons of practical driving instruction of at least 45 minutes’ duration.

The mandatory minimum number of lessons cannot be taken as indicative of a typical training course, as the total teaching time of 54 lessons of 45 minutes each is an absolute minimum.

Many learners will require further revision in both theoretical subjects and practical manoeuvres. In particular, when it comes to practical driving, learners may need up to twice as many driving lessons as specified in the minimum requirement.

children.title: 10.1.1 Requirements for obtaining a drivers license

pages.title: 10.1.1-1 B
pages.text: If you have not previously held a Driver's license for cars, you must have received instruction from an approved driving instructor prior to the driving test.

pages.title: 10.1.1-2 B
pages.text: The instruction must strictly follow the Danish Road Safety and Transport Agency’s regulations and cover both a theoretical and a practical syllabus. A module plan must be used in the instruction.

pages.title: 10.1.1-3 B
pages.text:
The module plan must be divided into theory lessons and practical lessons, i.e. driving lessons.

Upon completion of each module, the driving instructor must confirm, by signing the module plan, that the module has been completed with a satisfactory result.

pages.title: 10.1.1-4 B
pages.text: At the closed practice area and driving skills facility, apart from brief instruction from the driving instructor, you must be alone in the car during the practice drive.

pages.title: 10.1.1-5 B
pages.text: During practice driving on ordinary roads and streets, an approved driving instructor must sit next to you, and the driving instructor is considered to be the driver of the car in this context.

pages.title: 10.1.1-6 B
pages.text: If you do not already hold a motorcycle or tractor driver's license, you must, as a car driver, have completed a traffic-related first aid course. This course can help save the lives of other road users and may help to significantly reduce the extent of their injuries following a traffic accident.

pages.title: 3.1-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: As a driver, it is important to understand the manoeuvring characteristics of different vehicles and the driver’s field of vision, so that you can anticipate the challenges and risks they may pose in various traffic situations. This lesson covers the key manoeuvring characteristics of passenger cars, vans, Trucks, vehicles with trailers, tractors, motorcycles, mopeds and bicycles.

pages.title: 3.1.1-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: The term ‘speed characteristics’ encompasses acceleration, top speed and braking performance. • Acceleration refers to how quickly the vehicle can pick up speed. • Top speed indicates how fast the vehicle can travel in top gear. • Braking performance indicates how quickly the vehicle can slow down.

pages.title: 3.1.2-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: The vehicle’s steering characteristics include steering response, directional stability and crosswind sensitivity, which depend on the load distribution between the axles: •Steering response improves with increased weight on the rear axle. •Directional stability improves with increased weight on the front axle. •Crosswind sensitivity increases with more weight on the rear axle.

pages.title: 3.1.3-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: The driver’s ability to orientate themselves depends on sight and hearing and is affected by visibility in all directions as well as blind spots caused by the vehicle’s design. Glasses and headgear can restrict the field of vision, whilst high noise levels inside the vehicle can impair the ability to perceive important sounds such as horns and Emergency vehicles.

pages.title: 3.2.1-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Passenger cars and vans typically accelerate quickly. However, there are differences between vehicle types, as low-slung cars with wide tyres and a long wheelbase generally accelerate faster than tall cars with narrow tyres and a short wheelbase. Passenger cars and vans usually have a high top speed, as most can travel faster than 130 km/h, which is the highest general speed limit in Denmark.

pages.title: 3.2.1-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Passenger cars and vans typically have good braking performance, as the brakes on these vehicles are subject to higher standards compared to buses, trucks and tractors.

pages.title: 3.2.1-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: The steering characteristics of passenger cars and vans are so well developed that there is no significant difference in their responsiveness.

pages.title: 3.2.1-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Passenger cars and vans are generally characterized by directional stability, which means they maintain a steady course when driving in a straight line. However, directional stability and sensitivity to crosswinds may vary depending on the vehicle’s construction and load.

pages.title: 3.2.1-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: Passenger cars with trailers often have poorer acceleration, lower top speed and significantly poorer braking performance compared to cars without trailers. A car with a trailer may have a tendency to sway, so it is important to maintain extra side distance, especially when overtaking.

pages.title: 3.2.1-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: When braking heavily on a downhill slope or on slippery roads, trailers can easily skid and swing across the roadway.

pages.title: 3.2.1-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: Passenger cars and vans are generally not particularly sensitive to crosswinds. However, if the vehicle is heavily laden, so that a large proportion of the weight is on the rear axle, this can make the car more sensitive to crosswinds.

pages.title: 3.2.1-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: In passenger cars, the driver typically has a good view to the front and to the sides. However, there are some blind spots due to the car’s bodywork. The diagram shows the typical angles that are not immediately visible from the Driver's seat.

pages.title: 3.2.1-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: Even the narrow windscreen pillar can easily obscure a car, but by moving your head you can check what is hidden behind the pillars.

pages.title: 3.2.1-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: Passenger cars often have such wide corner pillars at the rear window that a cyclist can be hidden in the blind spot.

pages.title: 3.2.1-11 BCDBECE
pages.text: Dirty, misted or iced-up windows can significantly reduce the driver’s visibility.

pages.title: 3.2.1-12 BCDBECE
pages.text: A caravan or similar towed vehicle restricts rear visibility. Although the towing vehicle must be fitted with additional mirrors, many drivers are not used to relying solely on mirrors to check what is happening behind them.

pages.title: 3.2.1-13 BCDBECE
pages.text: Vans have poor rear visibility due to the enclosed cargo area without windows, as the driver can only use the side mirrors. The diagram shows the van’s blind spots.

pages.title: 3.2.1-14 BCDBECE
pages.text: Passenger cars and vans generally have a low noise level, so the driver can easily pick up signals from horns and Emergency vehicles. However, the use of, for example, a radio can reduce the driver’s ability to orientate themselves using sound.

pages.title: 3.2.2-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Trucks usually have poor acceleration, but an empty truck with a powerful engine can accelerate quite quickly over a short distance.

pages.title: 3.2.2-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: According to the law, trucks and buses have a relatively low top speed, which for trucks and many buses may not exceed 80 km/h, although these types of vehicles often exceed the speed limit. However, buses and certain trucks may be approved for 100 km/h, meaning they may travel at up to 100 km/h, but only on Motorways.

pages.title: 3.2.2-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: Trucks have poorer braking performance. By law, a passenger car must be able to stop within a maximum of 6 metres at a speed of 30 km/h. By comparison, a truck must use 10 metres to stop at the same speed.

pages.title: 3.2.2-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Buses, Trucks and truck and trailers require extra space to turn and perform other similar manoeuvres.

pages.title: 3.2.2-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: Large vehicles have high directional stability and need plenty of space to negotiate a bend.

pages.title: 3.2.2-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: Normally, large and heavy vehicles are not particularly sensitive to crosswinds, but trucks with light loads or empty trucks with high constructions can be much more sensitive to crosswinds.

pages.title: 3.2.2-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: The driver of a truck has a very good view to the front, but the large wing mirrors create some significant blind spots.

pages.title: 3.2.2-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: The view to the rear in the truck’s wing mirrors is limited, and there are large blind spots.

pages.title: 3.2.2-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: If, from the Driver's seat of a passenger car, you cannot see the lorry driver’s face in the wing mirror, there is danger that the lorry driver cannot see the passenger car either.

pages.title: 3.2.2-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: Some trucks may have such high noise levels or such well-insulated cabs that the driver may find it difficult to hear and locate horn signals, Emergency vehicles and the like.

pages.title: 3.2.3-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Trucks with trailers typically have poorer acceleration than trucks without trailers.

pages.title: 3.2.3-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Trucks and buses with trailers, like passenger cars with trailers, may have a tendency to sway and suffer from reduced directional stability.

pages.title: 3.2.3-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: Trailers attached to trucks and buses can easily skid and spin across the roadway in slippery conditions or during heavy braking on a hill.

pages.title: 3.2.4-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Tractors without trailers have a powerful engine that ensures rapid acceleration over short distances. However, their maximum speed is only 40 km/h, and they are therefore fitted with a red triangle at the rear to indicate that they are slow-moving vehicles.

pages.title: 3.2.4-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Older tractors may have rear lights and brake lights, but do not necessarily need to have Blinkers. However, the tractor must be fitted with a light bar, and the driver must use their arm to signal when turning.

pages.title: 3.2.4-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: Tractors have poor braking performance, as the Service brake often only acts on the rear wheels. If a tractor with a trailer brakes hard whilst turning, there is danger that the tractor may overturn.

pages.title: 3.2.4-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Tractors with various implements and/or trailers have unstable steering and a marked tendency to sway when driving straight ahead. This makes them dangerous to overtake if there is not enough space to maintain a safe side distance during the manoeuvre.

pages.title: 3.2.4-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: Tractors with a loading grab or similar equipment at the front or rear may tilt so much whilst driving that the front wheels lift off the road, thereby losing some of their steering ability.

pages.title: 3.2.4-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: Tractors with trailers, like trucks and buses, require a great deal of space when turning and performing similar manoeuvres.

pages.title: 3.2.4-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: Tractors may be fitted with implements that are often wider than the tractor itself, and when turning, these implements may encroach on other lanes.

pages.title: 3.2.4-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: From the tractor’s cab, there is usually a good view forwards, to the sides and backwards, with only a few blind spots.

pages.title: 3.2.4-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: A large and tall load on the Trailer can create significant blind spots to the rear.

pages.title: 3.2.4-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: The high noise level in the tractor cab, which often requires the use of ear defenders, makes it difficult or impossible for the driver to hear horn signals and similar sounds.

pages.title: 3.2.5-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Motorcycles have impressive acceleration and high top speeds, which can often take other road users by surprise.

pages.title: 3.2.5-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Motorcycles have poor braking performance, particularly in poor weather conditions, where the risk of skidding is high if the rider lacks experience and has not mastered the technique of using the hand and foot brakes simultaneously.

pages.title: 3.2.5-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: Large motorcycles are more stable in a straight line than small, light motorcycles, but it is important to note that, due to their relatively high speed, they require extra space when cornering.

pages.title: 3.2.5-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: All motorcycles are sensitive to crosswinds, so it is important to keep a good distance from the side, both when meeting oncoming traffic and when overtaking in strong crosswinds.

pages.title: 3.2.5-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: A crash helmet, visor, goggles and windscreen restrict the motorcyclist’s forward vision and create blind spots to the side and rear. At the same time, the helmet makes it difficult for the motorcyclist to hear audible signals.

pages.title: 3.2.5-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: In bad weather, dirt, rain or mist on motorcycle goggles or the visor can significantly impair the motorcyclist’s vision.

pages.title: 3.2.5-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: When riding without goggles or a visor, the motorcyclist tends to squint and turn their head even at low speeds, which significantly reduces their ability to orientate themselves.

pages.title: 3.2.5-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: It is not a legal requirement for all motorcycles to have side mirrors. Without side mirrors, a sharp turn of the head is required to look behind, which can negatively affect the motorcyclist’s steering.

pages.title: 3.2.5-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: A passenger on a motorcycle can hinder the rider’s ability to manoeuvre. If the passenger does not lean into the bend, it becomes more difficult to steer the motorcycle safely through

pages.title: 3.2.5-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: A motorcycle with a sidecar has different handling characteristics to a two-wheeler and has less Directional stability. When accelerating, it pulls to the right and when braking, to the left. In a right-hand bend, the sidecar may lift, whilst the rear wheel may lift in a left-hand bend

pages.title: 3.2.5-11 BCDBECE
pages.text: A motorcycle with a trailer, like a car with a trailer, has a tendency to sway. In addition, a motorcycle with a trailer often has poorer acceleration, a lower top speed and reduced braking performance.

pages.title: 3.2.6-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Mopeds are classified as ‘small mopeds’ and ‘large mopeds’. A large moped can easily be mistaken for a small motorbike or a small moped and can only be identified by the small white number plate at the rear.

pages.title: 3.2.6-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: A small moped, which has a maximum speed of 30 km/h, may either have no number plate or, if it was first registered after July 2006, have a yellow number plate with two letters and four digits.

pages.title: 3.2.6-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: A large moped, which can travel up to 45 km/h and therefore requires a motorcycle or car Driver's license, must be registered and have a small white number plate with two letters and three digits.

pages.title: 3.2.6-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: A large moped, even though its top speed is only 45 km/h, may have acceleration capabilities comparable to those of a small motorcycle.

pages.title: 3.2.6-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: Moped riders face the same visibility conditions as motorcyclists. The crash helmet restricts side and rear visibility, and motorcycle goggles or visors can further reduce visibility in poor weather.

pages.title: 3.2.6-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: Small mopeds and cyclists typically accelerate slowly.

pages.title: 3.2.6-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: Normally, a small moped travels faster than a bicycle, but electric bikes often travel just as fast as mopeds, and racing bikes can even be faster. It is important to be aware that some small mopeds are illegally modified so that they can travel significantly faster than the permitted 30 km/h.

pages.title: 3.2.6-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: In heavy traffic, small mopeds and cyclists travel at a relatively high speed compared to other road users.

pages.title: 3.2.6-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: Small mopeds and bicycles have poor braking performance, and there is danger of skidding during heavy braking.

pages.title: 3.2.7-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: A bicycle without a handbrake cannot stop when the pedal arm is vertical.

pages.title: 3.2.7-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Mopeds and bicycles are not particularly stable under conditions that affect direction and tend to wobble when travelling slowly. The same applies in windy conditions, as they are very sensitive to crosswinds.

pages.title: 3.2.7-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: Sensitivity to crosswinds and unstable handling become more pronounced for mopeds and bicycles when they are loaded with heavy luggage or children.

pages.title: 3.2.7-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Cyclists have optimal conditions for looking ahead, but looking behind requires a cumbersome turn of the head and body, which is often avoided. When the cyclist looks behind, this movement can affect the bike’s balance and increase the risk of wobbling.

pages.title: 3.2.7-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: Moped riders without goggles and cyclists tend, in rainy weather and similar conditions, to squint and turn their heads partially away from the road, which increases the risk of poor orientation.

pages.title: 3.2.7-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: Impractical clothing can also significantly reduce a cyclist’s ability to orientate themselves.

pages.title: 4.1.1-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Road safety is not just about the driver’s technical ability to handle the car, but just as much about how the driver perceives and assesses the traffic situation.

pages.title: 4.1.1-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Lack of attention, misunderstandings and misjudgements contribute to around a third of all accidents. During approximately a third of total driving time, unnecessary actions are performed that take the driver’s focus away from the traffic.

pages.title: 4.1.1-3 BCDCE
pages.text: The perception of the traffic situation is based primarily on visual impressions, so it is important to be aware of any visual impairments or reduced vision.

pages.title: 4.1.2-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Driving safety depends not only on the driver’s technical ability to control the car, but equally on how the driver perceives and assesses traffic conditions. Traffic perception is primarily based on visual impressions, and as a driver, one must be aware of possible visual impairments or reduced vision. Lack of attention, misperceptions and incorrect assessments play a major role in most road traffic accidents.

pages.title: 4.1.2-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Reaction time is the time that elapses from when a hazard is detected until the driver reacts to it (braking, steering, etc.). It can vary from a fraction of a second to several seconds. It is important to remember that the vehicle continues at the same speed throughout the reaction time.

pages.title: 4.1.3-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: One can normally only perceive and react to 2–3 things per second, so it is important to adjust one’s speed to this limited ability to perceive and react. In this case, there are only a few things one needs to perceive and perhaps react to.

pages.title: 4.1.3-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: A complex traffic situation is constantly changing and therefore requires extra attention and a quick reaction.

pages.title: 4.1.4-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Things or events that are particularly striking or catch one’s interest attract attention. Consequently, there is a risk of overlooking important details.

pages.title: 4.1.4-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: You can improve your perception by practising concentrating and focusing on the essential elements. That is to say, the details, warning signs and signals in the current traffic situation that are relevant to the manoeuvre you are in the process of performing.

pages.title: 4.1.4-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: When you are stationary at an Intersection waiting to make a left turn, it is important to focus on more than just oncoming traffic. Use the waiting time to also observe the traffic on the road you are about to turn into. Keep an eye on the Traffic Lights at regular intervals, and be aware of pedestrians approaching from behind who may cross the Roadway you are about to enter. Always take a critical view of your immediate assessment of the traffic situation.

pages.title: 4.1.4-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Visual acuity is only sufficient to clearly perceive all details in a small part of the field of vision. When you keep your head and eyes still and look straight ahead, your effective field of vision is almost 180 degrees, but at a speed of around 100 km/h, it is reduced to about 40 degrees. You should therefore avoid keeping your gaze fixed in one direction for too long.

pages.title: 4.1.5-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: A mobile phone call will always distract you from the traffic and require both attention and action, which can increase your Reaction time. It is illegal to use a hand-held mobile phone whilst driving. Avoid talking on a hands-free mobile phone in heavy traffic or other demanding situations where full concentration on driving is required. End the call and resume it when the vehicle is stationary.

pages.title: 4.1.6-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Various activities affect the ability to perceive and react. When the driver uses electronic devices such as a GPS, mobile phone or smartphone whilst driving, this can divert attention from the traffic. Lack of focus and distraction whilst driving are a significant cause of many accidents.

pages.title: 4.1.6-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Using a mobile phone is also a distraction.

pages.title: 4.1.6-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: Operating the car radio or having a conversation with a passenger can also divert some of the driver’s attention away from the traffic and contribute to the risk of a road traffic accident.

pages.title: 4.1.6-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Other passengers, particularly noisy children, but also animals, can be a distraction.

pages.title: 4.1.6-5 BCDCE
pages.text: Strong emotions such as excitement, grief or worry can impair concentration.

pages.title: 4.2.1-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: People tend to steer in the direction they are looking. This can be avoided by looking away from whatever you risk colliding with.

pages.title: 4.2.1-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: On long stretches of road, you should look as far ahead as possible.

pages.title: 4.2.1-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: If you focus on the cyclist, the link between your line of sight and the tendency to steer in the same direction may increase the risk of hitting the cyclist. Instead, you should look at the road well ahead of the cyclist.

pages.title: 4.2.1-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: When passing through narrow sections, it is important to focus your gaze in the middle of the narrowing, preferably on a point just beyond it, and avoid looking at the edges.

pages.title: 4.2.1-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: On a narrow road, you should not stare at oncoming traffic, but instead direct your gaze towards a point on the road behind you.

pages.title: 4.2.1-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: When driving through a bend, you should let your gaze follow the innermost and most curved edge of the road or the centre line.

pages.title: 4.2.1-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: When turning at an Intersection, do not spend too long looking for other road users, but instead direct your gaze towards the direction you are going.

pages.title: 4.3.1-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Distances of less than 50 m are usually judged fairly accurately.

pages.title: 4.3.1-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Distances over 50 metres are overestimated, meaning they are perceived as longer than they actually are. Therefore, the oncoming truck is closer than one might immediately think.

pages.title: 4.3.1-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: The estimation of distance is often based on the visual impression of the perspective and the size of the object in front; therefore, small vehicles may appear to be further away than they actually are.

pages.title: 4.3.1-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: In bad weather and darkness, where perspective and the size of objects are obscured or hidden, it becomes incredibly difficult to judge distances with any degree of accuracy.

pages.title: 4.3.2-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: One’s own speed is judged on the basis of both the car’s noise level and vibrations, as well as the distance to visible points along the road. Speeds below 50 km/h are assessed relatively accurately, whilst speeds above 50 km/h are often underestimated and thus perceived as lower than they actually are.

pages.title: 4.3.2-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: There is a risk of underestimating one’s own speed when driving on a road with few background landmarks and in a car with a low noise level. Furthermore, it is common to become speed-blind when, after driving at high speed for a long time, one enters an area where the speed must be reduced.

pages.title: 4.3.3-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Most people find it difficult to accurately judge the speed of cars that are more than 200 metres away.

pages.title: 4.4.1-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: As a driver, it is important to be aware of the key rules regarding driving and the consumption of alcohol, medication, stimulants or sedatives, drugs, as well as conditions such as fatigue, illness and similar conditions.

pages.title: 4.4.1-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Even small amounts of alcohol can impair your perception and reaction times, making it difficult to react correctly and quickly enough in challenging or unexpected situations, even at low Blood alcohol concentrations.

pages.title: 4.4.1-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: If you drive to a place where alcohol is served, you should decide in advance whether you intend to drive home again. If you choose to drive home, you should either avoid alcohol altogether or drink very little.

pages.title: 4.4.1-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: If your blood alcohol concentration is over 0.50 per mille or over 0.25 mg per litre of exhaled air whilst driving or attempting to drive, you will be punished for Driving under the influence (DUI).

pages.title: 4.4.1-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: If you are unable to drive safely, you may be prosecuted for Driving under the influence (DUI) even if your blood alcohol concentration is below 0.5.

pages.title: 4.4.1-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: A blood alcohol concentration of over 0.50 per mille and up to 2.00 per mille, corresponding to between 0.25 mg per litre of breath and 1.00 mg per litre of breath, is punishable on a first offence by a substantial fine

pages.title: 4.4.1-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: If your blood alcohol concentration is 2.01 or higher, you will be fined, sentenced to imprisonment and your car may be confiscated.

pages.title: 4.4.1-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: A blood alcohol concentration of over 0.50 and up to 1.20, corresponding to between 0.25 mg per litre of air and 0.60 mg per litre of air, results in a suspended driving ban for a first offence

pages.title: 4.4.1-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: A blood alcohol concentration of 1.21 per mille or above normally results in an unconditional disqualification from driving.

pages.title: 4.4.1-10 BCDCE
pages.text: First-time holders of a driver's license with a blood alcohol concentration between 0.20 and 1.20, i.e. holders of a Category A or B driver's license who have not held their first driver's license for three years, will be banned from driving.

pages.title: 4.4.1-11 BCDBECE
pages.text: The penalties for drink-driving will become significantly stricter in the event of repeated offences.

pages.title: 4.4.1-12 BCDBECE
pages.text: It is always necessary to complete an ANT course, which stands for Alcohol, Drugs and Traffic, in connection with Driving under the influence (DUI).

pages.title: 4.4.1-13 BCDBECE
pages.text: It is illegal to allow a person to drive a car if they have consumed so much alcohol that they are unable to drive safely.

pages.title: 4.4.1-14 BCDBECE
pages.text: The police may at any time require a driver to take a Breathalyzer test to check the level of alcohol in their breath.

pages.title: 4.4.2-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Taking substances that affect your mental state, such as drugs or certain types of medication, impairs your ability to drive and increases the risk of road accidents.

pages.title: 4.4.2-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: If you take various narcotic substances or mix them with alcohol, the effect on the person can be unpredictable, and the risk of accidents will in any case be significantly increased.

pages.title: 4.4.2-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: It is illegal to drive a car or even attempt to drive if you have taken substances that affect your consciousness and pose a danger to road safety.

pages.title: 4.4.2-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: If you take medication that affects your consciousness contrary to your doctor’s prescription, you may be subject to the rules on driving with substances affecting consciousness in your blood.

pages.title: 4.4.2-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: If substances affecting consciousness are detected in the blood, the first offence is punishable by a fine and an immediate disqualification from driving, which corresponds to the penalty for driving with a blood alcohol level of 1.21.

pages.title: 4.4.2-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: The penalties for driving with psychoactive substances in the blood become significantly stricter in the event of repeated offences.

pages.title: 4.4.2-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: It is prohibited to hand over the car to a person who has consumed psychoactive substances.

pages.title: 4.4.2-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: The police may at any time require the driver to undergo an eye test . . .

pages.title: 4.4.2-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: or to provide a saliva or sweat sample to check for the presence of substances that affect consciousness.

pages.title: 4.4.2-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: An ANT course must always be completed; this is a course on Alcohol, Drugs and Traffic, which must be undertaken in connection with driving under the influence of substances affecting consciousness.

pages.title: 4.4.3-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: You must not drive a car or attempt to do so if you are unable to do so in a fully responsible manner due to illness, fatigue, medication or the influence of stimulants or sedatives.

pages.title: 4.4.3-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Your perception and reaction times are impaired if you are ill or have taken nervous system or sleeping medication, strong cough or painkillers, or medication for allergies, travel sickness, seasickness or similar conditions.

pages.title: 4.4.3-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: The sedative effect of the medication is greatly increased if alcohol is consumed at the same time.

pages.title: 4.4.3-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Medicines that may impair alertness and reaction times are often marked with a red triangle. Always ask your doctor or pharmacist how the medicine affects your ability to drive.

pages.title: 4.4.3-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: Your perception and reaction times may be impaired if you are affected by a strong emotional experience, such as a traumatic event, or if you are suffering from both physical and mental fatigue, such as stress. You should therefore carefully consider leaving your car at home if you have experienced something traumatic, have not had enough sleep the night before, or if you are on your way home after a long and demanding day at work.

pages.title: 4.4.3-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: Many drivers tend to overestimate their abilities by driving long distances at times when they would normally be relaxing, resting or sleeping.

pages.title: 4.4.3-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: If, at the request of the police, a doctor assesses that you are unfit to drive safely, the penalty depends on the degree of impairment – slight, moderate, severe or intoxicated – and corresponds to the penalty for Driving under the influence (DUI)

pages.title: 4.4.3-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: It is not permitted to hand over the car to a person who, due to illness, fatigue or the consumption of medication or similar, is unable to drive the car in a safe and responsible manner.

children.title: 4.5 The behaviour of other road users

pages.title: 4.5.1-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: There are certain groups of road users who experience more accidents, either because they lack experience of navigating traffic, or because they have reached an age where it can be difficult to cope with the busy traffic of everyday life.

pages.title: 4.5.2-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Young children under the age of 5–6 lack both the mental and physical abilities to navigate traffic safely. Although they may appear cautious, they are still unreliable road users, as they cannot control impulsive actions such as running out into the road. They find it difficult to assess dangers and, due to their unsteady movements, are at risk of tripping or falling easily when walking or running.

pages.title: 4.5.2-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Young children in traffic are a clear warning sign, requiring extra attention, low speed and readiness to brake. Use the horn with caution, as noise can easily cause panic.

pages.title: 4.5.2-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: Younger schoolchildren aged 6 to 10 can often recognise an obvious danger, but find it difficult to anticipate a dangerous situation that is about to arise. They are slow to orientate themselves and therefore perceive situations more slowly. At the same time, they are unsure of their ability to judge speed and distance.

pages.title: 4.5.2-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Younger schoolchildren are generally familiar with the basic road rules, but they often find it difficult to understand that they themselves must be alert, even in places where others are obliged to give way, such as at Crosswalks and Traffic Lights. They also struggle to maintain concentration in traffic and may act impulsively on sudden impulses or prompts.

pages.title: 4.5.2-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: Most cycling accidents involve children aged 10–15, but children as young as 5–6 are already a vulnerable group. Many children do not receive enough practical training in cycling correctly and safely, partly because the transition from balance bikes to standard bicycles can be unclear.

pages.title: 4.5.2-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: Many children find it difficult to keep their balance, steer and brake. Even older schoolchildren aged 10–15 may have problems steering their bike if they have to look in a direction other than straight ahead, which often leads to poor awareness, particularly of what is happening behind them.

pages.title: 4.5.2-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: All children have a strong need to explore their own abilities and skills and therefore often use the bicycle as a means of experimenting and playing.

pages.title: 4.5.2-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: Although young people have the best-developed perception and reaction times, they are still among the most vulnerable road user groups. This is primarily due to a lack of experience and potential attitudinal challenges, particularly among moped riders aged 15–19.

pages.title: 4.5.2-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: Young people’s lack of experience often manifests itself as difficulties in adjusting their speed to the conditions, accurately assessing their own manoeuvring options, and being sufficiently critical of other Road users. Some young people are tempted to use the vehicle to test their abilities, seek thrills, cope with disappointment or assert themselves, which can lead to dangerous situations for themselves and others. This group also includes motorcyclists aged 18–22.

pages.title: 4.5.2-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: Most young moped riders, motorcyclists and car drivers have a positive attitude towards traffic, the rules of the road and the need to show consideration, but may find it difficult to translate this into their driving style due to a lack of awareness of the many dangers. Young people’s positive attitude often clashes with other road users’ lack of consideration and understanding. Among motorists, 18- to 24-year-olds are a particularly vulnerable group.

pages.title: 4.5.2-11 BCDBECE
pages.text: Older road users often have impaired vision and hearing and perceive and react slowly.

pages.title: 4.5.2-12 BCDBECE
pages.text: Many older road users have difficulty walking and fear falling, which makes them less attentive to traffic when stepping down from the curb or crossing the road at an intersection.

pages.title: 4.5.2-13 BCDBECE
pages.text: Many older people perceive crosswalks and traffic lights as particularly safe and cross the road without looking, relying entirely on the traffic lights.

pages.title: 4.5.2-14 BCDBECE
pages.text: Many older people fear traffic and are easily startled by cars that approach at speed, pass close by or brake suddenly, which can create dangerous panic situations.

pages.title: 4.6.1-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: The age of other road users can often be assessed based on their height, hair growth and colour, posture, gait and clothing. The use of walking sticks and similar aids may indicate reduced mobility.

pages.title: 4.6.1-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: The attention of other road users can be observed in the way they turn their heads or the direction of their gaze, and possibly by conspicuous objects or situations that clearly capture their interest.

pages.title: 4.6.1-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: The intentions of other road users can often be discerned through their actions, direction of movement and body language, combined with factors such as their age, level of attention and the general traffic situation.

pages.title: 4.6.1-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Road users with severe visual impairments can draw attention to this by using a white cane and/or the traffic badge for blind and partially sighted people. Since 1998, the ‘Man with the White Cane’ road safety badge has been the most widely used for blind and partially sighted people, but the old yellow badge with black dots is still used to some extent. The road safety badge is intended to ensure that visually impaired people are recognised in traffic, so that special consideration is shown towards them.

pages.title: 4.6.2-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: The completely unpredictable behaviour of small children requires that you always reduce your speed to a minimum and be ready to brake immediately.

pages.title: 4.6.2-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Many accidents involving older children occur when they cross the road after apparently having looked carefully. These accidents happen particularly on residential roads away from intersections, where children step out onto the road in front of or between parked cars.

pages.title: 4.6.2-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: Accidents often occur when older children cross the roadway at roads and intersections, both with and without traffic lights.

pages.title: 4.6.2-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Older children are particularly at risk when playing or walking in groups, as in these situations they often react impulsively and without paying attention to traffic.

pages.title: 4.6.2-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: Children on bicycles often fail to look around and give way to others.

pages.title: 4.6.2-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: Older people are particularly at risk when crossing the roadway, both at intersections and on stretches of road between intersections.

pages.title: 4.7.1-1 BCDCE
pages.text: Always be proactive and risk-aware. In unpredictable situations, you should be prepared, for example by moving your foot to the brake.

pages.title: 4.7.1-2 BCDCE
pages.text: You should be positive and helpful, for example by being considerate and helping other road users, even if they have made a mistake in traffic.

pages.title: 4.7.1-3 BCDCE
pages.text: It is important to be understanding of other road users’ challenges in traffic, such as a lack of local knowledge, and to ensure you keep a good distance from those who appear uncertain or inexperienced.

pages.title: 4.7.1-4 BCDCE
pages.text: It is important to be understanding of other road users’ lack of experience and to take into account that some, particularly older people, may be more cautious on the road.

pages.title: 4.7.1-5 BCDCE
pages.text: You should take extra care when passing Road Construction. It is important to reduce your speed significantly, especially when roadworkers are on or near the carriageway, and you must ensure you keep a safe distance from them whilst passing.

pages.title: 4.7.1-6 BCDCE
pages.text: You should be understanding of other road users’ desire to get ahead of you in traffic and refrain from using lights or the horn as a signal, even when a road user pulls in close in front of you and reduces the safety distance.

pages.title: 4.7.1-7 BCDCE
pages.text: You should never allow yourself to be influenced or become agitated by others’ mistakes or thoughtlessness, and you must avoid using abusive language, gesturing or making inappropriate expressions towards other Road users.

pages.title: 4.7.1-8 BCDCE
pages.text: You must never feel tempted, or allow yourself to be provoked, into committing reckless acts.

pages.title: 4.7.1-9 BCDCE
pages.text: One must be particularly helpful and considerate towards emergency vehicles.

pages.title: 4.7.2-1 BCDCE
pages.text: You must give ample space to large vehicles when they are performing specific manoeuvres such as turning, reversing and the like, even though they are the ones responsible.

pages.title: 4.7.2-2 BCDCE
pages.text: You should maintain a sufficient distance from other vehicles to avoid unnecessary acceleration and braking, which helps to reduce fuel consumption.

pages.title: 4.7.2-3 BCDCE
pages.text: It is important to assist other road users who appear to be having difficulty finding their way or have positioned themselves incorrectly, for example by allowing them to change lanes or adjust their position at an Intersection.

pages.title: 4.7.2-4 BCDCE
pages.text: You should avoid flashing your lights or using your horn, even if the car in front is slow to move off when the lights turn green.

pages.title: 4.7.3-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: There are many factors that influence how you behave in traffic and how safe a road user you are.

pages.title: 4.7.3-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Personal factors are of great significance, particularly self-control, but lifestyle, attitudes, gender, age, self-perception, sense of belonging and the car as an extension of the driver’s identity also influence the driver’s choices and behaviour on the road.

pages.title: 4.7.3-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: An unbalanced state of mind also plays a significant role. If you are in an unbalanced state due to strong emotions such as agitation, grief, worry or similar, the risk of accidents increases significantly.

pages.title: 4.7.3-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: The driver’s ability to anticipate and analyse risks, as well as the possible consequences, is crucial. This can reduce the risk of accidents and improve road safety. For example, failing to maintain a sufficient safety distance from the vehicle in front can have serious consequences.

pages.title: 4.7.3-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: A lack of experience or a tendency towards night blindness and similar conditions are examples of situations that require special precautions.

pages.title: 4.7.3-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: The driver’s knowledge of their own vehicle, or particularly a borrowed vehicle, is crucial for road safety. This includes an understanding of the vehicle’s design, equipment, load and state of maintenance. For example, knowledge of how the load affects the car’s handling, or how the ventilation system is used correctly, plays an important role in the driver’s visibility.

pages.title: 4.7.4-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Once you have gained some experience behind the wheel, it is easy to underestimate the risk in certain situations because things often go well. You simply become blind to the dangers.

pages.title: 4.7.4-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Risk blindness occurs when you choose a speed in bad weather or on slippery roads that is too fast to be able to stop safely before an obstacle. Therefore, it can be risky simply to follow the speed of other road users in such conditions.

pages.title: 4.7.4-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: Risk blindness is also evident when you drive too close to the Vehicle in front, making it impossible to avoid a collision if the Vehicle in front brakes suddenly.

pages.title: 4.7.4-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Risk blindness also manifests itself when the driver engages in activities in the car that have nothing to do with driving, meaning that for too long they do not pay the necessary attention to the road.

pages.title: 4.7.4-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: Risk blindness can also occur if, for example, you are too tired to drive safely and therefore overlook other dangers in traffic.

pages.title: 5.1.1-1 BCDCE
pages.text: The requirement for accessibility and safety on roads and streets cannot always be met, as traffic often develops faster than roads can be widened or altered. At the same time, society has limited funds available for both road construction and maintenance.

pages.title: 5.1.1-2 BCDCE
pages.text: Even if a road has all the facilities that should make it safe, the increased safety can often lead to heavier traffic and higher speeds. This, combined with the behaviour of other road users, can still create significant risks on that stretch of road.

pages.title: 5.1.2-1 BCDCE
pages.text: A driver will often be tempted to drive at the maximum permitted speed on a stretch of road. However, it is important always to consider whether the permitted speed is also safe, as road conditions may present risks that make it dangerous to drive indiscriminately at the highest permitted speed.

pages.title: 6.1.1-1 BBE
pages.text: The Road Traffic Act and the rules governing cars, drivers and driving apply on all streets, roads, Bicycle lanes, sidewalks, squares, bridges, tunnels, passages and paths or similar places where there is general traffic, regardless of whether these places are public or private.

pages.title: 6.1.2-1 BBE
pages.text: You must follow the driving instructions indicated by traffic signs, road markings, etc., as well as traffic signals.

pages.title: 6.1.2-2 BBE
pages.text: In certain situations, there may be a conflict between what the Road Traffic Act stipulates, what road markings and Traffic signs indicate, and the instructions given by the police. For example, the Road Traffic Act may require you to drive on the right-hand side of a pedestrian crossing, whilst a Traffic sign may indicate that you should drive on the left, or the police may prohibit passage altogether. Therefore, there is a hierarchy of priority: first, you must follow the police’s instructions, then Traffic signs and road markings, and finally the wording of the Road Traffic Act.

pages.title: 6.1.2-3 BBE
pages.text: Yellow road markings and traffic signs are used for temporary regulation, for example during Road Construction, and must be followed instead of the normal white lines and standard traffic signs.

pages.title: 6.1.2-4 BBE
pages.text: This prohibition sign means that driving is prohibited in both directions. If you continue to the other end of the road or street, you will encounter exactly the same prohibition sign.

pages.title: 6.1.2-5 B
pages.text: The ‘no entry in either direction’ sign may have a supplementary traffic sign allowing, for example, buses or taxis to proceed.

pages.title: 6.1.2-6 B
pages.text: In Denmark, there are environmental zones in many large cities where diesel-powered buses, trucks, vans and passenger cars must meet specific requirements regarding engine emissions of harmful substances or be fitted with a particulate filter in order to gain access.

pages.title: 6.1.2-7 B
pages.text: Passenger cars with diesel engines must have at least a Euro 5 engine or be fitted with a particulate filter

pages.title: 6.1.2-8 BBE
pages.text: The prohibition sign means ‘No entry’ for all vehicles. It is used where traffic from the opposite direction is permitted.

pages.title: 6.1.2-9 BBE
pages.text: At the opposite end of a street or road with No entry, there will be an information sign indicating that traffic is one-way on that stretch of road.

pages.title: 6.1.2-10 BBE
pages.text: The traffic sign indicates that it is a dead-end road.

pages.title: 6.1.2-11 BBE
pages.text: The prohibition sign prohibits the use of motor vehicles, such as cars and motorcycles, as well as tractors, motorised equipment and large mopeds.

pages.title: 6.1.2-12 BBE
pages.text: At the other end of a street or road where No entry is allowed for motor vehicles, tractors, motorised equipment and large mopeds, there will be an information sign indicating that traffic on that stretch is one-way, except for bicycles and small mopeds.

pages.title: 6.1.2-13 B
pages.text: The prohibition sign prohibits the passage of all vehicles and vehicle combinations exceeding the length specified on the sign. This means that the sign also applies to passenger cars and passenger cars with trailers if the vehicle or vehicle combination exceeds the specified length.

pages.title: 6.1.2-14 BBE
pages.text: The supplementary traffic sign indicates that the main sign applies only to certain road users – in this case, trucks.

pages.title: 6.1.2-15 BBE
pages.text: The supplementary traffic sign indicates that the main sign does not apply to that specific type of traffic.

pages.title: 6.1.2-16 BBE
pages.text: The supplementary traffic sign indicates that the information on the main sign applies to a nearby road.

pages.title: 6.1.2-17 BBE
pages.text: All types of prohibition, mandatory and warning signs may be displayed on square information signs.

pages.title: 6.1.2-18 BBE
pages.text: The sign "No transport of dangerous goods" means that vehicles carrying dangerous goods are not permitted to drive here. This includes products that may pose a risk during transport, such as fireworks, ammunition, gas cylinders, oxygen cylinders, petrol, diesel, fire-extinguishing fluid, non-water-based paint, turpentine, hydrochloric acid and lithium batteries.

pages.title: 6.1.2-19 BBE
pages.text: The sign shows a suggested route for vehicles carrying dangerous cargo.

pages.title: 1.2.10-1 B, 6.1.3-1 B
pages.text: A Category B driver's license allows you to drive a passenger car with up to 8 seats in addition to the driver’s seat.

pages.title: 1.2.10-2 B, 6.1.3-2 B
pages.text: A Category B driver's license also entitles you to drive a van with a maximum Permitted gross vehicle weight (GVW) of up to 3,500 kg.

pages.title: 1.2.10-3 B, 6.1.3-3 B
pages.text: The driver's license also entitles you to drive a car with a Trailer, provided the permitted gross vehicle weight (GVW) does not exceed 750 kg.

pages.title: 1.2.10-4 B, 6.1.3-4 B
pages.text: The driver's license also allows you to drive a car with a trailer that has a maximum permitted gross vehicle weight exceeding 750 kg, provided that the combined permitted gross vehicle weight of the car and trailer does not exceed 3500 kg.

pages.title: 1.2.10-5 B, 6.1.3-5 B
pages.text: The driver's license also authorises you to drive a 3-wheeled motorcycle of this type.

pages.title: 1.2.10-6 B, 6.1.3-6 B
pages.text: The driver's license also authorises the holder to drive a four-wheeled motorcycle, also known as a quadricycle, as well as an ATV (All-terrain vehicle).

pages.title: 1.2.10-7 B, 6.1.3-7 B
pages.text: A Category B driver's license allows you to drive a tractor with up to two trailers attached.

pages.title: 1.2.10-8 B, 6.1.3-8 B
pages.text: The driver's license also entitles you to drive motorised equipment ...

pages.title: 1.2.10-9 B, 6.1.3-9 B
pages.text: ... as well as large and small mopeds.

pages.title: 1.2.10-10 B, 6.1.3-10 B
pages.text: For some of these vehicles, special rules apply regarding the vehicle’s layout and equipment. These rules relate in particular to the vehicles’ length and width, brakes, lights, tyres, mirrors and any coupling to a Trailer.

children.title: 6.2 Safe and unimpeded flow of traffic

pages.title: 6.2.1-1 B
pages.text: You must always be considerate and vigilant in traffic so as not to cause danger, injury or inconvenience to others. This means that you have no rights in traffic; you have only obligations. You must therefore assist other road users so that traffic can flow as smoothly as possible.

pages.title: 6.2.1-2 B
pages.text: You must show particular consideration for those who find it difficult to cope in traffic, i.e. children, school crossing patrols, elderly people and disabled people.

pages.title: 6.2.2-1 B
pages.text: You are causing danger for… if your manner of driving creates a real risk of a collision or accident.

pages.title: 6.2.2-2 B
pages.text: You are causing an inconvenience by your manner of driving if you do not cause danger for… but whilst driving you get in the way of other road users and thereby force them to make way, move aside or hold back.

pages.title: 6.2.2-3 B
pages.text: There are certain manoeuvres where it can be difficult to completely avoid getting slightly in the way of others. This applies when pulling out from the kerb, changing lanes, stopping or slowing down rapidly. When performing these manoeuvres, you must ensure that you do not cause unnecessary inconvenience, as it is also known. The inconvenience you impose on others must therefore be necessary.

pages.title: 6.2.2-4 B
pages.text: Before reversing, you must ensure that the manoeuvre can be carried out without danger or inconvenience to others.

pages.title: 6.2.9-1 B, 6.2.8-1 CBE
pages.text: If you accidentally or through your own fault damage a traffic sign or similar signage, you should immediately arrange for it to be repaired. If this is not possible, you must contact the police as soon as possible and do everything you can to warn other road users.

pages.title: 6.2.9-2 B, 6.2.8-2 CBE
pages.text: If you damage someone else’s property or belongings, the person responsible must inform the owner or contact the police.

pages.title: 6.2.9-3 B, 6.2.8-3 CBE
pages.text: If you are involved in a road traffic accident, regardless of whether you are at fault or not, you must stop immediately and provide your name and address to the other parties involved if they ask for it.

pages.title: 6.2.9-4 B, 6.2.8-4 CBE
pages.text: Mark the scene of the accident so that others do not hit the people involved. Switch off the engine and avoid open flames or smoking due to the risk of fire from spilled fuel.

pages.title: 6.2.9-5 B, 6.2.8-5 CBE
pages.text: You should keep away from vehicles that may pose a risk of leaking dangerous cargo. These vehicles are marked with orange signs at both the front and rear.

pages.title: 6.2.9-6 B
pages.text: If you are involved in a road traffic accident, regardless of fault, you must stop immediately, assist any injured persons and – if the injuries are serious – report the accident to the police.

pages.title: 6.2.9-7 B
pages.text: If there are seriously injured or fatally injured persons, you must not alter the conditions or remove evidence at the accident site. However, it is permitted to move vehicles out of the way if they cause danger for traffic.

pages.title: 6.2.9-8 B
pages.text: If there are injured persons, assess their injuries and condition, and provide whatever assistance you are able to.

pages.title: 6.2.9-9 B
pages.text: If you cannot bear the sight of blood or injured people, you should ask other Road users for help with first aid and raising the alarm

pages.title: 6.2.9-10 B
pages.text: When you call the Emergency services on 1-1-2, you must state where the accident has occurred, what has happened, how many people have been injured, and where you are calling from.

pages.title: 6.2.10-1 B, 6.2.9-1 CBE
pages.text: The owner or registered user of a motor vehicle must have statutory third-party liability insurance covering any claims for compensation arising from accidents for which the driver is liable.

pages.title: 6.2.11-1 B, 6.2.10-1 CBE
pages.text: It is prohibited to allow persons who do not hold a valid Driver's license for the vehicle to drive it.

education.title: Module 2: Introductory theory and practical driving

pages.title: Introduction
pages.text:
Module 2: Introductory theory and practical driving

The instruction in Module 2 is designed to prepare you for the practical driving lessons.

You must be familiar with the car’s controls and be able to identify faults in the car that affect road safety and the vehicle’s handling, and you must be aware of the risks associated with the roads.

You must complete training on a closed practice area and become proficient in controlling the car at low speeds whilst performing manoeuvres that occur in normal traffic.

pages.title: 1.1.3-1 B
pages.text: In principle, the engine works by setting a number of pistons in motion when a mixture of air and fuel is ignited.

pages.title: 1.1.3-2 B
pages.text: The up-and-down movements of the pistons are converted into the rotary motion of a crankshaft.

pages.title: 1.1.3-3 B
pages.text: In a petrol engine, fuel mixed with air is drawn in through the carburettor or injected into the engine. The amount is regulated when the accelerator is pressed. Ignition occurs via a spark from the spark plug, which receives power from the battery when the ignition key is turned.

pages.title: 1.1.3-4 B
pages.text: In a diesel engine, clean air is drawn into the cylinder, and diesel is injected under high pressure by a pump. The fuel quantity is regulated via the accelerator. Ignition occurs by self-ignition due to the high pressure and temperature in the cylinder. When the engine is cold, diesel engines often require preheating in order to start.

pages.title: 1.1.3-5 B
pages.text: Electric cars have an electric motor powered by batteries; an electric motor can be combined with an internal combustion engine; such a combination of electric motor and internal combustion engine is called a hybrid car.

pages.title: 1.1.4-1 B
pages.text: The engine’s rotational movement is transmitted through the clutch and gearbox to the car’s drive wheels.

pages.title: 1.1.4-2 B
pages.text: The clutch works by pressing a clutch plate against the flywheel on the crankshaft, so that the engine’s rotation is transferred to the gearbox and the drive wheels. When the clutch pedal is pressed down, the connection is broken. When engaging, the pedal is lifted slowly so that the movement is transferred smoothly to the wheels.

pages.title: 1.1.4-3 B
pages.text: If the car has a hydraulic clutch, the fluid level in the clutch fluid reservoir must be sufficient.

pages.title: 1.1.4-4 B
pages.text: To protect the starter motor, the clutch pedal may be depressed fully when starting the engine. The clutch pedal must be depressed fully when changing gears to avoid damaging the gearbox. When the clutch is not in use, the pedal must not be used as a footrest, as this will quickly damage the clutch.

pages.title: 1.1.4-5 B
pages.text: Difficult gear changes accompanied by loud noises may indicate a fault with the clutch. Accelerating without the speed increasing suggests a fault in the clutch. Slow movement of the car in 1st gear, even though the clutch is fully depressed, also suggests a fault with the clutch.

pages.title: 1.1.4-6 B
pages.text: Cars with automatic transmission do not have a clutch pedal, only an accelerator and Brake pedal.

pages.title: 1.1.5-1 B
pages.text: The gearbox efficiently transfers the engine’s power to the wheels. At low speeds, lower gears are used, which provide more traction – just like the lower gears on a bicycle. At higher speeds, higher gears are used, which save fuel. Gears of different sizes enable gear changes. Reverse gear makes it possible to drive backwards.

pages.title: 1.1.5-2 B
pages.text: In cars with manual transmission, gears are changed using the gear lever, whilst gear changes occur automatically in cars with automatic transmission.

pages.title: 1.2.1-1 B
pages.text: Every car has a vehicle registration certificate, which acts as the car’s ‘identity’. · Older cars have a green certificate with all the information on the front. · Newer cars have a white A4 certificate with information on both the front and back.

pages.title: 1.2.1-2 B
pages.text: The vehicle registration certificate contains, among other things, information about the vehicle’s type, model, chassis number, registration number, etc.

pages.title: 1.2.1-3 B
pages.text: The owner of a car is the person named on the Vehicle registration certificate.

pages.title: 1.2.1-4 B
pages.text: A person may be listed as the user on the Vehicle registration certificate. If both a user and an owner are registered, the registered user bears legal responsibility for ensuring that the vehicle is in a roadworthy condition.

pages.title: 1.2.1-5 B
pages.text: The driver of a vehicle is the person driving the car; this may be the owner, the user or a completely different person.

pages.title: 1.2.1-6 B
pages.text: It is the owner or user of the vehicle listed on the vehicle registration certificate who is responsible for ensuring that the car is in a roadworthy condition, i.e. that the car meets the authorities’ requirements regarding its technical condition. The owner or registered user is also responsible for ensuring that statutory third-party liability insurance has been taken out and that any outstanding insurance premiums and road tax have been paid.

pages.title: 1.2.1-7 B
pages.text: It is the driver’s responsibility to ensure that the vehicle is in a safe condition, in particular that the steering, brakes, lights and horn, as well as any Coupling device, function safely and meet the legal requirements. This means that the driver is responsible for the technical aspects of the vehicle that can be checked. It is therefore necessary to be aware of the authorities’ requirements regarding the steering system, brakes, lights, etc. It is also important to recognise the signs of faults that may arise.

pages.title: 1.2.2-1 B
pages.text: The steering system must be easy, safe and quick to use. There must be no loose or worn parts that could make the steering imprecise.

pages.title: 1.2.2-2 B
pages.text: Play in the steering wheel means that you can turn the steering wheel a short distance without the wheels following. This may be a sign of wear in the Steering Unit. Manufacturers specify in the car’s manual how much play in the steering wheel is permitted.

pages.title: 1.2.2-3 B
pages.text: In the owner’s manuals for many passenger cars, the manufacturer has specified the maximum permitted play in the steering wheel for that particular model.

pages.title: 1.2.2-4 B
pages.text: If the play in the steering wheel is greater than that specified in the owner’s manual, it constitutes significant play in the steering wheel, which is therefore illegal.

pages.title: 1.2.2-5 B
pages.text: Older cars and trucks use the classic steering system with many mechanical links between the steering wheel and the wheels.

pages.title: 1.2.2-6 B
pages.text: Modern cars: Have Sterring Racks, which are more direct and precise. The Sterring Rack moves sideways when you turn the steering wheel.

pages.title: 1.2.2-7 B
pages.text: Most cars have Power steering, which makes it easier to turn the steering wheel – either hydraulic (fluid-powered) or electric. If the Power steering fails, the car should still be steerable, but continuing to drive may be irresponsible and therefore illegal.

pages.title: 1.2.2-8 B
pages.text: If the car is fitted with hydraulic Power steering, the fluid level in the reservoir must comply with the car manufacturer’s specifications. This is checked either by ensuring the fluid level is between the minimum and maximum marks, or by checking that the warning light for this is not illuminated. If there is too little power steering fluid in the system, the steering mechanism must be inspected.

pages.title: 1.2.2-9 B
pages.text: In newer cars, there should normally be no Play in the steering wheel; in cars with Power steering, check for Play in the steering mechanism with the engine running.

pages.title: 1.2.2-10 B
pages.text: Heavy or difficult steering is a sign of a fault in the steering system. Heavy or difficult steering may be caused by: – Insufficient power steering fluid – A broken or worn V-belt – A fault in the electrical system

pages.title: 1.2.2-11 B
pages.text: Cars are often fitted with Electronic Stability Control (ESC). ESC helps to prevent skidding. The system uses sensors to detect how the car is moving and corrects the vehicle using the brakes and engine if it is about to lose grip.

pages.title: 1.2.2-12 B
pages.text: The ESC system is fitted with a warning light. If this light is on continuously, there may be a fault in the ESC system, and the car manufacturer’s instructions must be followed.

pages.title: 1.2.2-13 B
pages.text: Incorrect tyre pressure or incorrect placement of heavy cargo can alter the car’s steering characteristics. If the tyre pressure is incorrect or the car is unevenly loaded, it may become: – Oversteering (turns too much) – Understeering (turns too little)

pages.title: 1.2.2-14 B
pages.text: If there is abnormal wear on one side of the front tyres, this may be a sign of incorrect alignment of the Steering Unit.

pages.title: 1.2.2-15 B
pages.text: When driving at low speed, the steering wheel should turn easily from side to side without meeting uneven resistance or making unusual noises.

pages.title: 1.2.2-16 B
pages.text: The steering system is checked by observing whether the wheels immediately follow the movements of the steering wheel. If the wheels do not immediately follow the movements of the steering wheel, this may be a sign of play in the steering connections.

pages.title: 1.2.3-1 B
pages.text: The car must be fitted with a Service brake, an Emergency brake and a Parking brake. The three types of brakes: •Service brake: Used during normal driving and must act on all wheels. •Emergency brake: Takes over if the Service brake fails. •Parking brake: Keeps the car stationary when parked.

pages.title: 1.2.3-2 B
pages.text: The Service brake must act on all wheels and be capable of braking the car safely, quickly and effectively at all speeds and under all loads.

pages.title: 1.2.3-3 B
pages.text: The service brake is typically a hydraulic brake with two separate circuits. When you press the Brake pedal, pressure is transmitted via brake fluid to the wheels, causing them to brake. If one circuit fails (e.g. due to a leak), the other can still brake the car – but with reduced effectiveness.

pages.title: 1.2.3-4 B
pages.text: The disc brake is a relatively simple design in which the brake fluid presses the brake lining against the rotating brake disc behind the wheels.

pages.title: 1.2.3-5 B
pages.text: Drum brake: A drum that rotates with the wheel, with Brake shoes pressing from the inside out.

pages.title: 1.2.3-6 B
pages.text: When the driver presses the Brake pedal, a piston in the master cylinder is actuated. The piston creates pressure in the Brake fluid through the master cylinder’s pipes and hoses, and at the wheel brake, the wheel cylinder pistons either push the brake shoes outwards against the brake drums on the drum brake or the brake pads inwards against the brake discs on the disc brake.

pages.title: 1.2.3-7 B
pages.text: A hydraulic service brake may be vacuum- or electrically-assisted. The vacuum booster is located between the Brake pedal and the master cylinder and is connected to the engine’s intake. Two chambers separated by a diaphragm control the vacuum: When braking, atmospheric pressure is applied behind the diaphragm, increasing the pressure on the master cylinder. When the pedal is released, the vacuum is restored on both sides.

pages.title: 1.2.3-8 B
pages.text: The fluid level in the brake fluid reservoir must be between the minimum and maximum marks. When the brake pedal is pressed hard, it must not be possible to press it all the way to the floor. The pedal must feel firm and hard to press and must not slowly sink towards the floor when pressed for a prolonged period.

pages.title: 1.2.3-9 B
pages.text: If the car is fitted with a vacuum booster, check this with the engine switched off. With the engine switched off, press the Brake pedal several times; it should become harder to press as the Vacuum brake booster equalises the pressure. Start the engine whilst pressing the Brake pedal. Once the engine has started, the Brake pedal should become softer to press and the pedal should sink slightly towards the floor.

pages.title: 1.2.3-10 B
pages.text: During light braking on a dry, level road, the car must not pull to one side. Pulling to one side in such a situation may indicate moisture or dirt on the brake lining. Uneven braking or sudden jerking from one or more wheels may be caused by faults in the Brake drums, brake discs or brake linings.

pages.title: 1.2.3-11 B
pages.text: If the brake pedal can suddenly be pressed further down than usual, this is a sign that one of the brake circuits is faulty.

pages.title: 1.2.3-12 B
pages.text: The parking brake is mechanical and, by means of rods or cables, activates the brakes on the wheels of an axle.

pages.title: 1.2.3-13 B
pages.text: The parking brake may be electrically operated via a switch and is released either by the switch or by engaging a gear and pressing the accelerator.

pages.title: 1.2.3-14 B
pages.text: The parking brake must be capable of holding the car stationary on a sloping road.

pages.title: 1.2.3-15 B
pages.text: When the handbrake is applied, force is transmitted via a cable to a lever arm in the Brake drum. In drum brakes, the arm pushes the brake shoes out against the drum; in disc brakes, the pads are pressed against the disc.

pages.title: 1.2.3-16 B
pages.text: The handbrake lever must not be able to be pulled all the way up, and it must be possible to keep it engaged.

pages.title: 1.2.3-17 B
pages.text: The emergency brake may be integrated into the Service brake, or may be integrated into the Parking brake, or be a separate braking system. The emergency brake must be capable of stopping the vehicle safely if the Service brake fails.

pages.title: 1.2.3-18 B
pages.text: All brakes may be designed as ABS brakes, which prevent the wheels from locking during braking. The system uses sensors at the wheels and an electronic control unit that automatically adjusts the braking pressure if a wheel is about to lock.

pages.title: 1.2.3-19 B
pages.text: If the ABS warning light comes on suddenly, or if it does not go out shortly after starting, this indicates a fault in the ABS system, and driving to the nearest Repair shop is permitted.

pages.title: 1.2.3-20 B
pages.text: Brake Assist, also known as BAS, is an electronic system that measures the vehicle’s speed and the driver’s pressure on the Brake pedal. In the event of sudden braking, the system increases the brake pressure to the maximum by fully activating the brakes, ensuring the fastest possible deceleration.

pages.title: 1.2.4-1 B
pages.text: The car must only be fitted with Mandatory or Permitted lights.

pages.title: 1.2.4-2 B
pages.text: Lights in a pair must be of the same colour and intensity, and all the vehicle’s lights must be capable of functioning.

pages.title: 1.2.4-3 B
pages.text: The vehicle must have two main-beam headlamps.

pages.title: 1.2.4-4 B
pages.text: The high beam must emit a white or yellowish light and must clearly illuminate the road at least 100 m in front of the vehicle.

pages.title: 1.2.4-5 B
pages.text: The high beam must be fitted with an indicator light that illuminates when the high beam is switched on. As a rule, the light in the indicator is blue.

pages.title: 1.2.4-6 B
pages.text: The car must have two dipped-beam headlamps.

pages.title: 1.2.4-7 B
pages.text: The low-beam headlights must be white or yellowish and must clearly illuminate the road at least 30 metres in front of the car without causing glare.

pages.title: 1.2.4-8 B
pages.text: The low-beam headlights must be asymmetrical. This means that the light must shine further ahead on the right-hand side of the road.

pages.title: 1.2.4-9 B
pages.text: The low-beam headlights must have a 1% gradient. This is checked by standing close to the headlamp and placing a finger on the sharp transition between light and dark on the leg. Then step a few metres away from the headlamp, where the sharp transition between light and dark must now have dropped by the same number of centimetres.

pages.title: 1.2.4-10 B
pages.text: The car must be fitted with 2 Position lights.

pages.title: 1.2.4-11 B
pages.text: The position lights must be white, visible from at least 300 metres and must not dazzle. If they are integrated into a yellowish dipped or high beam headlamp, they must also be yellowish.

pages.title: 1.2.4-12 B
pages.text: The vehicle must have two rear lights.

pages.title: 1.2.4-13 B
pages.text: The rear lights must emit a red light and be clearly visible from a distance of at least 300 metres without being dazzling.

pages.title: 1.2.4-14 B
pages.text: At the rear, the car must have at least one number plate lamp with a white light, which must illuminate the number plate so that it can be clearly read.

pages.title: 1.2.4-15 B
pages.text: The number plate light must be powerful enough to ensure that the number plate can be read from a distance of at least 20 metres.

pages.title: 1.2.4-16 B
pages.text: If the vehicle is more than 2.10 m wide, it must be fitted with 2 white front-facing and 2 red Rear-facing marker lights, which must be clearly visible from a distance of at least 300 m without causing glare.

pages.title: 1.2.4-17 B
pages.text: The vehicle may only be fitted with mandatory or permitted reflectors. At the rear, the vehicle must have two red reflectors.

pages.title: 1.2.4-18 B
pages.text: The mandatory reflectors must be approved and must not be triangular.

pages.title: 1.2.4-19 B
pages.text: Any yellow side reflectors must be approved and correctly positioned on the sides of the vehicle. Side reflectors may be replaced by yellow Side marker lights that are clearly visible from a distance of at least 300 m without causing glare.

pages.title: 1.2.4-20 B
pages.text: Vehicles over 6 metres in length must be fitted with both side reflectors and Side marker lights.

pages.title: 1.2.4-21 B
pages.text: The vehicle must be fitted with 3 red stop lights at the rear; however, older vehicles may have just 2 stop lights.

pages.title: 1.2.4-22 B
pages.text: The brake lights must shine significantly brighter than the rear lights when the Brake pedal is pressed. The rear lights and brake lights may be incorporated into the same pair of lights.

pages.title: 1.2.4-23 B
pages.text: The car must have 2 Blinkers at the front, 2 Blinkers at the rear and 1 Blinker on each side

pages.title: 1.2.4-24 B
pages.text: If the indicators are flashing significantly faster than usual, this is usually a sign that one or more indicators are not working.

pages.title: 1.2.4-25 B
pages.text: The indicator must be fitted with a warning light or audible warning.

pages.title: 1.2.4-26 B
pages.text: The indicator light or audible warning must change frequency or remain lit continuously if there is a fault with the Blinkers.

pages.title: 1.2.4-27 B
pages.text: In addition to the mandatory high beam headlamps, low-beam headlights, position lights and any marker lamps, the vehicle up ahead may be fitted with additional high beam headlamps, daytime running lamps, overtaking indicators, fog lamps, parking lamps, and search and work lamps.

pages.title: 1.2.4-28 B
