pages.text: In addition to the mandatory rear lights, brake lights and any Outline marker lights, the rear of the vehicle may be fitted with additional rear lights, rear fog lights, reversing lights and brake lights.

pages.title: 1.2.4-29 B
pages.text: The horn must produce a clear, continuous tone.

pages.title: 1.2.5-1 B
pages.text: The engine must not be soiled by leaking oil, as this creates a risk of fire in the engine compartment.

pages.title: 1.2.5-2 B
pages.text: The engine’s lubricating oil must be checked at regular intervals. Too little lubricating oil can cause engine damage. The engine is usually fitted with a dipstick for checking the lubricating oil level.

pages.title: 1.2.5-3 B
pages.text: Sufficient engine oil must be added. This can be checked by the minimum and maximum marks on the dipstick, the car’s warning light, or by following the instructions in the owner’s manual.

pages.title: 1.2.5-4 B
pages.text: It is important to check the engine coolant at regular intervals, as too little coolant can cause engine damage. If the engine is hot, it is dangerous to open the radiator cap, as there is excess pressure in the cooling system, meaning the scalding hot coolant risks spraying out.

pages.title: 1.2.5-5 B
pages.text: Most cars have an expansion tank next to the radiator where you can check the coolant level. Coolant must be topped up in accordance with the instructions in the owner’s manual.

pages.title: 1.2.5-6 B
pages.text: The exhaust system has two functions: to reduce the noise from the engine’s exhaust and to carry away the harmful gases produced during combustion so that they do not pose a danger to the driver and passengers. It must be fitted with a silencer, and the exhaust must be leak-free and correctly secured in brackets and straps.

pages.title: 1.2.5-7 B
pages.text: The engine must not make unnecessary noise or emit smoke. White smoke is water vapour and disappears once the engine warms up. Blue smoke may indicate wear, whilst black smoke is caused by poor combustion – often due to engine faults, a clogged air filter for the compressor or an active choke.

pages.title: 1.2.5-8 B
pages.text: Leaks in the exhaust system can allow dangerous carbon monoxide to enter the car. Check for leaks by holding a cloth over the exhaust; hissing sounds or extra noise indicate faults in the system or the silencer.

pages.title: 1.2.5-9 B
pages.text: If you drive with the boot lid open, there is also a risk of carbon monoxide entering the car, leading to carbon monoxide poisoning.

pages.title: 1.2.5-10 B
pages.text: Since 1990, petrol-powered passenger cars have been required to have a catalytic converter to meet exhaust emission standards. The catalytic converter, which is fitted to the exhaust pipe, contains a ceramic body with precious metals. Here, 70–85% of hydrocarbons, nitrogen oxides and carbon monoxide are converted into water vapour through a chemical process, which is why it is called a three-way catalytic converter.

pages.title: 1.2.5-11 B
pages.text: If the car is fitted with a catalytic converter, only unleaded petrol must be used. If leaded petrol is used, the catalytic converter will be damaged.

pages.title: 1.2.5-12 B
pages.text: If the car is fitted with a catalytic converter, attempting to push or tow the car will result in the catalytic converter being destroyed, as there is a risk of ignition of petrol vapours inside the catalytic converter.

pages.title: 1.2.5-13 B
pages.text: As the catalytic converter becomes extremely hot – up to 800–900 degrees – you should not park the car over dry grass, withered leaves or similar, as there is a risk of fire.

pages.title: 1.2.5-14 B
pages.text: The driver of a motor vehicle must at all times ensure that the vehicle is in a roadworthy condition with regard to noise emissions, and with regard to the vehicle’s engine and emission control equipment, which affect the vehicle’s emissions of air pollutants

pages.title: 1.2.6-1 B, 1.5.1-1 BE
pages.text: As a driver, you must drive in such a way that you do not cause unnecessary noise or pollute with smoke and exhaust fumes. This is a matter of consideration for both the environment and other people.

pages.title: 1.2.6-2 B, 1.5.1-2 BE
pages.text: The Road Traffic Act prohibits unnecessary and disruptive driving in built-up areas. If driving is necessary, the driver must drive in such a way as to cause the least possible disturbance to others.

pages.title: 1.2.6-3 B, 1.5.1-3 BE
pages.text: Do not leave the engine idling for long periods; only start the car when you are ready to drive. In Copenhagen and Aarhus, for example, the engine may only be left idling for a maximum of one minute.

pages.title: 1.2.6-4 B, 1.5.1-4 BE
pages.text: Driving style has a significant impact on fuel consumption. High speeds and aggressive driving with heavy acceleration result in increased fuel consumption of 5–10%, and in some cases as much as 25%. When slowing down, fuel consumption can be reduced by releasing the accelerator completely without taking your foot off the clutch.

pages.title: 1.2.6-5 B, 1.5.1-5 BE
pages.text: Energy-efficient driving technique means generally avoiding unnecessary and repeated changes in speed

pages.title: 1.2.6-6 B, 1.5.1-6 BE
pages.text: High speeds and aggressive driving with heavy acceleration, e.g. when overtaking, lead to increased fuel consumption, whilst Energy-efficient driving techniques can generally result in fuel savings of 5–10% and, in many cases, up to 25%.

pages.title: 1.2.6-7 B, 1.5.1-7 BE
pages.text: When approaching traffic lights, consider whether it will be necessary to stop. Slow down well in advance rather than braking hard.

pages.title: 1.2.6-8 B, 1.5.1-8 BE
pages.text: The engine should be switched off if you are stationary for a long time – for example, at level crossings or red lights. Some cars do this automatically.

pages.title: 1.2.6-9 B, 1.5.1-9 BE
pages.text: Accelerate quickly with the accelerator pedal pressed about halfway down, and select a high gear as soon as possible – this saves fuel. The correct gear selection might be to change from, for example, 2nd to 4th or 3rd to 4th gear.

pages.title: 1.2.6-10 B, 1.5.1-11 BE
pages.text: Keep an eye on the car’s fuel consumption gauge – it can help you drive more economically.

pages.title: 1.2.6-11 B, 1.5.1-12 BE
pages.text: Heavy items in the car and extra equipment on the roof (such as a roof box) increase fuel consumption. Remove anything you don’t need.

pages.title: 1.2.6-12 B, 1.5.1-13 BE
pages.text: Tyres with too low a pressure use more fuel and affect the car’s handling. Check tyre pressure regularly.

pages.title: 1.2.6-13 B, 1.5.1-14 BE
pages.text: When driving with the air conditioning or climate control and other power-consuming equipment switched on, fuel consumption increases.

pages.title: 1.2.6-14 B
pages.text: Short journeys and unnecessary trips use extra fuel and cause unnecessary wear and tear on the car. Combine your errands.

pages.title: 1.2.6-15 B, 1.5.1-15 BE
pages.text: If you can, drive outside rush hour. It saves time, energy and is better for the environment.

pages.title: 1.2.6-16 B
pages.text: Carpooling to and from work means fewer cars on the roads, lower fuel consumption and less environmental impact.

pages.title: 1.2.6-17 B, 1.5.1-16 BE
pages.text: If possible, you should choose the most fuel-efficient and least polluting vehicle when buying a new car

pages.title: 1.2.7-1 B
pages.text: Tyres, wheel rims and wheel bearings must be intact and undamaged. This means that none of these parts must have visible damage such as cracks, dents or wear that could affect safety.

pages.title: 1.2.7-2 B
pages.text: Tyres are classified by type according to their construction and intended use. There are two basic types of tyre construction: radial tyres and Diagonal tires.

pages.title: 1.2.7-3 B
pages.text: Depending on their use, radial tires and diagonal tires may be constructed as • Standard tires without ‘M S’ marking • Off-road and winter tires with ‘M S’ marking • Tyres for temporary use, known as emergency spare wheels.

pages.title: 1.2.7-4 B
pages.text: From 1 July 2025, a new law came into force regarding winter tyres in Denmark. From now on, it is prohibited to drive on summer tyres when the roads are covered in snow, ice or slush. At the same time, M S-marked tyres without the snowflake symbol are no longer approved as suitable for winter use. The Danish Road Safety and Transport Agency therefore recommends: Change to winter tyres in good time if you cannot do without your car when there is a risk of snow, ice and slush. If you do not change to winter tyres, it is important that you do not drive on days when there is a risk of snow, ice and slush.

pages.title: 1.2.7-5 B
pages.text: There are certain requirements for tyres that must always be met, otherwise you risk a fine from the police. Here is an overview of these requirements: • Tyres must be suitable for the current road conditions, e.g. winter conditions. • Tyres, rims and wheel bearings must be intact and undamaged. • Tyres must match the rim in size and design. • Tyres must be clearly marked with the size specification and the name or logo of the manufacturer or retreading company. • The tread depth must be at least 1.6 mm. • Tyre pressure must comply with the vehicle manufacturer’s specifications. Tyre pressure is a crucial factor for the vehicle’s stability and braking performance.

pages.title: 1.2.7-6 B
pages.text: Winter tyres are marked either ‘M S’ (mud and snow) or ‘M S’ and 3 P M S F (Three-Peak Mountain Snowflake). The 3 P M S F snowflake symbol is easy to recognise: a snowflake surrounded by three mountain peaks. According to the legislation, this symbol is always accompanied by the M S marking. This means that the tyre is particularly suitable for harsh winter conditions, i.e. where there is snow and ice on the roads. Information regarding the “3 P M S F” marking will appear on the tyre label, which accompanies new tyres upon marketing and sale.

pages.title: 1.2.7-7 B
pages.text: You should switch to summer tyres once the risk of frost has passed, typically during the spring. If you keep winter tyres on your car, this can lead to poorer braking performance, higher fuel consumption and a greater impact on the environment and climate. Some tyres are marketed as all-season tyres, but as this is a marketing term, the labelling – and therefore the properties – vary between different brands. It is therefore important to check the tyre labelling, especially if they are to be used in winter conditions. When the police advise against all driving due to extreme winter weather, their instructions should be followed. If driving is absolutely necessary, it should only be done with tyres marked ‘3PMSF’ and with winter equipment, as driving otherwise may be illegal.

pages.title: 1.2.7-8 B
pages.text: Passenger cars with a maximum permitted gross vehicle weight of 3,500 kg and vans with a maximum permitted gross vehicle weight of 3,000 kg must be fitted with tyres of the same type on the same axle, with the exception of the spare wheel. Tyres on the same axle must match each other in terms of construction type – for example, radial tires and Diagonal tires must not be mixed.

pages.title: 1.2.7-9 B
pages.text: Studded tyres may only be used between 1 November and 15 April and, in such cases, must be fitted to all wheels, including any attached Trailer. This is to prevent damage to the roads and to ensure that Road grip is consistent across the entire Truck and trailer combination.

pages.title: 1.2.7-10 B
pages.text: Tyres must be inflated to the pressure specified by the vehicle manufacturer. Correct tyre pressure is important for safety, handling and fuel consumption.

pages.title: 1.2.7-11 B
pages.text: Tyres must have a minimum tread depth of 1.6 mm on all wheels, as indicated by the Treadwear indicators where applicable. Treadwear indicators on the tyre show when the minimum limit has been reached. Below this, the tyre is illegal and dangerous.

pages.title: 1.2.7-12 B
pages.text: Uneven or uneven wear on tyres indicates a fault. Uneven wear is almost always a sign of a fault elsewhere on the car.

pages.title: 1.2.7-13 B
pages.text: Neutral steering means that the car follows the direction intended by the steering wheel.

pages.title: 1.2.7-14 B
pages.text: If the car is oversteering, it means that it is overreacting, i.e. turning more sharply than the steering input intends. This may be due to low tyre pressure in the rear tyres or incorrect load, so that a significant proportion of the weight is on the rear tyres.

pages.title: 1.2.7-15 B
pages.text: Oversteering or understeering, as well as increased sensitivity to Crosswinds, can be caused by incorrect tyre pressure. If the car handles differently than usual or is greatly affected by Crosswinds, this may be due to tyre pressure that is too low or too high.

pages.title: 1.2.7-16 B
pages.text: The car must be fitted with Shock absorbers on all wheels. This applies to both passenger cars and vans – it is a legal requirement and important for stability and safety.

pages.title: 1.2.7-17 B
pages.text: Shock absorbers reduce the movement of the suspension and help maintain contact between the tyres and the road. A shock absorber consists of a piston with narrow valves that regulate the flow of hydraulic oil during compression and extension. This creates resistance, which limits the movement of the spring.

pages.title: 1.2.7-18 B
pages.text: The shock absorbers are checked by pressing the car down over each wheel. When released, the body should settle immediately

pages.title: 1.2.7-19 B
pages.text: Squeaking noises whilst driving are a sign of faults in the springs or Shock absorbers. This could be worn parts, rust or breakage, which requires inspection and possibly replacement.

pages.title: 1.2.7-20 B
pages.text: If the shock absorbers are faulty, this may be indicated not only by squeaking noises whilst driving, but also by abnormal patchy wear on the tyre. When the tyre loses contact with the road, it strikes the ground at different points, causing uneven wear on the tyre.

pages.title: 1.2.8-1 B
pages.text: The bodywork comprises the roof, sides with fenders, bonnet, boot lid, doors and underbody.

pages.title: 1.2.8-2 B
pages.text: Doors, bonnet and boot lid must be fitted with locks so that they can be kept closed whilst the vehicle is in motion.

pages.title: 1.2.8-3 B
pages.text: The bodywork must not be damaged to such an extent that it causes danger for road safety.

pages.title: 1.2.8-4 B
pages.text: The bodywork must not be corroded to such an extent that it causes danger for road safety.

pages.title: 1.2.9-1 B
pages.text: As a general rule, the windscreen must be intact and free from damage. A damaged windscreen can distort the view and increase the risk of accidents, particularly in sunlight or when driving into the light. The aim is to ensure unobstructed and clear visibility.

pages.title: 1.2.9-2 B
pages.text: The windscreen must be kept clean using windscreen washer and wipers. Dirt, rain and snow must be able to be removed quickly whilst driving. Without functioning windscreen washer and wipers, visibility can quickly become poor.

pages.title: 1.2.9-3 B
pages.text: There must be a sufficient supply of washer fluid. Without fluid, the wipers cannot clean the windscreen effectively. This is particularly critical when there is dirt, salt or insects on the windscreen.

pages.title: 1.2.9-4 B
pages.text: If the windscreen cannot be kept clean, this is a sign of a fault in the windscreen washer and wipers. Problems with the equipment must be detected and resolved quickly to avoid reduced visibility. It is a matter of safety awareness and maintenance.

pages.title: 1.2.9-5 B
pages.text: Passenger cars must be fitted with an exterior mirror on the left-hand side. The left-hand side mirror is essential for checking what is behind you and when overtaking. Without it, you are blind in a critical area.

pages.title: 1.2.9-6 B
pages.text: There must also be a rear view mirror. The rear view mirror provides a view to the rear and is important when, for example, changing lanes or parking. Together with the side mirrors, it ensures a full field of vision.

pages.title: 1.2.9-7 B
pages.text: The mirrors must be clean, undamaged and correctly adjusted. A mirror without a clear view is useless. Clean and undamaged mirrors ensure that you can react correctly to traffic approaching from behind.

pages.title: 1.2.9-8 B
pages.text: The car must normally be fitted with approved seat belts in all seating positions. Seat belts save lives. They prevent passengers from being thrown about or out of the car in the event of a collision.

pages.title: 1.2.9-9 B
pages.text: Seat belts must be free from damage. A damaged seat belt may fail in an accident. It must be able to withstand strong jolts without breaking.

pages.title: 1.2.9-10 B
pages.text: The car must be fitted with seat belts on all forward-facing seats. Cars first registered on or after 1 October 1999 must also have seat belts on rear-facing seats.

pages.title: 1.2.9-11 B
pages.text: The car must be fitted with headrests on the front seats; the mandatory headrests must not be removed if the seat is in use. Headrests prevent whiplash in the event of a rear-end collision.

pages.title: 1.2.9-12 B
pages.text: When driving, you should carry an approved Warning triangle so that you have it to hand in situations where you are required to set it up. In the event of a breakdown or accident, you must warn other road users. The Warning triangle increases visibility and safety, especially in the dark and in bad weather.

pages.title: 1.2.10-1 B, 6.1.3-1 B
pages.text: A Category B driver's license allows you to drive a passenger car with up to 8 seats in addition to the driver’s seat.

pages.title: 1.2.10-2 B, 6.1.3-2 B
pages.text: A Category B driver's license also entitles you to drive a van with a maximum Permitted gross vehicle weight (GVW) of up to 3,500 kg.

pages.title: 1.2.10-3 B, 6.1.3-3 B
pages.text: The driver's license also entitles you to drive a car with a Trailer, provided the permitted gross vehicle weight (GVW) does not exceed 750 kg.

pages.title: 1.2.10-4 B, 6.1.3-4 B
pages.text: The driver's license also allows you to drive a car with a trailer that has a maximum permitted gross vehicle weight exceeding 750 kg, provided that the combined permitted gross vehicle weight of the car and trailer does not exceed 3500 kg.

pages.title: 1.2.10-5 B, 6.1.3-5 B
pages.text: The driver's license also authorises you to drive a 3-wheeled motorcycle of this type.

pages.title: 1.2.10-6 B, 6.1.3-6 B
pages.text: The driver's license also authorises the holder to drive a four-wheeled motorcycle, also known as a quadricycle, as well as an ATV (All-terrain vehicle).

pages.title: 1.2.10-7 B, 6.1.3-7 B
pages.text: A Category B driver's license allows you to drive a tractor with up to two trailers attached.

pages.title: 1.2.10-8 B, 6.1.3-8 B
pages.text: The driver's license also entitles you to drive motorised equipment ...

pages.title: 1.2.10-9 B, 6.1.3-9 B
pages.text: ... as well as large and small mopeds.

pages.title: 1.2.10-10 B, 6.1.3-10 B
pages.text: For some of these vehicles, special rules apply regarding the vehicle’s layout and equipment. These rules relate in particular to the vehicles’ length and width, brakes, lights, tyres, mirrors and any coupling to a Trailer.

pages.title: 1.3.1-1 B
pages.text: Before you can drive a car on the road, it must be registered with the authorities (the Danish Motor Vehicle Agency), and a vehicle registration certificate must be issued – an official document showing that the car is approved and registered for use on the road.

pages.title: 1.3.1-2 B
pages.text: The vehicle registration certificate contains important information about the car, e.g.: The car’s kerb weight (what it weighs without a load) The car’s Gross vehicle weight (GVW) (how much it is allowed to weigh, including passengers and luggage) How heavy a Trailer the car is allowed to tow

pages.title: 1.3.1-3 B
pages.text: You can check the vehicle registration certificates of the car and the Trailer to see if they are legally permitted to be coupled together. If the Trailer is too heavy, it is not legal – it can be dangerous and unlawful.

pages.title: 1.3.1-4 B
pages.text: When driving with a trailer, you must carry both the car’s and the trailer’s vehicle registration certificates in the car. If you are driving abroad, you must have either: The original certificate, or A duplicate (copy issued by SKAT)

pages.title: 1.3.1-5 B
pages.text: If you are only driving in Denmark, you do not need to carry the original certificates. Copies are sufficient. This also applies to digital copies

pages.title: 1.3.1-6 B
pages.text: Several countries require you to carry the original Vehicle registration certificate when driving in their country – for example, Germany, France and Spain. It is therefore important to check the requirements of the country you are travelling to.

children.title: 5.2 Elements of risk on the road

pages.title: 5.2-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: The requirements for accessibility and safety on roads and streets cannot always be met, as traffic growth generally outpaces the rate at which roads can be expanded or modified. Nor is society able to provide unlimited funds for road construction and maintenance.

pages.title: 5.2-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Even if a road is equipped with all the facilities that should make it a safe road, the built-in safety features will often lead to heavier traffic and higher speeds, and this, combined with the behaviour of other road users, may mean that there are still significant risks along that stretch of road.

pages.title: 5.2-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: As a driver, one must be critical of the temptation to drive at the maximum permitted speed on a stretch of road, as road conditions may involve certain risks that mean driving at the highest permitted speed without caution will be associated with considerable danger. In a later lesson, we will look at these risks in more detail.

pages.title: 5.2.1-1 BCDCE
pages.text: In theory lessons, the following terms are used in connection with these specific risk factors on the roads: - the road’s surroundings - the road’s equipment or standard - the road’s alignment - the road’s use - the road’s type and class.

pages.title: 5.2.1-2 BCDCE
pages.text: The road environment refers to built-up areas and their density, vegetation, wooded areas, open fields, etc. along roads and streets. In certain situations, these environments may constitute risk factors that drivers must be able to recognise and respond to sensibly.

pages.title: 5.2.1-3 BCDCE
pages.text: Road infrastructure refers, for example, to road markings, sidewalks, bicycle lanes, crosswalks and street lighting, all of which can help to improve safety. The width of the roadway, the type of surface and its condition form part of the road standard and also play a role in the risks that may be associated with the road.

pages.title: 5.2.1-4 BCDCE
pages.text: The way in which the road passes through junctions, bends, narrowings, over hills, past level crossings and through Roundabouts and tunnels is referred to as the road’s alignment. The road’s alignment entails certain risks to which drivers must be alert and able to react appropriately.

pages.title: 5.2.1-5 BCDCE
pages.text: The use of the road, including traffic density and type, which is often influenced by local destinations such as schools, stations, bus terminals, shopping centres and sports grounds, also constitutes risk factors to which drivers should pay particular attention.

pages.title: 5.2.1-6 BCDCE
pages.text: The type and class of the road refer to how roads are divided into categories such as Motorways, Expressways, main roads and traffic-calmed areas such as quiet roads, play and recreation areas, and pedestrianised streets. Each road type has its own specific rules and risk factors.

pages.title: 5.2.2-1 BCDCE
pages.text: Risk conditions relating to the road’s surroundings refer to conditions such as any built-up areas, their density, vegetation, wooded areas, open fields and similar features along streets and roads.

pages.title: 5.2.2-2 BCDCE
pages.text: A significant proportion of road traffic accidents occur in urban areas, and the number of accidents relative to traffic volume is highest on roads in built-up areas.

pages.title: 5.2.2-3 BCDCE
pages.text: The risk of accidents in urban areas is high on this type of shopping street, where there is mixed traffic both along and across the street.

pages.title: 5.2.2-4 BCDCE
pages.text: Even on residential roads with both high- and low-rise buildings, there is a significant risk of road traffic accidents, particularly at junctions.

pages.title: 5.2.2-5 BCDCE
pages.text: Most accidents involving young children on residential roads occur on the stretches between junctions.

pages.title: 5.2.2-6 BCDCE
pages.text: The risk conditions in the road environment outside urban areas are typically most critical during the transition from autumn to winter and from winter to spring, particularly when the temperature fluctuates around freezing point.

pages.title: 5.2.2-7 BCDCE
pages.text: During the transitional periods between autumn and winter and between winter and spring, there is a particular risk of slippery patches on the roads, especially where the road passes through or alongside wooded areas.

pages.title: 5.2.2-8 BCDCE
pages.text: In autumn, roads are often slippery and greasy due to fallen leaves, particularly where the road passes through or alongside wooded areas.

pages.title: 5.2.2-9 BCDCE
pages.text: If the road passes through damp meadows or alongside marshes, there is a high risk of patchy slippery road surfaces during the transition from autumn to winter and from winter to spring due to high humidity.

pages.title: 5.2.2-10 BCDCE
pages.text: Depressions in the terrain can often lead to high humidity and thus a risk of slippery roads, particularly when the temperature is close to freezing.

pages.title: 5.2.2-11 BCDCE
pages.text: On road sections near lakes and beaches, humidity will also be relatively high, which increases the risk of patchy slippery road surfaces.

pages.title: 5.2.2-12 BCDCE
pages.text: On sunken roads and beneath bridges and viaducts, the sun and wind struggle to dry the moisture on the roadway, increasing the risk of patchy slippery conditions.

pages.title: 5.2.2-13 BCDCE
pages.text: When the road crosses a bridge, there is a high risk of the roadway on the bridge becoming patchily slippery during periods when temperatures are around freezing point. The cold from both the top and underside of the bridge can quickly cause moisture on the roadway to freeze into ice.

pages.title: 5.2.2-14 BCDCE
pages.text: Even if the roadway has a good surface, soil spilled from field work, particularly in the spring and autumn when farmers are working with tractors and similar machinery, can result in significantly poorer road grip, requiring drivers to adjust their speed.

children.title: 5.2.3 The Equipment or Standard of the Road

pages.title: 5.2.3-1 BCDCE
pages.text: Road infrastructure, or the lack thereof, plays a role in risk conditions: Is the roadway narrow or wide? Are there Road markings, sidewalks, Bicycle lanes, crosswalks and street lighting? The type and condition of the road surface also affect risk conditions and thus the choice of speed.

pages.title: 5.2.3-2 BCDCE
pages.text: Roads without sidewalks pose a risk that pedestrians on the right-hand side of the road may be hit by vehicles. Pedestrians should walk on the left-hand side against the flow of traffic when using roads without sidewalks, but they often walk on the right-hand side with their backs to oncoming traffic.

pages.title: 5.2.3-3 BCDCE
pages.text: The risk of hitting pedestrians on the roadway is particularly high in the dark, as many pedestrians fail to use reflectors or reflective strips.

pages.title: 5.2.3-4 BCDCE
pages.text: Both in urban areas and in the countryside, the risk of cyclists being hit is twice as high on roads without Bicycle lanes, and the risk of moped riders being hit is also higher.

pages.title: 5.2.3-5 BCDCE
pages.text: Unless the road layout clearly indicates that it is a Bicycle lane, a Bicycle lane must be marked with a ‘Bicycle lane’ sign or a white bicycle symbol and be demarcated by a curb or a wide Solid side line. Unless otherwise indicated, both cyclists and small mopeds must use the Bicycle lane.

pages.title: 5.2.3-6 BCDCE
pages.text: The supplementary traffic sign here indicates that it is a two-way Bicycle lane, with traffic in both directions.

pages.title: 5.2.3-7 BCDCE
pages.text: The supplementary traffic sign indicates that the two-way bicycle lane ends.

pages.title: 5.2.3-8 BCDCE
pages.text: Cycle lanes at intersections are marked with a wide broken line, blue colour or both.

pages.title: 5.2.3-9 BCDCE
pages.text: Super bicycle lanes are bicycle lanes of particularly high quality; they are marked with this route identifier.

pages.title: 5.2.3-10 BCDCE
pages.text: Cyclists and moped riders who ride from a bicycle lane onto the Roadway have an unconditional Duty to give way to all traffic, but they do not always comply with it.

pages.title: 5.2.3-11 BCDCE
pages.text: Pedestrian crosswalks on stretches between junctions are used by only a few pedestrians if the detour to the crosswalk is longer than the width of the road. Consequently, there is a greater risk of pedestrians being hit in the areas immediately before and after the crosswalk compared with stretches without a crosswalk.

pages.title: 5.2.3-12 BCDCE
pages.text: Pedestrians often cross the road even when there is a footbridge or underpass, as these are only used to any significant extent if they genuinely save time, which is rarely the case.

pages.title: 5.2.3-13 BCDCE
pages.text: Particularly outside urban areas, the risk of accidents is higher on roads without road markings.

pages.title: 5.2.3-14 BCDCE
pages.text: Road markings improve road safety as they guide drivers to the correct position and manoeuvres.

pages.title: 5.2.3-15 BCDCE
pages.text: Road markings are particularly helpful in the dark and in poor lighting conditions.

pages.title: 5.2.3-16 BCDCE
pages.text: Wide, four-lane roads are generally no safer than two-lane roads.

pages.title: 5.2.3-17 BCDCE
pages.text: On narrow roads, there is a greater risk of single-vehicle accidents, head-on collisions and collisions with moped riders, cyclists and pedestrians.

pages.title: 5.2.3-18 BCDCE
pages.text: The risk of accidents on narrow roads is greatest at the junctions of minor side roads and at entrances and exits from properties.

pages.title: 5.2.3-19 BCDCE
pages.text: Standard four-lane roads with a median are not significantly safer than roads without a median. However, the median reduces the risk of head-on collisions and prevents left turns onto and off minor side roads.

pages.title: 5.2.3-20 BCDCE
pages.text: A median without crash barriers or fencing does not significantly reduce the risk of accidents involving pedestrians, cyclists and moped riders crossing the road at an intersection.

pages.title: 5.2.3-21 BCDCE
pages.text: The risk of accidents in the dark is approximately twice as high on unlit roads as on lit roads.

pages.title: 5.2.3-22 BCDCE
pages.text: The risk of accidents on unlit roads is particularly high when encountering vehicles that cause glare.

pages.title: 5.2.3-23 BCDCE
pages.text: On unlit roads, there are many collisions involving pedestrians crossing intersections.

pages.title: 5.2.3-24 BCDCE
pages.text: Even if the road is lit, it can be difficult to see clearly in rainy weather and similar conditions due to light reflections.

pages.title: 5.2.3-25 BCDCE
pages.text: The road surface and its condition play a crucial role in road grip. Road grip is created both through friction (resistance to sliding) between the tyres and the roadway and by the tyres gripping the unevenness of the roadway. Acceleration, steering and braking can only function via Road grip, which is therefore a prerequisite for any manoeuvre.

pages.title: 5.2.3-26 BCDCE
pages.text: Dirt and gravel roads have poor road grip, so it is important to start off carefully to avoid wheel spin and to drive slowly to avoid skidding when cornering or braking.

pages.title: 5.2.3-27 BCDCE
pages.text: Cobblestones provide better road grip than dirt and Gravel roads, but they quickly become slippery when wet.

pages.title: 5.2.3-28 BCDCE
pages.text: The best road grip is achieved on a rough asphalt surface with coarse gravel.

pages.title: 5.2.3-29 BCDCE
pages.text: On a newly laid asphalt surface with small stones that have not yet been pressed into the surface, there is a risk of stone chips if you drive at speeds above 40 km/h.

pages.title: 5.2.3-30 BCDCE
pages.text: In spring, the road surface is often pitted and uneven due to winter frost and gritting. This uneven and pitted surface results in poorer road grip, so speed should be reduced.

pages.title: 5.2.3-31 BCDCE
pages.text: A rain shower following a dry spell can make the road surface slippery due to the mixture of water, dust, worn rubber and oil spills.

pages.title: 5.2.3-32 BCDCE
pages.text: High temperatures and poor asphalt quality can cause the asphalt surface to melt, making the roads extremely slippery.

pages.title: 5.2.3-33 BCDCE
pages.text: Even with a good roadway, soil spilled from field work, construction sites or similar can lead to significantly reduced road grip, requiring drivers to adjust their speed accordingly.

pages.title: 5.2.3-34 BCDCE
pages.text: Wooded areas and dense vegetation can, at certain times of the year, lead to slippery and greasy roads when trees shed their seeds and leaves fall.

pages.title: 5.2.3-35 BCDCE
pages.text: Regardless of the type of road surface you are driving on, compacted snow and ice provide very poor road grip, meaning that even at low speeds there is a risk of skidding when cornering and braking.

pages.title: 5.2.3-36 BCDCE
pages.text: When switching from a road with good road grip, such as tarmac, to a road with cobblestones and consequently poorer friction, there is a risk of the car skidding if you have not adjusted your speed before the bend.

pages.title: 5.2.3-37 BCDCE
pages.text: Where there are speed bumps, these should be passed at the maximum permitted or indicated speed for that location. If buses and large trucks are to pass without causing significant disruption, they cannot pass the speed bumps at the same speed as passenger cars, but must drive at a significantly lower speed.

pages.title: 5.2.3-38 BCDCE
pages.text: If the speed is too high, it can be uncomfortable for both the driver and passengers. Furthermore, excessive speed can lead to back injuries for the occupants of the vehicle and cause damage to the vehicle.

pages.title: 5.2.3-39 BCDCE
pages.text: When trucks and large buses have to pass speed bumps, they cannot do so at the same speed as passenger cars, but must drive considerably more slowly.

pages.title: 5.2.4-1 BCDCE
pages.text: The road layout, which includes junctions, narrowings, tunnels, bends, hills, level crossings and Roundabouts, presents hazards that require drivers to adjust their speed to the prevailing conditions.

pages.title: 5.2.4-2 BCDCE
pages.text: Road intersections, both in urban and rural areas, are the locations where most accidents occur, as traffic from multiple directions converges and both pedestrians and traffic cross each other’s paths. When approaching an intersection, you must adjust your speed according to visibility and the Rules for the duty to give way at the location.

pages.title: 5.2.4-3 BCDCE
pages.text: In the countryside, junctions with four side roads and no traffic lights are the type where the highest number of road accidents occur under conditions of high traffic volume.

pages.title: 5.2.4-4 BCDCE
pages.text: Junctions with narrow roads are generally just as dangerous as junctions with wide roads.

pages.title: 5.2.4-5 BCDCE
pages.text: Intersections without road markings, turning lanes, Hatched road markings or pedestrian refuges are more hazardous than those with these markings. The markings make it easier for traffic to orientate itself and position its vehicles correctly.

pages.title: 5.2.4-6 BCDCE
pages.text: Road junctions with Traffic Lights reduce the risk of accidents between vehicles travelling straight ahead on separate roads, but at the same time increase the risk of accidents involving vehicles turning left that do not give way to oncoming traffic.

pages.title: 5.2.4-7 BCDCE
pages.text: When approaching a bend in the road, it is important to adjust your speed to the sharpness of the bend and keep as far to the right as possible.

pages.title: 5.2.4-8 BCDCE
pages.text: Curved roads are generally considered dangerous, and the sharper the bend, the greater the risk of accidents. A sharp bend is particularly dangerous if it is on a road that otherwise has only gentle curves and good visibility.

pages.title: 5.2.4-9 BCDCE
pages.text: Curved roads on narrow roads with visibility of only 100 metres or less are more dangerous than bends with better visibility.

pages.title: 5.2.4-10 BCDCE
pages.text: Sharp bends in the countryside without kerb markings are more risky than bends with Solid side lines, kerb posts or direction arrows. Bends where the roadway slopes outwards towards the outside of the bend are particularly dangerous, as they make it harder to steer through the bend, even at normal speeds.

pages.title: 5.2.4-11 BCDCE
pages.text: Road narrowings pose a risk in overtaking situations and a risk of collision with Traffic that is pushing or forcing its way in from the left or right.

pages.title: 5.2.4-12 BCDCE
pages.text: Hilltops are generally considered dangerous due to the limited visibility. When approaching a hilltop, you must adjust your speed to the short sight distance and keep as far to the right as possible to allow for any oncoming traffic.

pages.title: 5.2.4-13 BCDCE
pages.text: When approaching a level crossing, there is always a risk of collision with trains or rail vehicles. You must therefore adjust your speed so that you can stop in time if the signals are activated or if you see or hear a train approaching.

pages.title: 5.2.4-14 BCDCE
pages.text: The risk of an accident is particularly high at Railroad crossings without barriers.

pages.title: 5.2.4-15 BCDCE
pages.text: Level crossings with barriers are safer than those with only light and sound signals, as these can be more easily overlooked in bright sunlight or overlooked if there is a lot of noise in the car. However, you must remember that even technical measures such as signals and barriers can fail.

pages.title: 5.2.4-16 BCDCE
pages.text: Roundabouts significantly reduce the risk of accidents among motorists compared to ordinary junctions with give-way rules. For cyclists, however, the risk is not reduced, as they are often hit by motorists either entering or exiting the roundabout.

pages.title: 5.2.4-17 BCDCE
pages.text: The risk of accidents when driving through a tunnel is particularly high when entering from full daylight, as visual acuity is reduced. Even if the tunnel is lit, the eyes may struggle to adjust to the changed lighting conditions.

pages.title: 5.2.4-18 BCDCE
pages.text: Tunnels can be dangerous because many road users forget to ensure their vehicle has enough fuel. The limited space in the tunnel and reduced visual acuity also increase the risk of colliding with a stationary vehicle.

pages.title: 5.2.5-1 BCDCE
pages.text: Most accidents occur on roads with heavy traffic, and the risk increases the more mixed the traffic is.

pages.title: 5.2.5-2 BCDCE
pages.text: Some roads in a local area attract specific groups of road users, which can increase the risk of accidents. This applies, for example, to school routes, roads used by ferry traffic or heavy goods vehicles, access and exit roads, shopping streets and similar.

pages.title: 5.2.5-3 BCDCE
pages.text: Local destinations such as schools, sports grounds, bus stops, train stations, large workplaces, care homes, cinemas and other entertainment venues often lead to inattentive behaviour among road users who are focused on reaching these places.

children.title: 5.2.6 The Type or Class of Roads

pages.title: 5.2.6-1 BCDCE
pages.text: Using traffic signs, roads can be classified into the following types: • Motorways • Expressways • Main roads • Tunnels • Speed-restricted areas • Cycle lanes • Residential areas and • Pedestrianised streets.

pages.title: 5.2.6-2 BCDCE
pages.text: The ‘Motorway’ sign can be either green or blue and is placed at the start of the Motorway and at all slip roads. It indicates that the special rules for driving on motorways apply.

pages.title: 5.2.6-3 BCDCE
pages.text: The sign "Expressway" indicates that you are entering an Expressway where the special rules for driving on expressways apply.

pages.title: 5.2.6-4 BCDCE
pages.text: Main roads are marked with a yellow information sign indicating that traffic coming from the side roads must give way to all traffic, and that outside built-up areas, parking on the roadway is not permitted.

pages.title: 5.2.6-5 BCDCE
pages.text: The sign “Speed-restricted area” marks an area where the road has been designed, using chicanes or speed bumps, so that it is not suitable for driving at speeds higher than those indicated on the sign, for example 30 km/h.

pages.title: 5.2.6-6 BCDCE
pages.text: The sign "Residential area" marks an area where it is permitted to stay and play across the entire width of the road. Driving here must be at very low speed, and drivers must exercise extra care and consideration for pedestrians.

pages.title: 5.2.6-7 BCDCE
pages.text: The sign "Pedestrian zone" indicates that the area is for pedestrians only. However, the sign may also indicate permission to drive at specific times or under special conditions.

pages.title: 5.2.6-8 BCDCE
pages.text: The warning sign indicates that there is a tunnel further ahead on the road.

pages.title: 6.2.3-1 B, 6.2.6-1 CDBE
pages.text: When driving outside of the lighting-up time, i.e. between sunrise and sunset in good visibility conditions, low-beam headlights must be used as driving lights. Alternatively, special driving lights or the car’s fog lights may be used.

pages.title: 6.2.3-2 B, 6.2.6-2 CDBE
pages.text: If it is necessary to warn of a danger, you should alert others by briefly sounding the horn or flashing your headlights. The use of the horn in other situations is not permitted.

pages.title: 6.2.3-3 B, 6.2.6-3 CDBE
pages.text: During the lighting-up time, Traffic Lights should be used instead of audible signals, unless there is an imminent danger.

pages.title: 6.2.4-1 B, 6.2.6-4 CDBE
pages.text: The use of Blinkers is mandatory when it can serve as a guide to others. In addition, there are a wide range of manoeuvres where Blinkers must always be used.

pages.title: 6.2.4-2 B, 6.2.6-5 CDBE
pages.text: Before pulling out from the kerb, before turning round and before turning, you must signal with your Blinkers.

pages.title: 6.2.4-3 B, 6.2.6-6 CDBE
pages.text: On Motorways, you must always use your Blinkers when changing lanes and whenever there is a significant change in the position of your vehicle, such as when entering or exiting the Motorway. On other roads, you must signal when necessary to guide other traffic.

pages.title: 6.2.4-4 B, 6.2.6-7 CDBE
pages.text: In the event of unexpected traffic congestion on a Motorway or other danger, Hazard warning lights must be used. On other roads outside Built-up areas, Hazard warning lights may also be used. Signals must be given clearly and unambiguously well in advance of a manoeuvre and must be stopped once the manoeuvre is complete.

pages.title: 6.2.4-5 B, 6.2.6-8 CDBE
pages.text: Before entering a Roundabout, and if you are taking the first exit, you must indicate right. If you are taking the last exit, you may indicate left. When leaving the Roundabout after the first exit, start indicating right from the centre of the side road, before the exit you wish to take.

pages.title: 6.2.4-6 B, 6.2.6-9 CDBE
pages.text: When stopping or slowing down rapidly, signal with your brake lights.

pages.title: 6.2.5-1 B, 6.2.6-10 CDBE
pages.text: Lighting-up time is from sunset to sunrise . . . .

pages.title: 6.2.5-2 B, 6.2.6-11 CDBE
pages.text: Lighting-up time is also when the headlights must be used due to darkness, fog, mist, rain or other poor visibility conditions.

pages.title: 6.2.5-3 B, 6.2.6-12 CDBE
pages.text: When driving during the lighting-up time, i.e. from sunset to sunrise, or when the car’s lights must be used due to darkness, fog, mist, rain or similar poor light or visibility conditions, at least Low-beam headlights must be used.

pages.title: 6.2.5-4 B, 6.2.6-13 CDBE
pages.text: When driving outside the Lighting-up time, you must use low-beam headlights. Alternatively, you may use special driving lights or fog lights.

children.title: 6.2.6 Free passage for certain types of road users

pages.title: 6.2.6-1 B
pages.text: There are certain road users to whom you must give way. This means you must hold back and make room for them, for example groups of children under the supervision of a leader.

pages.title: 6.2.6-2 B
pages.text: You must also ensure that you give way or make room for convoys of the armed forces and emergency services.

pages.title: 6.2.6-3 B
pages.text: You must likewise hold back or make way for other organised processions.

pages.title: 6.2.6-4 B
pages.text: You must also give way to funeral processions.

pages.title: 6.2.6-5 B
pages.text: You should ensure that the road is kept clear in good time and stop, if necessary, to allow Emergency vehicles to pass.

pages.title: 6.2.6-6 B
pages.text: It is important to avoid driving so close to an accident scene that you hinder rescue and clearance work.

pages.title: 6.2.7-1 B
pages.text: A car must not exceed 2.55 m in width, 12 m in length and 4 m in height – with or without a load

pages.title: 6.2.7-2 B
pages.text: The weight of the car, including passengers, luggage or other cargo, must not exceed the maximum permitted Gross vehicle weight (GVW) stated on the vehicle registration certificate.

pages.title: 6.2.7-3 B
pages.text: Passengers and luggage must be placed in the car in such a way that the driver has a clear view and easy access to manoeuvre the car.

pages.title: 6.2.7-4 B
pages.text: Passengers must not be carried in numbers or positioned in a manner that may pose a danger to themselves or others. No more passengers may be carried than there are seats with associated seat belts.

pages.title: 6.2.7-5 B
pages.text: If a seat is fitted with a seat belt, it must be worn by the person sitting there, together with a booster seat if necessary.

pages.title: 6.2.7-6 B
pages.text: Children under 3 years of age must use a harness, child seat or other approved safety equipment in the front seat that is suitable for their height and weight.

pages.title: 6.2.7-7 B
pages.text: Children under 3 years of age must use safety equipment in preference to other passengers.

pages.title: 6.2.7-8 B
pages.text: Cars with airbags must carry a warning against fitting rear-facing child seats, unless the airbags are automatically deactivated when a rear-facing child seat is fitted.

pages.title: 6.2.7-9 B
pages.text: It is the driver’s responsibility to ensure that passengers under 15 years of age wear a seat belt.

pages.title: 6.2.7-10 B
pages.text: The seat Headrest must be adjusted to suit the individual user in order to provide optimum protection.

pages.title: 6.2.7-11 B
pages.text: Cargo and luggage must be placed so that it does not obstruct blinkers, lights or the number plate. It must be secured so that it does not make unnecessary noise, drag on the road or risk falling off.

pages.title: 6.2.7-12 B
pages.text: In cases where the cargo covers one or more mandatory lights or reflectors, a light bar must be fitted to the rear of the cargo. If the cargo also covers the number plate, the light bar must also be fitted with a third number plate.

pages.title: 6.2.7-13 B
pages.text: When loading cargo, the general rule is to place the heaviest items at the bottom and as far forward as possible. Cargo must also be secured to prevent it from sliding forward during braking.

pages.title: 6.2.7-14 B
pages.text: If anything is dropped or spilled on the road and poses a danger to traffic, it must be removed immediately. If this is not possible, you must warn others of the danger by means of markings or similar.

pages.title: 6.2.7-15 B
pages.text: Cargo that protrudes more than 1 metre to the front and rear, and more than 15 cm beyond the sides of the vehicle, must be marked.

pages.title: 6.2.7-16 B
pages.text: For commercial transport and transport during the lighting-up time, a white cylinder with two red reflective bands must be used as a marker. During the lighting-up time, the white cylinder must also be fitted with a white light at the front and a red light at the rear.

pages.title: 6.2.7-17 B
pages.text: The white cylinder with two red reflective bands must be at least 30 cm high and at least 10 cm in diameter.

pages.title: 6.2.7-18 B
pages.text: For non-commercial transport outside the Lighting-up time, marking may be carried out using a cloth or by some other clear means.

pages.title: 6.2.7-19 B
pages.text: As a private individual, you may often find yourself in a situation where you need to transport dangerous cargo in your car. “Dangerous cargo” is the transport industry’s term for products that may pose a risk during transport. The transport of dangerous cargo must always follow specific rules.

pages.title: 6.2.7-20 B
pages.text: Examples of dangerous cargo include fireworks, ammunition, gas cylinders, petrol, diesel, fire extinguishing fluid, non-water-based paint, turpentine, hydrochloric acid and lithium batteries.

pages.title: 6.2.7-21 B
pages.text: Private individuals may transport dangerous cargo by car subject to certain rules. The cargo must be intended for personal or domestic use, including leisure and sporting activities. The dangerous cargo must be packaged for retail sale, which means that, as a general rule, it must be in the original packaging that consumers can buy in shops. A maximum of 240 litres of flammable liquids may be transported in refillable containers, with a maximum of 60 litres per container.

pages.title: 6.2.7-22 B
pages.text: During transport, dangerous cargo must be securely fastened or positioned so that it cannot tip over or shift. There must be no leakage of the contents under normal transport conditions. Spills or leaks of dangerous cargo must be reported immediately to 1-1-2 if they cannot be removed or rendered harmless immediately.

pages.title: 6.2.7-23 B
pages.text: More information about private individuals’ transport of dangerous goods by road can be obtained from the Agency's website: www.brs.dk.

pages.title: 6.2.7-24 B
pages.text: A maximum of one trailer can be connected to a car; and only if the car is approved to tow a trailer.

pages.title: 6.2.8-1 B, 6.2.7-1 CDBE
pages.text: If the car breaks down or an accident occurs in a place where stopping and parking are prohibited, the car must be moved away as quickly as possible. On a Motorway, the car should be removed from the Roadway if at all possible.

pages.title: 6.2.8-2 B, 6.2.7-2 CDBE
pages.text: If the car is causing a danger or inconvenience to traffic, you must immediately set up a Warning triangle at least 50 metres behind the car on ordinary roads and at least 100 metres on a Motorway. As a supplement to the Warning triangle, you may use the car’s Hazard warning lights.

pages.title: 6.2.8-3 B, 6.2.7-3 CDBE
pages.text: In the event of unexpected traffic jams or other sudden hazards on roads other than Motorways and outside Built-up areas, the Hazard warning lights may be used to warn other road users of the danger. On Motorways, the Hazard warning lights must always be used in the event of unexpected traffic jams or other immediate dangers.

pages.title: 6.2.8-4 B, 6.2.7-4 CDBE
pages.text: If the car breaks down or similar on a level crossing or other crossing with tracks, you must warn the train driver of the danger as best you can.

pages.title: 6.2.8-5 B, 6.2.7-5 CDBE
pages.text: It is lawful to use a car to tow a broken-down car, tractor or motorised implement, provided that the brakes and Steering Unit of the towed vehicle are in good working order.

pages.title: 6.2.8-6 B, 6.2.7-6 CDBE
pages.text: Towing must be carried out using a sturdy rope, tow bar or similar device.

pages.title: 6.2.8-7 B, 6.2.7-7 CDBE
pages.text: The distance between the vehicles must not exceed 4 metres, and if the distance is more than 2 metres, the rope must be clearly marked. The driver of the towed vehicle must hold a valid Driver's license for that vehicle, and the speed during towing must not exceed 30 km/h.

education.title: Module 3: Basic theory and practical driving module

pages.title: Introduction
pages.text:
Module 3: Basic theory and practical driving module.

The instruction in Module 3 is designed to equip you with the skills to adapt your driving to changing traffic conditions and applicable traffic regulations in a safe, considerate, energy-efficient and Environmentally friendly manner, whilst performing all standard manoeuvres in a light/less congested area.

children.title: 7.1 Moving off and stopping by the roadside

pages.title: 7.1-1 B
pages.text: You must always use your blinkers before setting off. As a rule, you should wait to switch on your blinkers until All clear, so that you can set off. Switch off your blinkers once you have started moving.

pages.title: 7.1-2 B
pages.text: If traffic is heavy, you can use your blinkers to signal that you are about to set off, so that other road users can make way. However, it is important that the use of the blinkers does not create danger or cause unnecessary inconvenience, and it does not give you the right to cause a hindrance when setting off.

pages.title: 7.1-3 B
pages.text: There are several risks associated with setting off that you should be aware of. Many accidents occur because the person setting off underestimates their speed and the distance to vehicles approaching from behind.

pages.title: 7.1-4 BBE
pages.text: It is easy to become impatient when traffic is heavy, which can result in misjudging the situation. If the engine has just started and is still cold, there is a risk of the engine stalling whilst starting off, which may pose a danger to vehicles behind.

pages.title: 7.1-5 BBE
pages.text: Before setting off, you must ensure that you can do so without risk or unnecessary inconvenience, which means that vehicles behind you should not normally be forced to slow down. It is not enough just to look ahead and behind in the Mirrors – it is important to turn your head and check whether there is anyone in your blind spots.

pages.title: 7.1-6 B
pages.text: Here it appears that the road is all clear, but before setting off it is important to turn your head and check your blind spot.

pages.title: 7.1-7 B
pages.text: There is a cyclist in the side mirror, but if there is no one in the blind spot, you can drive off, as the cyclist is far enough away for you to set off without causing any unnecessary inconvenience.

pages.title: 7.1-8 B
pages.text: In this case, the cyclist is so close that setting off would cause unnecessary inconvenience.

pages.title: 7.1-9 BBE
pages.text: Even if there is no one in the blind spot, due to the distance from the vehicle approaching from behind and its speed, you risk causing unnecessary inconvenience if you set off.

pages.title: 7.1-10 B
pages.text: If there is no one in the blind spot, you may set off due to the speed of the vehicle approaching from behind. This is done by accelerating so quickly that the vehicle approaching from behind does not need to slow down.

pages.title: 7.1-11 BBE
pages.text: If the roadway is wet or slippery, reduced traction means you cannot accelerate as quickly as normal, and you risk wheel spin when pulling away, so there must be a considerable distance to vehicles approaching from behind when you pull away.

pages.title: 7.1-12 BBE
pages.text: When setting off on narrow roads and streets, it is important to pay particular attention to oncoming traffic if setting off could pose a risk or cause unnecessary inconvenience to them. Due to the limited space for manoeuvring, you must wait to set off until the oncoming vehicle has passed.

pages.title: 7.1-13 BBE
pages.text: You must always indicate with your Blinkers when setting off from the kerb, regardless of whether there are other road users or not.

pages.title: 7.2-1 B
pages.text: The kerb marks the part of the roadway to be used by cars, motorbikes and large mopeds.

pages.title: 7.2-2 B
pages.text: The wide kerb line indicates that there is space to the right of the kerb line for cyclists and pedestrians.

pages.title: 7.2-3 B
pages.text: If there is no dedicated lane (Bus lane, turning lane or Bicycle lane) to the right of the solid edge line, tractors and motorised equipment must keep as far to the right of the Roadway as possible, so that they are driving on top of the edge line.

pages.title: 7.2-4 B
pages.text: The narrow edge line is a warning sign, as cyclists and pedestrians use the same part of the Roadway as cars.

pages.title: 7.2-5 B
pages.text: The solid edge line may only be crossed when stopping or parking, or when entering or turning off the road.

pages.title: 7.2-6 B
pages.text: If there is no dedicated lane (Bus lane, turning lane or Bicycle lane) to the right of the solid edge line, it is permitted to cross the edge line when overtaking on the right of a vehicle turning left.

pages.title: 7.2-7 B
pages.text: Where there are no lane markings, there are as many lanes as there is space for rows of four-wheeled vehicles.

pages.title: 7.2-8 B
pages.text: The lane markings, consisting of a short line with a long gap, indicate the separation between lanes. It is permitted to cross the lane markings to change lanes.

pages.title: 7.2-9 B
pages.text: The warning line, the long dash with a short gap, indicates that you must take particular care when crossing the line due to poor visibility or because you are about to encounter a stop line.

pages.title: 7.2-10 B
pages.text: The stop line must not be crossed, not even when turning, swerving or driving across the line.

pages.title: 7.2-11 B
pages.text: However, it is permitted to cross the stop line where special conditions make it necessary, e.g. when passing Road Construction or an illegally stopped or parked vehicle. When crossing a stop line, you must be particularly vigilant.

pages.title: 7.2-12 B
pages.text: The sign indicates that you must drive past the sign in the direction the arrow points.

pages.title: 7.2-13 B
pages.text: The sign indicates that you may choose which side to pass the sign on.

pages.title: 7.2-14 B
pages.text: The information sign indicates that you must enter the Crawler lane if you are driving slower than the speed indicated on the sign, and that you must leave the Crawler lane again if you are driving faster than the indicated speed.

pages.title: 7.2-15 B
pages.text: You must pass traffic lights, traffic signals or similar on the right, unless the road is one-way or otherwise indicated by road markings such as Traffic signs or Road markings.

pages.title: 7.2-16 BBE
pages.text: Traffic must, taking into account other traffic and the conditions in general, keep as far to the right of the Roadway as possible; that is to say, one must normally use the right-hand lane.

pages.title: 7.2-17 BBE
pages.text: Where the roadway is divided into lanes by means of lane markings, you must position yourself in the centre of the marked lane.

pages.title: 7.2-18 B
pages.text: When driving, you must avoid keeping your eyes fixed immediately in front of the car, but instead look far up ahead at short intervals and, as far as possible, be aware of road and traffic conditions 8 to 12 seconds up ahead. You should also anticipate traffic conditions to avoid significant and unnecessary reductions in speed, thereby achieving fuel savings.

pages.title: 7.2-19 B
pages.text: It is important to keep your eyes moving and also to stay aware of what is happening to the sides and behind you using the mirrors, so that you have plenty of time to carry out your manoeuvres.

pages.title: 7.2-20 B
pages.text: When turning the steering wheel to make steering corrections or to change lanes, it is important to turn the wheel smoothly and avoid jerky movements – the higher the speed, the smoother the movements.

pages.title: 7.2-21 BBE
pages.text: The left-hand lane is only used when overtaking, for example, stationary vehicles, and you should return to the right-hand lane after passing the obstacles.

pages.title: 7.2-22 BBE
pages.text: However, if there are several parked vehicles in the right-hand lane, you should not keep changing lanes every time you pass a stationary car, but wait to move back into the right-hand lane until you have passed the row of obstacles and the right-hand lane is clear of obstacles.

pages.title: 7.2-23 BBE
pages.text: When overtaking, for example, cyclists or other slow-moving road users, use the left-hand lane to overtake, and return to the right-hand lane when it can be done without danger or inconvenience to the vehicle being overtaken.

pages.title: 7.2-24 BBE
pages.text: If you are to continue straight ahead at this Intersection, it would not be advisable to position yourself in the right-hand lane because of the cyclists. Here, choosing the left-hand lane means you are positioned as far to the right as possible, taking into account these slow-moving road users and their tendency to swerve when setting off when the lights change.

pages.title: 7.2-25 BBE
pages.text: If you are going straight ahead at this Intersection, it would also be advisable to position yourself in the left-hand lane, where you are positioned as far to the right as possible, taking into account the slowly accelerating truck waiting at the traffic lights.

pages.title: 7.2-26 BBE
pages.text: When proceeding straight ahead at the Intersection and positioning yourself in the left-hand lane, you should also position yourself as far to the right as possible, taking into account the passenger car indicating right and therefore starting slowly when the lights turn green.

pages.title: 7.2-27 BBE
pages.text: When approaching this intersection, it is also advisable to position yourself in the left-hand lane, as the right-hand lane on the other side of the intersection is occupied by stationary vehicles.

pages.title: 7.2-28 BBE
pages.text: When approaching a blind bend on a country road, you must adjust your speed and move as far to the right of the Roadway as possible to avoid dangerous encounters with oncoming traffic.

pages.title: 7.2-29 BBE
pages.text: The same applies when approaching a blind hilltop. In addition to adjusting your speed, you must move as far to the right as possible to avoid potentially dangerous oncoming traffic.

pages.title: 7.2-30 BBE
pages.text: A “2-in-1 road” is a single-lane road with two-way traffic. The carriageway is bordered on both sides by wide hard shoulders, marked with broad broken solid side lines. The wide hard shoulders serve both as a passing area when oncoming traffic needs to pass each other and as a traffic area for vulnerable road users.

pages.title: 7.2-31 BBE
pages.text: On a ‘2-minus-1 road’, drivers must position themselves in the centre of the roadway between the wide broken edge lines . . .

pages.title: 7.2-32 BBE
pages.text: in a passing situation, you must adjust your speed . . .

pages.title: 7.2-33 BBE
pages.text: and, taking into account any vulnerable road users at the roadside, move out over the wide dotted line to maintain a safe Side distance from oncoming traffic . . .

pages.title: 7.2-34 BBE
pages.text: After passing oncoming traffic, move back into the centre of the roadway and, at the end of the ‘2-lane road’, return to the right-hand lane.

pages.title: 7.2-35 BBE
pages.text: Driving on a “2-lane road with one lane closed”.

children.title: 7.3 Your Speed while driving straight ahead

pages.title: 7.3-1 B
pages.text: Young drivers often experience single-vehicle accidents in which, with no other vehicle involved, they suddenly lose control of the car and end up off the road or collide with an obstacle. These accidents are primarily caused by excessive speed in relation to the conditions, possibly combined with Driving under the influence (DUI). Most single-vehicle accidents occur on straight stretches of road, but on bends they typically happen when the car drifts out to the outside of the bend, where the roadside is least curved. Narrow roads also see more single-vehicle accidents than wide roads.

pages.title: 7.3-2 B
pages.text: When choosing a speed, one should be aware of: - Inattention - Misjudgement of one’s own speed. - Misjudgement of the sharpness of a curved road. - Misjudgement of Road grip. - Incorrect tyre pressure, worn tyres and incorrect load. - Fatigue. - The influence of alcohol or drugs.

pages.title: 7.3-3 B
pages.text: The Road Traffic Act requires drivers to always adapt their speed to the conditions and ensure that their speed never exceeds the level at which they have full control of the vehicle. It must also be possible to stop the vehicle within the visible distance and before any obstacles that may be encountered. In the following, we will take a closer look at the risks associated with choosing a speed.

pages.title: 7.3-4 BBE
pages.text: In Denmark, the following general speed limits apply: 50 km/h in built-up areas, 80 km/h outside built-up areas and on dual carriageways, and 130 km/h on Expressways.

pages.title: 7.3-5 BBE
pages.text: However, certain vehicles are subject to a specific speed limit: Motorcycles with trailers, passenger/van and trucks with trailers, as well as buses, may not exceed 80 km/h. Small cars and buses with an approved Tempo 100 permit may drive up to 100 km/h on Motorways – This applies to both Danish and foreign vehicles.

pages.title: 7.3-6 BBE
pages.text: The information sign indicates that you are entering a built-up area where the general speed limit is 50 km/h.

pages.title: 7.3-7 BBE
pages.text: Within built-up areas, road signs may indicate a lower local speed limit than the general one.

pages.title: 7.3-8 B
pages.text: Local speed limits may be displayed on variable message signs

pages.title: 7.3-9 B
pages.text: Signs may indicate a higher local speed limit than the general limit. The local speed limit applies on that stretch of road until it is lifted by an end-of-limit sign or a new speed limit. If you turn off a road with a local speed limit and there are no signs on the new road, the general speed limit applies.

pages.title: 7.3-10 BBE
pages.text: When a local speed limit ends, this is indicated by a sign – after which the general speed limit applies.

pages.title: 7.3-11 BBE
pages.text: The end sign may have a Supplementary traffic sign specifying that it is located in a Built-up area, which means that the general speed limit after the sign is 50 km/h.

pages.title: 7.3-12 BBE
pages.text: This sign supersedes all prohibition signs on the previous stretch of road, except for no stopping and no parking signs. The general speed limit therefore applies after the sign.

pages.title: 7.3-13 BBE
pages.text: The information sign indicates that you are leaving a Built-up area, and the general speed limit of 80 km/h then applies. The sign marking the end of a Built-up area simultaneously cancels any local speed limit.

pages.title: 7.3-14 B
pages.text: If there is a sign indicating the local speed limit immediately after the information sign, it is the local speed limit that applies.

pages.title: 7.3-15 B
pages.text: However, a supplementary traffic sign may indicate that the local speed limit applies only to specific types of vehicles.

pages.title: 7.3-16 B
pages.text: On certain stretches of country road outside Built-up areas, the local speed limit may be up to 90 km/h.

pages.title: 7.3-17 B
pages.text: The sign indicates that automatic speed enforcement may be in operation, either via a mobile speed camera van or a fixed-position speed camera, where drivers’ speeds are recorded automatically. The data collected is used both for issuing fines and for statistical purposes.

pages.title: 7.3-18 BBE
pages.text: The “Recommended speed” sign indicates that the road is not suitable for driving faster than the speed indicated on the sign.

pages.title: 7.3-19 BBE
pages.text: The stretch of road with the recommended speed applies until you pass the “Recommended speed ends” sign.

pages.title: 7.3-20 BBE
pages.text: A supplementary traffic sign may indicate the stretch of road with a recommended speed, which therefore does not always end with the 'Recommended speed ends' sign.

pages.title: 7.3-21 B
pages.text: Road grip plays an important role in choosing a speed. There are several warning signs indicating that you should pay extra attention to the roadway surface and its condition, as there may be a risk of reduced traction.

pages.title: 7.3-22 B
pages.text: The ‘Slippery road’ warning sign warns that the road may be particularly slippery. The reason must always be stated on a Supplementary traffic sign, as here with ‘Slippery in wet conditions’. If the conditions on the Supplementary traffic sign are not met, e.g. if the road is dry, the sign has no bearing on the choice of speed.

pages.title: 7.3-23 B
pages.text: The roadway becomes particularly slippery when there is a risk of black ice.

pages.title: 7.3-24 B
pages.text: The supplementary traffic sign indicates that the roadway is particularly slippery as it crosses a wooden bridge.

pages.title: 7.3-25 B
pages.text: The ‘Uneven Road’ warning sign warns of dangerous speed bumps or unevenness on the road, where poor road contact may occur if driving too fast.

pages.title: 7.3-26 B
pages.text: When there are "rumble strips" on the road, it means you should be extra careful and perhaps slow down.

pages.title: 7.3-27 B
pages.text: The "Bump" warning sign indicates that there are speed bumps up ahead. These speed bumps should only be passed at the speed limit or the speed indicated at that location.

pages.title: 7.3-28 B
pages.text: The "Loose stones" warning sign warns of a particular risk of stone chips.

pages.title: 7.3-29 B
pages.text: When the “Loose stones” warning sign is in place, it is recommended to reduce speed to around 40 km/h, regardless of whether there is a local speed limit or not.

pages.title: 7.3-30 B
pages.text: The "Dangerous verge" warning sign may have a supplementary traffic sign, such as "High shoulder" or "Soft shoulder", explaining why the shoulder is dangerous.

pages.title: 7.3-31 B
pages.text: The road layout also plays a significant role in determining speed; by road layout we mean: • Junctions • Curved roads • Narrow sections • Hills • Level crossings • Roundabouts • Tunnels

pages.title: 7.3-32 BBE
pages.text: When approaching a junction, you must adjust your speed to suit the conditions. The warning sign “Dangerous intersection” indicates that it is the crossing traffic that must give way, but the sign is erected because the crossing traffic has poor visibility and may therefore find it difficult to comply with the right of way, or because accidents frequently occur at that intersection.

pages.title: 7.3-33 B
pages.text: The "Dangerous junction" warning sign may also indicate that it is a T-junction where traffic coming from the side roads must give way to all traffic. It also shows which direction the crossing traffic is coming from.

pages.title: 7.3-34 BBE
pages.text: When approaching a curved road, speed must be adjusted to the sharpness of the road so that it can be negotiated at a steady and constant speed without having to brake or accelerate. If conditions permit, you should keep as far to the right of the road as possible, and at the end of the curved road you may accelerate slightly.

pages.title: 7.3-35 B
pages.text: The warning sign "Dangerous bend in the road" indicates that there is a dangerous right-hand bend up ahead.

pages.title: 7.3-36 B
pages.text: Here, the warning sign indicates that a dangerous left-hand bend is approaching.

pages.title: 7.3-37 B
pages.text: The "Dangerous bend in the road" warning sign indicates that there are two or more dangerous bends, with the first bend being to the left. A supplementary traffic sign may indicate the length of the stretch with dangerous bends or the number of bends on the route.

pages.title: 7.3-38 BBE
pages.text: Below the “Dangerous bend in the road” warning sign, a supplementary traffic sign may be erected indicating the speed at which the bend or bends can normally be negotiated. The speed indicated on the information sign is a guide, so that drivers can adjust their speed according to the vehicle’s load, etc.

pages.title: 7.3-39 B
pages.text: Directional arrows, background marking plates, edge marking plates and barrier arms are used to mark curved roads where road users must make a significant change of direction. This may be at obstacles in front of road junctions or at points where the roadway suddenly narrows.

pages.title: 7.3-40 B
pages.text: Edge marking plates are used to mark obstacles on the road, such as here at a traffic island. The direction of the stripes indicates which side vehicles must pass the edge marking post on, namely the side towards which the stripes slope, in this case to the left.

pages.title: 7.3-41 B
pages.text: The markings on the kerb marker here show that drivers may drive either to the right or left of the marker.

pages.title: 7.3-42 B
pages.text: Background marking plates designed as directional arrows and kerb marking plates are also used to reinforce the marking of, for example, bends.

pages.title: 7.3-43 B
pages.text: The background marking here indicates that the road takes a sharp bend to the right.

pages.title: 7.3-44 B
pages.text: The ‘Steep incline’ warning sign indicates the maximum gradient.

pages.title: 7.3-45 BBE
pages.text: When approaching a hill, you may need to change to a lower gear. If you need to change gear whilst climbing the hill, do so in good time to avoid the engine stalling. When approaching the top of a hill with limited visibility, slow down so that you can stop within the distance you can see, and keep as far to the right of the Roadway as possible whilst passing the top of the hill.

pages.title: 7.3-46 B
pages.text: The “Steep descent” warning sign indicates the maximum gradient.

pages.title: 7.3-47 B
pages.text: When driving down steep hills, use the same gear you used to drive up the hill to make use of the engine’s braking effect.

pages.title: 7.3-48 B
pages.text: The "Narrow road" warning sign indicates that the narrowing is on the right-hand side of the road.

pages.title: 7.3-49 B
pages.text: The "Narrow road" warning sign indicates that the narrowing is on the left-hand side.

pages.title: 7.3-50 B
pages.text: Here, the warning sign indicates that the narrowing occurs on both sides.

pages.title: 7.3-51 B
pages.text: "Narrow road" warning signs may have a Supplementary traffic sign indicating the clear width of the narrowed section.

pages.title: 7.3-52 BBE
pages.text: When approaching a level crossing, speed must be reduced to such a level that you can stop in time if the signal lights up, the barriers lower, or if you can see or hear a train approaching.

pages.title: 7.3-53 B
pages.text: The warning sign “Railroad crossing” without barriers warns of a railroad crossing up ahead.

pages.title: 7.3-54 B
pages.text: The warning sign “Level crossing with barriers” warns of a level crossing up ahead.

pages.title: 7.3-55 B
pages.text: In conjunction with the “Level crossing” warning signs, distance markers with 3, 2 or 1 slashes are often used. The sign with 3 slashes is placed below the warning sign, whilst the other two signs indicate 2/3 and 1/3 of the distance from the warning sign to the crossing, respectively.

pages.title: 7.3-56 B
pages.text: At railroad crossings without Blinkers and barriers, there may be a Supplementary traffic sign with the text “Look out for trains”.

pages.title: 7.3-57 B
pages.text: The “Railway crossing” warning sign may have a Supplementary traffic sign indicating that a full stop must be made before crossing the railway crossing.

pages.title: 7.3-58 B
pages.text: A cross mark immediately before the level crossing indicates that it is a single-track level crossing.

pages.title: 7.3-59 B
pages.text: This cross-mark immediately before the level crossing indicates that it is a multi-track level crossing.

pages.title: 7.3-60 B
pages.text: If there is a ‘Full Stop’ sign at the level crossing, traffic must come to a complete stop at the stop line before crossing the level crossing.

pages.title: 7.3-61 B
pages.text: The supplementary traffic sign “Electrified track” is used where there are live wires at the level crossing. The distance indicated on the sign specifies the safe clearance height beneath the live wires.

pages.title: 7.3-62 B
pages.text: The flashing light may display a red flashing light, possibly combined with a bell signal. When the light flashes and the bell sounds, road users must stop at the Stopline, or if there is no Stopline, at a safe distance before the signal.

pages.title: 7.3-63 B
pages.text: The “Other danger” warning sign with the “Track” Supplementary traffic sign indicates that there is a level crossing where railway staff will warn road users with a flag, signal lamp or by other means when a train is approaching the crossing.

pages.title: 7.3-64 B
pages.text: The “Roundabout” warning sign warns of a Roundabout up ahead.

pages.title: 7.3-65 B
pages.text: The “Other danger” warning sign always has a Supplementary traffic sign describing the type of danger, typically a danger not covered by the other warning signs.

pages.title: 7.3-66 B
pages.text: The warning sign indicates that there is a "Danger". The reason is always stated on a Supplementary traffic sign.

pages.title: 7.3-67 B
pages.text: The "Rockfall" warning sign indicates that there is danger of falling rocks on the roadway.

pages.title: 7.3-68 BBE
pages.text: The “Crosswind” warning sign is placed at particularly exposed locations such as bridges and embankments, where strong crosswinds may occur and risk blowing the vehicle off course, especially at high speed.

pages.title: 7.3-69 B
pages.text: The “Crosswind” warning sign may be supplemented by a wind sock at locations where there is a risk of strong crosswinds.

pages.title: 7.3-70 B
pages.text: The "Traffic Light" warning sign is erected where the signal may be difficult to see.

pages.title: 7.3-71 B
pages.text: The “Harbour Quay” warning sign marks a ferry berth, quay or similar. The sign is normally placed right at the edge of the quay or similar area.

pages.title: 7.3-72 B
pages.text: The "Lifting Bridge" warning sign is found at bridges that can be opened. In front of the bridge, there is a double flashing red stop signal, which is activated to inform Road users to stop before the Stopline or, if there is no Stopline, at a safe distance from the signal.

pages.title: 7.3-73 B
