pages.text: The warning sign "Crosswalk" warns of a crosswalk up ahead.

pages.title: 7.3-74 B
pages.text: The “Crosswalk” information sign is located at the crosswalk itself. It may be suspended and supplemented with a yellow flashing light or placed at the edge of the Roadway.

pages.title: 7.3-75 B
pages.text: The “Crosswalk” information sign may be mounted on a blue and white post to highlight the location of the crosswalk.

children.title: 7.6 Driving past stationary vehicles and pedestrians etc.

pages.title: 7.6-1 B
pages.text: There are many collisions involving stationary vehicles, particularly on the right-hand side of the road, and there are also a number of accidents involving cars or road users setting off from the roadside just as you are passing them. Other parties involved are pedestrians, particularly the elderly and children who step out onto the Roadway, partially obscured by a stationary vehicle.

pages.title: 7.6-2 BBE
pages.text: When passing stationary vehicles, you must ensure you maintain an appropriately low speed and a safe Side distance.

pages.title: 7.6-3 BBE
pages.text: You should be alert to pedestrians who may step out onto the road behind the parked car.

pages.title: 7.6-4 B
pages.text: People in a stationary car may pose a hazard.

pages.title: 7.6-5 B
pages.text: In this situation, there is a risk that the side door of the parked car may suddenly open. If necessary, you can signal your intention to overtake whilst being ready to brake.

pages.title: 7.6-6 B
pages.text: Visible exhaust fumes, illuminated brake lights and perhaps Blinkers may indicate that the driver is preparing to drive off.

pages.title: 7.6-7 B
pages.text: The sign indicates that the bicycle lane ends and cyclists and small mopeds are joining the Roadway.

pages.title: 7.6-8 B
pages.text: The supplementary traffic sign warns of the risk of cyclists crossing the roadway.

pages.title: 7.6-9 B
pages.text: When a cyclist is standing at the side of the road with one foot on the pedal, this may be a sign that they are ready to set off.

pages.title: 7.6-10 B
pages.text: When cyclists and moped riders set off from the roadside, you should be aware of their tendency to swerve.

pages.title: 7.6-11 BBE
pages.text: When passing pedestrians at the roadside, you should keep a good side distance to ensure they have the necessary space.

pages.title: 7.6-12 B
pages.text: In poor road conditions or similar situations, you should adjust your speed so that others are not splashed as far as possible.

pages.title: 7.6-13 BBE
pages.text: When passing pedestrians at an intersection, you must give them time to cross and avoid driving too close to them.

pages.title: 7.6-14 B
pages.text: The sign warns of children and is placed near schools, after-school clubs, playgrounds and similar areas.

pages.title: 7.6-15 B
pages.text: Children can often be impulsive and unpredictable in traffic, especially when in groups. It is therefore important to drive slowly and keep a safe distance from them.

pages.title: 7.6-16 B
pages.text: When school crossing patrols are on duty, drivers must respect their signals and either slow down or stop if the patrol is helping pupils cross the road. When approaching an area where the school crossing patrol is working, you must drive slowly enough to clearly signal that you intend to slow down.

pages.title: 7.6-17 B
pages.text: When school crossing patrols are on duty, a warning sign regarding children may be in place, supplemented by two alternating flashing yellow lights.

pages.title: 7.6-18 B
pages.text: The warning sign indicates that there may be pedestrians on the road and is placed particularly in areas with restricted visibility.

pages.title: 7.6-19 BBE
pages.text: When approaching a rider or a horse-drawn vehicle from behind, you should adjust your speed in good time and, whilst overtaking, maintain a steady speed and keep a considerable side distance.

pages.title: 7.6-20 B
pages.text: The sign warns that there may be wildlife on the roadway. There is often a supplementary traffic sign indicating the length of the stretch to which the warning applies.

pages.title: 7.6-21 B
pages.text: The sign warns of daily cattle crossings and is placed in areas with poor visibility.

pages.title: 7.6-22 B
pages.text: The sign warns of Road Construction.

pages.title: 7.6-23 BBE
pages.text: When driving past Road Construction, it is important to maintain a suitably low speed and keep a safe distance from the Road Construction.

pages.title: 7.6-24 B
pages.text: The sign warns of a crosswalk and is placed where it may be difficult to spot the crosswalk in good time, as well as in places where one would not immediately expect a crosswalk to be located.

pages.title: 7.6-25 B
pages.text: An information sign is placed on both sides of the Roadway at the crosswalk.

pages.title: 7.6-26 B
pages.text: The information sign may be mounted on a blue and white striped pedestrian post to clarify the location of the Crosswalk.

pages.title: 7.6-27 B
pages.text: The information sign may hang over the Crosswalk and may be fitted with a yellow flashing light.

pages.title: 7.6-28 B
pages.text: When approaching a crosswalk, you should keep an eye out for pedestrians. If there are no pedestrians at or in the crosswalk, you may continue driving.

pages.title: 7.6-29 BBE
pages.text: If there are pedestrians, you must slow down and approach the crosswalk at a suitably low speed so that pedestrians who are either already in the crosswalk or about to step into it can see that you intend to stop.

pages.title: 7.6-30 BBE
pages.text: If there are pedestrians in the crossing or clearly stepping into it, you must not pose any danger or inconvenience to them. This means that you must not force pedestrians to stop or change their speed whilst crossing the Roadway.

pages.title: 7.6-31 B
pages.text: It is important to be aware that pedestrians often choose to cross the road right next to the crosswalk if they feel that using the crosswalk involves a slight detour.

pages.title: 7.6-32 BBE
pages.text: Traffic approaching a bus stop in a built-up area where a bus is stationary must reduce its speed and, if necessary, stop completely if the bus signals with its blinkers that it is about to move off so that it can leave the stop.

pages.title: 7.6-33 B
pages.text: When approaching a bus stationary at a bus stop, you must adjust your speed and look for signs that the bus is about to move off. For example, whether the brake lights have stopped flashing, whether the driver is looking in their wing mirror, or similar. If the left-hand blinkers come on, you may need to stop completely to allow the bus to pull out from the bus stop.

pages.title: 7.6-34 B
pages.text: When approaching a bus that is either pulling into a bus stop or is already stopped there, you should be aware of pedestrians crossing the road to catch the bus.

pages.title: 7.6-35 B
pages.text: When passing a bus that is stopped at a bus stop, you should be aware of passengers crossing the road both in front of and behind the bus.

pages.title: 7.6-36 B
pages.text: School bus signs with yellow flashing lights must be fitted to the front and rear of vehicles used as school buses or similar for transporting children to and from school. The flashing lights warn that children may be crossing the Roadway to or from the bus.

pages.title: 7.7-1 B
pages.text: Many accidents occur in meeting situations on narrow two-lane roads. The other parties involved are often cars and vans, but a number of trucks and two-wheeled vehicles are also involved. In addition, many collisions occur with oncoming traffic that is overtaking, turning or reversing, as well as with pedestrians at the roadside.

pages.title: 7.7-2 B
pages.text: Broken long lines indicate poor visibility and are used as a centre line on narrow roads.

pages.title: 7.7-3 B
pages.text: The broken long lines serve as a warning of an approaching solid line. When crossing a broken long line, it is important to be extra vigilant. Driving over the centre of the road always poses a risk to oncoming traffic and should therefore be avoided or at least kept to a minimum.

pages.title: 7.7-4 B
pages.text: The solid line must not be crossed unless special circumstances, such as Road Construction or illegally parked vehicles, make it necessary.

pages.title: 7.7-5 BBE
pages.text: The warning sign “Oncoming traffic” is erected where a one-way road ends and the median ceases. This means that in situations where vehicles meet, there is a risk of coming into close proximity with oncoming traffic.

pages.title: 7.7-6 BBE
pages.text: When you encounter oncoming traffic on narrow roads, it is a good idea to slow down and keep to the right to create sufficient distance. Avoid looking directly at the oncoming vehicle, as this may cause you to unconsciously turn in their direction. Instead, focus your gaze on the centre of the open Roadway to maintain stable steering.

pages.title: 7.7-7 BBE
pages.text: When passing large vehicles, be aware of the wind turbulence they can create, as this can cause you to be blown off course.

pages.title: 7.7-8 BBE
pages.text: When approaching a bend, you must adjust your speed to avoid crossing the centre of the road due to centrifugal force.

pages.title: 7.7-9 BBE
pages.text: When approaching a curved road, be aware that oncoming traffic may cut the corner and come close to or cross the centre of the road. It is therefore important to slow down to avoid meeting in the middle of the curved road, where the risk of a collision is greatest.

pages.title: 7.7-10 BBE
pages.text: On narrow roads without road markings, there is a risk that oncoming traffic may cross the centre of the road due to high speed. You should therefore adjust your speed to avoid meeting oncoming traffic precisely where, after the bend, they are closest to the centre of the road.

pages.title: 7.7-11 B
pages.text: On slippery and greasy roads, there is a greater risk that oncoming traffic will come closer to or cross the centre of the road, compared with a dry road surface.

pages.title: 7.7-12 B
pages.text: In this situation, you should be aware that oncoming traffic may move closer to the centre of the road to avoid the puddle at the side of the road.

pages.title: 7.7-13 B
pages.text: If the kerb is uneven or full of potholes, you should expect oncoming traffic to keep a distance from the kerb and therefore may come closer to the centre of the road.

pages.title: 7.7-14 B
pages.text: Large vehicles such as buses, trucks and truck and trailers are very stable in their direction of travel and require plenty of space when cornering. Consequently, they often end up close to or over the centre of the road when negotiating a bend. It is important to avoid situations where you meet them whilst they are close to the centre of the road.

pages.title: 7.7-15 B
pages.text: Motorcycles are generally not very stable in terms of direction, but larger and heavier motorcycles have better directional stability than smaller and lighter models. This can increase the risk in oncoming traffic situations, especially just before and during bends.

pages.title: 7.7-16 B
pages.text: Particularly when emerging from a sheltered area, strong crosswinds can easily push you off course.

pages.title: 7.7-17 B
pages.text: When a car is reversing out of a driveway, you should expect oncoming traffic to approach the centre of the road.

pages.title: 7.7-18 BBE
pages.text: For example, when on hills or in bends you encounter a slow-moving tractor with a line of cars behind it, which have long been unable to overtake, you should expect that one or more oncoming vehicles behind the tractor will pull out towards the centre of the road to overtake.

pages.title: 7.7-19 B
pages.text: You should also be prepared for the oncoming traffic to move towards the centre of the road to overtake, well before the cyclist.

pages.title: 7.7-20 B
pages.text: If you encounter a cyclist in your lane, you must adjust your speed to avoid passing both the oncoming traffic and the cyclist at the same time. If it is not possible to overtake the cyclist before the encounter, you should slow down and stay behind the cyclist until the oncoming traffic has passed.

pages.title: 7.7-21 B
pages.text: The sign indicates that the road narrows on the right-hand side.

pages.title: 7.7-22 B
pages.text: The sign indicates that the road narrows on the left-hand side.

pages.title: 7.7-23 B
pages.text: Here, the sign indicates that the road narrows on both sides.

pages.title: 7.7-24 BBE
pages.text: The supplementary traffic sign indicates the maximum width available on the roadway.

pages.title: 7.7-25 BBE
pages.text: Traffic whose half of the carriageway is blocked must give way to oncoming traffic.

pages.title: 7.7-26 B
pages.text: In situations where oncoming traffic encounters an obstruction in their lane, it is the oncoming traffic that must give way. However, it is important to be aware that the oncoming traffic will often move towards the centre of the road well before reaching the obstruction.

pages.title: 7.7-27 B
pages.text: In a situation where the road narrows on both sides, the driver who reaches the narrowing last must give way to the oncoming traffic that is closest to the narrowing.

pages.title: 7.7-28 BBE
pages.text: The sign indicates that you may only enter the stretch of road if you can do so without forcing oncoming traffic to stop.

pages.title: 7.7-29 BBE
pages.text: The information sign indicates that oncoming traffic must give way, as they have the sign ‘Give way to oncoming traffic’.

pages.title: 7.7-30 B
pages.text: The “Give way to oncoming traffic” sign is erected in connection with Road Construction in the oncoming traffic lane, and therefore overrides the rule in the Road Traffic Act that drivers whose lane is blocked must give way.

pages.title: 7.7-31 B
pages.text: The information sign “oncoming traffic must give way” is placed at Road Construction in one’s own lane and therefore overrides the rule in the Road Traffic Act that the driver whose lane is blocked must give way.

pages.title: 7.7-32 BBE
pages.text: This prohibition sign prohibits vehicles with a width, including load, exceeding the limit specified on the sign from proceeding.

pages.title: 7.7-33 BBE
pages.text: Lane signals regulate the direction of traffic on reversible (two-way) lanes. They may display a red cross, a yellow diagonal arrow or a green arrow, which hangs over the relevant lane. An intersection with a red cross means that driving in that lane is prohibited. A yellow flashing diagonal arrow indicates that you must change lanes as soon as possible in the direction the arrow points. A green arrow indicates that the lane is open to traffic.

pages.title: 7.7-34 BBE
pages.text: Lane signals help to direct traffic into specific lanes or stop it completely. If the signal shows a red cross, drivers must move into an open lane. If no lane is open, they must stop immediately.

children.title: 7.8 Driving ahead of or behind other vehicles

pages.title: 7.8-1 B
pages.text: Traffic must not unnecessarily disrupt the normal flow of traffic by driving at an extremely low speed without reasonable cause. This means that, as far as possible, you should maintain the average speed or the highest permitted and safe speed on that stretch of road.

pages.title: 7.8-2 BBE
pages.text: The distance to the Vehicle in front must be sufficient to ensure there is no risk of a collision if the Vehicle in front reduces speed or stops. This means that you must maintain a distance of at least 2 seconds from the Vehicle in front.

pages.title: 7.8-3 B
pages.text: You calculate the distance to the Vehicle in front by starting to count “twenty-one, twenty-two” when the Vehicle in front passes a fixed object, such as a Traffic sign. If you reach the object yourself before you have counted to twenty-two, the distance is too short.

pages.title: 7.8-4 BBE
pages.text: Vehicles with special speed limits, such as buses, lorries and cars with trailers, must maintain an additional safety distance outside built-up areas. This is to allow space for an overtaking vehicle to pull in between the slow-moving vehicle and the vehicle in front.

pages.title: 7.8-5 B
pages.text: To ensure that a 2-second distance from the Vehicle in front is sufficient, it is important not only to keep your eyes on the car in front, but also to look as far ahead on the road as possible. Keep an eye on road and traffic conditions further ahead so that you can react in good time to potential dangers.

pages.title: 7.8-6 BBE
pages.text: When driving behind a vehicle that obstructs your view ahead, it is therefore necessary to maintain a distance of more than 2 seconds.

pages.title: 7.8-7 BBE
pages.text: In conditions of reduced visibility, such as heavy rain or fog, a 2-second distance from the Vehicle in front is not sufficient. In such cases, you should maintain a greater distance.

pages.title: 7.8-8 BBE
pages.text: On slippery and greasy roads, a 2-second distance from the Vehicle in front is also insufficient; here too, you must maintain a greater distance.

pages.title: 7.8-9 BBE
pages.text: When approaching a hilltop with limited visibility, you must be prepared for the vehicle in front to suddenly slow down. It is therefore important to increase the distance to the vehicle in front whilst driving up the hill.

pages.title: 7.8-10 B
pages.text: When approaching a curved road, you must be prepared for the Vehicle in front to suddenly slow down. It is therefore important to maintain a greater distance from the Vehicle in front when approaching the curved road.

pages.title: 7.8-11 B
pages.text: When approaching an intersection, you must be prepared for the Vehicle in front to slow down suddenly, either because of crossing traffic or because the driver is braking to turn at the Intersection. It is therefore important to increase the distance to the Vehicle in front when approaching the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.8-12 B
pages.text: When approaching a level crossing, you must be prepared for the signals to change suddenly or for a train to approach, which may cause the Vehicle in front to brake abruptly.

pages.title: 7.8-13 B
pages.text: When approaching a parked vehicle at the side of the road, you should increase the distance to the Vehicle in front to ensure a sufficient Safety distance in case it brakes suddenly.

pages.title: 7.8-14 B
pages.text: When approaching traffic lights, you should increase the distance to the car in front to ensure you have enough space if the lights change and the Vehicle in front brakes suddenly.

pages.title: 7.8-15 B
pages.text: When approaching a traffic light-controlled intersection with a green light, you should ensure there is sufficient distance to the vehicle behind you in case you need to brake due to the signal turning amber.

pages.title: 7.8-16 B
pages.text: If you are so close to the Stopline when the light changes to amber that there is a risk of being hit by the vehicle behind you if you brake, you must continue into the Intersection, even though an amber light means stop.

pages.title: 7.8-17 B
pages.text: When approaching an area where children are present or moving about near the road, you should reduce your speed and increase the distance to the Vehicle in front. This allows you to react in the event that the children’s behaviour causes the Vehicle in front to brake.

pages.title: 7.8-18 B
pages.text: When driving behind a driver who is unfamiliar with the area, you should expect that they may find it difficult to orientate themselves and may therefore suddenly make unexpected manoeuvres such as braking, changing lanes or turning. It is therefore important to maintain a safety distance of more than 2 seconds.

pages.title: 7.8-19 B
pages.text: It is important to check your mirrors regularly and only briefly, so that you are always aware of the distance, speed and intentions of the vehicle behind you. If the distance is insufficient, this may be because your own speed is not adapted to the conditions and may be too low, in which case you need to increase your speed.

pages.title: 7.8-20 B
pages.text: If a truck or bus, which has poorer braking performance than a passenger car, is close behind, it is dangerous to brake suddenly. If it is not possible to increase your speed, you should keep as far to the right of the road as possible so that the vehicle behind can overtake.

pages.title: 7.8-21 B
pages.text: If a vehicle behind you starts to overtake, you must not increase your speed. You should keep as far to the right of the road as possible to make overtaking easier.

pages.title: 7.8-22 B
pages.text: When being overtaken, there is a risk that the overtaking vehicle may pull in sharply in front of you, leaving an insufficient safety distance.

pages.title: 7.8-23 B
pages.text: When traffic is moving at low speed or in a wide vehicle, such as a car with a Caravan, on a narrow or winding road, you must be extra vigilant of vehicles behind you. You can make overtaking easier by slowing down, pulling right over to the side or, if necessary, stopping.

pages.title: 7.8-24 BBE
pages.text: If the roadway is marked with a wide solid side line and there is no dedicated lane to the right of it, it is permitted to cross the solid side line whilst driving at low speed or in a particularly wide vehicle to facilitate overtaking.

pages.title: 7.8-25 B
pages.text: The sign indicates that there is a particular risk of traffic congestion.

pages.title: 7.8-26 B
pages.text: When driving in traffic congestion, it is particularly important to maintain a suitable safety distance from the vehicle in front, as there is a high risk of a pile-up if the vehicle in front brakes suddenly.

pages.title: 7.8-27 B
pages.text: You must maintain a safe safety distance from the vehicle in front, which usually means a time gap of around two seconds under normal conditions. However, the distance should be increased if road and traffic conditions, weather or road surface conditions require it.

pages.title: 7.4-1 BBE
pages.text: When changing your position on the roadway, either to prepare for a turn or because the number of lanes is reduced, the manoeuvre can often seem surprising, as other Traffic users expect you to stay in your lane. Depending on the conditions, there are two different rules that apply when changing your position: the rule for changing lanes or the merging rule.

pages.title: 7.4-2 B
pages.text: When changing lanes, there must be enough space so that others are not inconvenienced. Vehicles approaching from behind must not be forced to brake. Check the traffic well in advance, indicate well in advance, change lanes calmly and cancel the indicator once the lane change is complete.

pages.title: 7.4-3 B
pages.text: Where the merging rule applies, you must adjust your speed to the traffic in the parallel lane and use a suitable gap to merge. Drivers in the other lane must facilitate the merge by, for example, adjusting their speed and thereby creating space.

pages.title: 7.4-4 BBE
pages.text: On roads where the roadway is divided into lanes by means of road markings, a lane change is made when crossing the lane lines.

pages.title: 7.4-5 BBE
pages.text: Here, the lane is blocked by a stationary vehicle. A lane change must be made at the intersection to drive past the stationary car.

pages.title: 7.4-6 BBE
pages.text: Here, the innermost part of the roadway is also blocked by a stationary vehicle. Even though the roadway is not divided into lanes by lane markings, there are as many lanes as there is room for rows of four-wheeled vehicles. The rule on changing lanes therefore applies when passing the passenger car.

pages.title: 7.4-7 BBE
pages.text: Here, the innermost lane is blocked by Road Construction. Even though there are no marked lane lines, the rule on changing lanes also applies here.

pages.title: 7.4-8 B
pages.text: The warning sign indicates that the road narrows further ahead, but it does not specify whether the lane-change rule or the merging rule applies. It is the roadway markings that determine which rule to use.

pages.title: 7.4-9 BBE
pages.text: Where the number of lanes decreases and the road markings continue through to the narrowing, the lane-change rule must be followed.

pages.title: 7.4-10 B
pages.text: Here, the lane markings continue all the way to the Hatched road markings, so you must follow the rule for changing lanes.

pages.title: 7.4-11 B
pages.text: The arrows here indicate that the lane is about to end, but the arrows do not indicate which rule applies when the lane ends; it is the lane markings that determine this.

pages.title: 7.4-12 B
pages.text: In some cases, an information sign may be erected showing how the lane configuration will be further ahead. It also indicates that drivers must follow the rules for changing lanes, which can be clearly seen from the lane markings on the sign.

pages.title: 7.4-13 BBE
pages.text: Here, the information sign indicates that the left-hand lane ends 200 m further ahead and that the rules for changing lanes must be followed.

pages.title: 7.4-14 B
pages.text: Some acceleration lanes are marked by a wide dotted edge line that runs all the way to the end of the lane. Traffic in the acceleration lane must follow the rules for changing lanes when it crosses the wide edge line. In some cases, the lane to the right of the edge line may be a combined entry and exit lane; in such cases, traffic wishing to move into the exit lane must also follow the rules for changing lanes, without causing danger or unnecessary inconvenience.

pages.title: 7.4-15 B
pages.text: Before changing lanes, you must ensure that this can be done without causing danger or unnecessary inconvenience. Even if the side mirror appears clear, you must check your blind spots by turning your head before changing lanes.

pages.title: 7.4-16 BBE
pages.text: Where the number of lanes is reduced and there are no lane markings, or where the lane markings cease before the narrowing, the merging rule must be followed. Here, you must adjust your speed to match that of the traffic in the adjacent lane and allow sufficient space to merge. Traffic in the adjacent lane must assist the vehicle wishing to merge, for example by adjusting their speed to make room.

pages.title: 7.4-17 B
pages.text: Here the lane markings end, and therefore the merging rule applies as you approach the narrowing.

pages.title: 7.4-18 B
pages.text: Here, the roadway is not divided at all by lane markings; the merging rule applies here too.

pages.title: 7.4-19 BBE
pages.text: In some cases, an information sign may be erected showing how the lanes will be arranged further ahead. The sign also indicates that the merging rule must be followed, as there are no lane markings on the sign.

pages.title: 7.4-20 B
pages.text: The arrow indicates that the left-hand lane ends. It is clear from the information sign and the end of the lane markings that the merge rule applies at the narrowing. Please note that if you change to the right-hand lane before the narrowing, you must follow the rules for changing lanes.

pages.title: 7.4-21 B
pages.text: The information sign regarding the merge rule may also look like this.

pages.title: 7.4-22 BBE
pages.text: Where two roadways merge without the wide broken edge line being carried through, the merging rule also applies.

pages.title: 7.4-23 BBE
pages.text: This information sign indicates that two roadways merge and that, with due regard for other road users, drivers must follow the merging rule.

pages.title: 7.4-24 B
pages.text: Where merging is mandatory, traffic must merge, showing due consideration to others, if necessary by adjusting their speed. Well in advance of the lanes merging, check your wing mirrors and blind spots to ensure it is safe to merge with traffic approaching from behind.

pages.title: 7.4-25 BBE
pages.text: The information sign indicates that the road is equipped with a Crawler lane.

pages.title: 7.4-26 BBE
pages.text: Vehicles that cannot travel at least at the speed indicated on the round regulatory sign must use the Crawler lane. The speed indicated as the minimum speed outside the Crawler lane is the maximum speed within the Crawler lane. When crossing the wide dotted edge line marking the boundary of the Crawler lane, the rules for changing lanes must be followed.

pages.title: 7.4-27 BBE
pages.text: Where the Crawler lane ends, the design of the wide edge line determines whether there is an obligation to merge or whether the rules for changing lanes must be followed. Here, the information sign indicates that you must change lanes when leaving the Crawler lane at the top of the hill.

pages.title: 7.10-1 BCDCE
pages.text: Rumble strips are narrow, noise-producing strips across the driving direction, indicating that you must exercise particular caution.

pages.title: 7.10-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: The sign indicates that you are entering an area with speed-reducing measures such as speed bumps or road narrowings, where it is typically not possible to drive faster than the specified speed.

pages.title: 7.10-3 BCDCE
pages.text: The specified speed in speed-reducing zones may vary depending on the speed-reducing measures in place.

pages.title: 7.10-4 BCDCE
pages.text: Square boxes across the direction of travel indicate that there are speed bumps on the road.

pages.title: 7.10-5 BCDCE
pages.text: However, speed bumps are not always marked with these square panels.

pages.title: 7.10-6 BCDCE
pages.text: Speed-reducing measures may also include road narrowings and chicanes.

pages.title: 7.10-7 BCDCE
pages.text: Speed-reducing measures may also consist of a combination of road narrowings and Speed bumps.

pages.title: 7.10-8 BCDCE
pages.text: The sign indicates that you are leaving an area with speed-reducing measures.

pages.title: 7.10-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: The sign indicates that motor vehicles must give way to people resting and playing, including both children and adults, and driving is normally restricted to speeds below 15 km/h. Parking is only permitted in the specially marked spaces.

pages.title: 7.10-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: The sign indicates that the play and recreation area ends. When leaving a play and recreation area, you have a duty to give way to all traffic.

pages.title: 7.10-11 BCDBECE
pages.text: The ‘Bicycle Lane’ sign indicates an area where the roadway is reserved for bicycles and small Mopeds.

pages.title: 7.10-12 BCDBECE
pages.text: The ‘Bicycle Street’ sign with a Supplementary traffic sign permitting local traffic for other vehicles is permitted. Vehicles must travel at the same speed as cyclists and moped riders, which is normally under 30 km/h. All road users must exercise extra care and consideration for one another and must not unnecessarily obstruct traffic flow. Parking in a cycle lane is only permitted in specially marked spaces.

pages.title: 7.10-13 BCDCE
pages.text: The sign indicates the end of a cycle street.

pages.title: 7.10-14 BCDBECE
pages.text: The sign indicates that this is a pedestrian zone where driving is prohibited, as the area is reserved for pedestrians.

pages.title: 7.10-15 BCDCE
pages.text: A pedestrian zone may also be marked with the traffic sign “No entry in either direction” with a Supplementary traffic sign indicating that it is a pedestrian zone.

pages.title: 7.10-16 BCDBECE
pages.text: A supplementary traffic sign may indicate that driving into a pedestrian zone is permitted at certain times. Driving must only take place at very low speeds, typically under 15 km/h, and parking is only permitted in the specially marked spaces.

pages.title: 7.10-17 BCDBECE
pages.text: The sign indicates that the pedestrian street ends. When driving out of a pedestrian street, you have the duty to give way to all traffic.

pages.title: 7.10-18 BCDBECE
pages.text: When driving on or crossing a pedestrian zone, the driver must ensure that pedestrians do not enter the vehicle’s danger zone, and driving may only continue once the pedestrians have made way.

pages.title: 7.10-19 BCDCE
pages.text: The sign simply indicates that an environmental road has been constructed, where there may be pedestrian crossings, medians or similar obstacles on the Roadway. No special traffic rules apply within the area.

pages.title: 7.11-1 B
pages.text: When two vehicles are travelling in opposite directions at an uncontrolled traffic light-controlled intersection, there are clear rules about who must give way. Either one road user has a duty to give way to all traffic, or the right-of-way rule applies.

pages.title: 7.11-2 B
pages.text: Where the right-of-way rule applies, you must give way to traffic from the right whilst ensuring that traffic from the left complies with its duty to give way. You may only proceed when doing so poses no danger or inconvenience to traffic from the right.

pages.title: 7.11-3 B
pages.text: There are several different traffic signs indicating a duty to give way to all traffic, such as ‘Full Stop’ and the ‘Give Way’ sign. The ‘Give Way’ sign may also have a supplementary traffic sign describing special conditions.

pages.title: 7.11-4 B
pages.text: When approaching a full stop Intersection, there may be a warning marking on the Roadway indicating that you must come to a complete stop at the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-5 B
pages.text: Advance warning of a “Full stop” may also be indicated on a give way sign with a Supplementary traffic sign showing the word “Stop” and the distance to the Intersection where a full stop is required.

pages.title: 7.11-6 BBE
pages.text: Where a "Full Stop" sign is erected, you must come to a complete stop at the Stopline, and you have a Duty to give way to all traffic when entering or crossing the intersecting road.

pages.title: 7.11-7 B
pages.text: Duty to give way to all traffic may be indicated in advance by a triangular symbol, often with a distance marking, painted on the Roadway.

pages.title: 7.11-8 B
pages.text: On certain roads, "rumble strips" have been installed when approaching an Intersection with a Duty to give way to all traffic. Rumble strips are noise-producing strips across the road that signal that you must be extra vigilant.

pages.title: 7.11-9 B
pages.text: Advance warning of the Duty to give way to all traffic may be marked with a give-way sign, where the distance to the give-way point is indicated on a Supplementary traffic sign.

pages.title: 7.11-10 BBE
pages.text: The ‘Duty to give way to all traffic’ sign indicates that you must always give way to traffic approaching from both directions when entering or crossing the road. The give-way sign is usually supplemented by give-way lines, also known as give way lines.

pages.title: 7.11-11 BBE
pages.text: When crossing a two-way bicycle lane, you always have an unconditional duty to give way to all traffic, which is indicated by the "Duty to give way to all traffic" sign and the sub-sign "Two-way bicycle lane".

pages.title: 7.11-12 BBE
pages.text: On minor roads, the Duty to give way to all traffic may be indicated by a Give way line alone.

pages.title: 7.11-13 BBE
pages.text: When driving out of a road and passing a sidewalk, bicycle lane or shoulder that is higher than the roadway of the intersecting road, you have an absolute duty to give way to all traffic. The raised level may be indicated by the sidewalk continuing across the crossing, or by the crossing being surfaced with a material that is clearly distinct from the side road. The crossing may also be narrower than the usual width of the road.

pages.title: 7.11-14 BBE
pages.text: When driving out of a road and crossing a Sidewalk, you must not only give way but also ensure you give way to pedestrians walking on the Sidewalk.

pages.title: 7.11-15 BBE
pages.text: When exiting a petrol station or similar area outside the normal road network, you also have a duty to give way to all traffic.

pages.title: 7.11-16 BBE
pages.text: When exiting a car park, you also have a duty to give way to all traffic.

pages.title: 7.11-17 BBE
pages.text: When driving from a footpath, Dirt road, gravel road or other clearly minor roads, you always have a duty to give way to all traffic.

pages.title: 7.11-18 BBE
pages.text: Traffic leaving a property or plot of land always has a duty to give way to all traffic. They must also ensure they give way to pedestrians on the road they are joining.

pages.title: 7.11-19 BBE
pages.text: When exiting a pedestrianised street, traffic has an unconditional duty to give way to all traffic.

pages.title: 7.11-20 BBE
pages.text: When driving out of a playground or recreational area, you also have a Duty to give way to all traffic.

pages.title: 7.11-21 B
pages.text: If visibility at an intersection with a Duty to give way to all traffic is such that you can properly assess the traffic situation whilst moving forward, you do not need to come to a complete stop unless traffic conditions require it.

pages.title: 7.11-22 B
pages.text: When approaching a junction where you have to give way, you must adjust your speed so that it is clear to other road users that you have to give way and will hold back.

pages.title: 7.11-23 B
pages.text: If necessary to get a clear view of both sides of the crossing road, you may drive slightly over the give way lines until you have a sufficient view.

pages.title: 7.11-24 B
pages.text: If pedestrians are crossing the roadway, you must give them time to cross before driving right up to the give-way line.

pages.title: 7.11-25 B
pages.text: If you have a Duty to give way to all traffic at an Intersection with a Crosswalk, you should, where possible, avoid stopping in the Crosswalk when giving way, unless it is necessary to gain a clear view of the traffic.

pages.title: 7.11-26 BBE
pages.text: At blind intersections such as this, where road users on the intersecting road have a duty to give way to all traffic, you should not assume that they will necessarily comply with their duty to give way – especially children on bicycles. It is therefore important to take your foot off the accelerator in good time and position your foot ready to brake, whilst looking to both sides, before proceeding into the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-27 B
pages.text: When driving behind other vehicles and approaching a junction, you must ensure you maintain a greater distance from the car in front well in advance, as it may suddenly brake for crossing traffic.

pages.title: 7.11-28 B
pages.text: If the car in front indicates shortly before an Intersection, be aware that this may signal that it is turning into a driveway or similar before the Intersection itself.

pages.title: 7.11-29 BBE
pages.text: If none of the traffic has a duty to give way to all traffic, the right-of-way rule applies, which means you must give way to traffic coming from the right. At the same time, you must ensure that traffic from the left observes their right of way.

pages.title: 7.11-30 BBE
pages.text: The right-of-way rule also applies in places where road markings are not visible, e.g. due to snowy weather or similar conditions.

pages.title: 7.11-31 B
pages.text: At this intersection, you must give way to traffic coming from the right. It may be tempting to carry on driving when road users from the side road have slowed down significantly before turning.

pages.title: 7.11-32 B
pages.text: When approaching a T-junction from a side road where you must give way to the right, you cannot expect road users on the main road to necessarily comply with their duty to give way.

pages.title: 7.11-33 BBE
pages.text: The sign "Dangerous Intersection" means that crossing traffic has a Duty to give way to all traffic, but it can often be difficult to get your bearings at the Intersection. You should therefore pay extra attention to crossing traffic, as they may have difficulty complying with their Duty to give way.

pages.title: 7.11-34 B
pages.text: The sign may be placed before a T-junction, and in this case indicates from which direction the crossing traffic is coming.

pages.title: 7.11-35 BBE
pages.text: The ‘Main Road’ sign indicates that you are on a main road, which means that crossing traffic has a Duty to give way to all traffic, unless otherwise indicated by road markings.

pages.title: 7.11-36 BBE
pages.text: The give way sign indicates that the main road ends, meaning that there may be other give way obligations at the upcoming intersections.

pages.title: 7.11-37 BBE
pages.text: The sign indicates that there is a traffic light ahead, particularly in places with poor visibility or where one would not expect to find a traffic light.

pages.title: 7.11-38 B
pages.text: The following types of signals are used: main signals, green-on-red signals, arrow signals for road users travelling in the direction of the arrow, cycle signals for cyclists and small mopeds, pedestrian signals, and bus signals with a white light, which apply only to buses operating under a concession.

pages.title: 7.11-39 B
pages.text: When approaching a traffic light-controlled intersection, it is important to pay attention to the traffic lights and adjust your speed so that you can stop in time if the light turns amber.

pages.title: 7.11-40 B
pages.text: When the traffic light turns amber, this means you must stop, as it indicates that the light will soon turn red. However, you must not stop if there is a risk of being hit from behind.

pages.title: 7.11-41 B
pages.text: When the traffic light is red, vehicles must stop at the stop line.

pages.title: 7.11-42 B
pages.text: When the traffic lights show red and amber simultaneously, this indicates that the lights are about to turn green.

pages.title: 7.11-43 B
pages.text: At some intersections, the traffic lights are designed as arrow signals, where traffic must follow the signal that applies to its intended direction of travel through the intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-44 B
pages.text: A ‘minus green’ signal, also known as a ‘repetition signal’, located in the furthest corner of the Intersection, displays only yellow and red lights. It indicates to drivers turning left at the Intersection which Traffic Light signal oncoming traffic has. When the signal is off, oncoming traffic has a green light.

pages.title: 7.11-45 B
pages.text: The police may direct traffic using hand signals. When one or both arms are stretched out across the driving direction, this means stop. Even if the signal is only given briefly, you must not drive towards the police officer’s back or chest until a clear signal is given.

pages.title: 7.11-46 B
pages.text: When one arm is raised, this means stop in all directions, and the Intersection must be cleared of traffic.

pages.title: 7.11-47 B
pages.text: You may only proceed once the police officer has turned and signalled for traffic in the cross-traffic direction to stop, and has then indicated with a waving motion that you may continue through the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-48 BBE
pages.text: At traffic light-controlled intersections, there may be give-way signs in place, but the sign is irrelevant when the traffic lights are in operation.

pages.title: 7.11-49 BBE
pages.text: Only if the traffic lights are out of order do drivers encountering the give way sign have an unconditional duty to give way at the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-50 BBE
pages.text: The supplementary traffic sign “Light rail” indicates that a light rail line has been constructed on the cross-road, where light rail vehicles are permitted to travel in both directions.

pages.title: 7.11-51 BBE
pages.text: If the traffic lights are out of order and there are no give-way signs giving one direction of traffic the Duty to give way to all traffic applies at the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-52 BBE
pages.text: The supplementary traffic sign indicates that there are a particularly high number of traffic accidents at the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-53 B
pages.text: To enable drivers to familiarise themselves with the lane layout at an Intersection in good time, an information sign stating ‘Lane layout at Intersection’ may be erected before the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-54 B
pages.text: At larger intersections, arrow markings may be displayed above the lanes to indicate the driving directions within the intersection for which the lanes are intended.

pages.title: 7.11-55 B
pages.text: When approaching the Intersection, you must position yourself appropriately in good time in relation to your intended route and the general traffic conditions.

pages.title: 7.11-56 B
pages.text: At the intersection, the roadway is divided into approach lanes by solid lines. It is permitted to change lanes across the lane and broken long lines, but it is not permitted to cross the solid line.

pages.title: 7.11-57 B
pages.text: The wide kerb line demarcates special lanes, e.g. turning lanes. It is only permitted to cross the kerb line where it is broken at an intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-58 B
pages.text: Turning lanes may only be used by traffic intending to turn in the direction of the arrow.

pages.title: 7.11-59 B
pages.text: If the turning lane is marked with double turning arrows, the lane applies to two consecutive intersections.

pages.title: 7.11-60 B
pages.text: The turning lane may be marked with lane arrows indicating a no-turn restriction, showing that it is prohibited to turn at the first Intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-61 B
pages.text: The turning lane may also be a combined bus and turning lane, where the arrow above the word ‘bus’ indicates that the bus proceeds straight ahead at the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-62 B
pages.text: The blue mandatory sign on the right indicates that you must go straight ahead at this Intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-63 B
pages.text: Here, the mandatory sign indicates that you must drive in the direction of the arrow.

pages.title: 7.11-64 B
pages.text: Here, turning right is mandatory at the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-65 B
pages.text: The sign indicates that it is prohibited to turn right at the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-66 B
pages.text: The sign indicates that it is prohibited to turn left at the Intersection, and that no turning is allowed at the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.11-67 B
pages.text: At this Intersection, turning left is mandatory.

pages.title: 7.11-68 B
pages.text: Direction signs help you find your way to geographical destinations, such as ports, airports, places of interest and service facilities. They are located at junctions.

pages.title: 7.11-69 B
pages.text: Exit signs indicate the way to geographical destinations and are placed at the start of an Exit lane.

pages.title: 7.11-70 B
pages.text: Distance signs indicate the distance to the destination, as well as the route number and other information.

pages.title: 7.11-71 B
pages.text: Orientation signs are available as ‘Portal orientation signs’ suspended above the Roadway, ‘Diagram orientation signs’, ‘Lane orientation signs’ and ‘Table orientation signs’, all of which are erected before junctions and provide information on the direction to geographical destinations.

pages.title: 7.11-72 B
pages.text: "Distance signs" are erected particularly after major junctions and indicate the route number and distance to locations.

pages.title: 7.12-1 B
pages.text: Many accidents occur, particularly among young drivers, when driving straight ahead at intersections. The other party is often traffic moving from the right, where many turn left regardless of the Rules for the duty to give way. Almost as often, the other party is coming from the left or is oncoming traffic turning left without giving way. Other parties involved include pedestrians crossing the Roadway both before and after the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.12-2 BBE
pages.text: When approaching an Intersection, it is important not simply to follow the car in front, but instead to ensure you look carefully to both sides before entering the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.12-3 BBE
pages.text: You should not expect drivers at the intersection to always give way. Therefore, at intersections with poor visibility, it is important to adjust your speed and look carefully to both sides before entering the intersection.

pages.title: 7.12-4 B
pages.text: Children and older people on bicycles often find it difficult to assess the situation due to their age. They perceive and react more slowly, which makes it challenging for them to give way.

pages.title: 7.12-5 B
pages.text: When driving behind a cyclist and intending to continue straight ahead through the Intersection, you can expect the cyclist to suddenly turn left at the Intersection without signalling or looking.

pages.title: 7.12-6 B
pages.text: Particularly in bad weather, motorcyclists and moped riders, due to their helmets and goggles, find it difficult to orientate themselves properly and thus struggle to give way.

pages.title: 7.12-7 BBE
pages.text: At this Intersection, there is a right-of-way rule, so it is important to slow down well in advance to clearly show drivers approaching from the right that you are both able and willing to give way to traffic from the right. At the same time, you must look to the left to ensure that drivers approaching from that direction are both able and willing to give way.

pages.title: 7.12-8 B
pages.text: When you have a duty to give way to all traffic, you must slow down to signal to other road users that you are both able and willing to comply with your duty to give way.

pages.title: 7.12-9 BBE
pages.text: When joining a road with a two-way bicycle lane, you always have an unconditional duty to give way to all traffic. It is important to be extra vigilant, as cyclists may approach from both the right and the left.

pages.title: 7.12-10 B
pages.text: When proceeding straight ahead at a large intersection with a wide median and having an unconditional duty to give way to all traffic, it may be a good idea in heavy traffic to move forward to the centre of the intersection when there is a break in the traffic from the left. Here, you can wait for a break in the traffic from the right before continuing across the intersection.

pages.title: 7.12-11 BBE
pages.text: When crossing a road where you have a Duty to give way to all traffic, you may be so focused on the cars that you overlook pedestrians crossing the road on the opposite side of the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.12-12 BBE
pages.text: When driving straight ahead at an Intersection, oncoming traffic intending to turn left must hold back, but you should expect that turning road users may misjudge the traffic situation and turn without due care.

pages.title: 7.12-13 BBE
pages.text: Buses, trucks and trailers take a long time to clear the Intersection when turning.

pages.title: 7.12-14 B
pages.text: If several oncoming traffic vehicles are turning and the vehicle at the front turns, one or more of the vehicles behind may follow the front vehicle without thinking.

pages.title: 7.12-15 BBE
pages.text: Oncoming cyclists turning left may be partially obscured by other oncoming traffic and therefore easy to overlook.

pages.title: 7.12-16 B
pages.text: When proceeding straight ahead at an Intersection, you should position yourself correctly in good time. This means that, taking into account other traffic and the general conditions, you should position yourself as far to the right of the Roadway as possible.

pages.title: 7.12-17 B
pages.text: In this situation, due to the cyclist, it would not be appropriate to position yourself in the far-right lane.

pages.title: 7.12-18 B
pages.text: The passenger car indicating right at the Intersection is driving slowly and is taking a long time to clear the Intersection. Therefore, the correct position when driving straight ahead at this Intersection would be in lane 2, next to the turning car.

pages.title: 7.12-19 B
pages.text: The truck at the intersection is accelerating slowly and driving slowly, so it would be most appropriate to choose lane 2 and drive up alongside the truck.

pages.title: 7.12-20 B
pages.text: If there are parked cars after the Intersection, it is not advisable to choose the far-right lane. Instead, change to lane 2 well in advance of the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.12-21 B
pages.text: Even if the Vehicle in front appears to be going straight ahead at the Intersection, you should be prepared for the possibility that it may turn right immediately after the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.12-22 BBE
pages.text: A red light means stop and indicates that you must stop at the Stopline or at a safe distance from the Intersection if there is no Stopline.

pages.title: 7.12-23 BBE
pages.text: A red/amber light also means stop, but also indicates that the light is about to change to green.

pages.title: 7.12-24 B
pages.text: When approaching traffic lights, you must adjust your speed and pay extra attention to the Traffic Light so that you can adapt your driving to what the Traffic Light shows.

pages.title: 7.12-25 BBE
pages.text: A green light means go, but only if the road is clear.

pages.title: 7.12-26 BBE
pages.text: It is not permitted to proceed when the light is green if heavy, slow-moving traffic prevents you from crossing the entire road before the signal changes. Otherwise, you risk ending up in the middle of the Intersection and blocking cross-traffic.

pages.title: 7.12-27 BBE
pages.text: Even if the light is green at the Intersection, you should be prepared for the possibility that crossing traffic may not observe their Duty to stop.

pages.title: 7.12-28 B
pages.text: A yellow light means stop and indicates that the light is about to turn red.

pages.title: 7.12-29 B
pages.text: You should not stop at a yellow light if you are so far forward that it is not possible to stop at the Stopline, or if you risk being hit by vehicles approaching from behind that are close behind you.

pages.title: 7.12-30 B
pages.text: Signals without a green phase, also known as ‘minus green’ signals, are located in the left-hand corner of an Intersection with an extended green phase for oncoming traffic. They indicate to vehicles turning left, which are waiting in the middle of the Intersection, when the lights will change to amber and red for oncoming traffic.

pages.title: 7.13-1 B
pages.text: When turning right, the main other road users to watch out for are cyclists and moped riders who are continuing straight ahead on the right-hand side of the turning vehicle. Many accidents also occur when a vehicle approaching from behind collides with the vehicle turning right. In addition, accidents occur involving road users approaching from both the right and left at the Intersection – often motorists from the right and cyclists or moped riders from the left. Finally, the driver must be aware of pedestrians crossing the lane into which the vehicle is turning.

pages.title: 7.13-2 BBE
pages.text: When approaching an Intersection and intending to turn right, it is important to check your surroundings well in advance. Look behind you in the Mirrors, check your blind spots, and turn your head to make sure the way is clear. You must then indicate your intention to turn right using the Blinkers.

pages.title: 7.13-3 B
pages.text: When approaching an intersection, you should keep close to the edge of the carriageway or the curb to prevent cyclists and moped riders from overtaking on the right-hand side of the car.

pages.title: 7.13-4 BBE
pages.text: If there are cyclists on the roadway and it is not possible to overtake them safely before reaching the correct position for the right turn, you must pull in behind the cyclists and position yourself close to the Curb to prevent other cyclists approaching from behind from overtaking on the right.

pages.title: 7.13-5 BBE
pages.text: If you are turning right from a road with a Bicycle lane that ends before the junction, it may be necessary to slow down and possibly stop completely at the end of the Bicycle lane. Where it can be done without danger or unnecessary inconvenience to those approaching from behind, you should position yourself behind the cyclist close to the Curb to prevent other cyclists approaching from behind from overtaking on the right.

pages.title: 7.13-6 BBE
pages.text: When turning right from a road with a bicycle lane that continues into the Intersection, you must not create a danger or inconvenience for cyclists going straight ahead. It may therefore be necessary to stop completely before making the right-hand turn.

pages.title: 7.13-7 B
pages.text: Even if you have positioned yourself close to the curb as you approach the Intersection, you must remember to check your mirrors and blind spot to ensure there is All clear to complete the right-hand turn.

pages.title: 7.13-8 BBE
pages.text: When turning right, you must allow pedestrians crossing the Roadway sufficient time to cross the Roadway.

pages.title: 7.13-9 B
pages.text: If there is a crosswalk on the road you are turning into, you must give way to pedestrians in the crosswalk and those who are clearly about to step into it.

pages.title: 7.13-10 B
pages.text: If there are no cyclists approaching from behind, you must drive right up to the crosswalk and stop to let pedestrians cross before making the right-hand turn.

pages.title: 7.13-11 BBE
pages.text: Once the turn is complete, stop signalling and move into the right-hand Roadway, unless you are immediately turning left.

pages.title: 7.13-12 BBE
pages.text: If there is an obstruction in the right-hand lane, e.g. a parked vehicle, you should move into the second lane whilst still turning.

pages.title: 7.13-13 B
pages.text: If there is an obstruction in the lane near the corner and there is oncoming traffic, it may be necessary to wait to make the right turn until the oncoming vehicle has passed the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.13-14 B
pages.text: When turning from a road with high friction onto a road with low friction, where there is a risk of skidding, you must adjust your speed to maintain Road grip.

pages.title: 7.13-15 B
pages.text: When turning right from a road where you have the Duty to give way to all traffic, it is important to assess whether there is enough space in the traffic from the left to complete the turn without forcing other drivers to slow down or change their position.

pages.title: 7.13-16 BBE
pages.text: When approaching a traffic light-controlled intersection and intending to turn right, it is important to pay attention to the traffic lights and the conditions at the intersection. If there is a right-turn lane, you must use this from the start, but it is permitted to change lanes where the solid side line is broken.

pages.title: 7.13-17 BBE
pages.text: If there are several turning lanes, you should choose the one that best suits your route after the right turn under the conditions.

pages.title: 7.13-18 B
pages.text: The right-turn lane may serve as a combined bus and turning lane. The arrow above the word ‘bus’ indicates that the bus is travelling straight ahead through the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.13-19 B
pages.text: The turning lane may be located to the right of a bus lane. In such cases, you must change lanes across the bus lane without causing danger or creating unnecessary inconvenience for the traffic driving in the bus lane.

pages.title: 7.13-20 B
pages.text: The arrow marking here indicates that the turning lane must be used, regardless of whether you are turning right at the first Intersection or at the next one. If you are turning at Intersection number two, you must wait to indicate until you have cleared the first Intersection.

pages.title: 7.13-21 B
pages.text: The arrow marking here indicates that it is prohibited to turn right at the first Intersection.

pages.title: 7.13-22 B
pages.text: When the light is green and you have checked your mirrors and blind spots to ensure All clear, you can proceed with the right-hand turn.

pages.title: 7.13-23 B
pages.text: If you need to give way to cyclists going straight ahead or pedestrians in the crosswalk, you should move forward into the Intersection when the light is green and stop to wait for all clear so that you can complete the right-hand turn.

pages.title: 7.13-24 B
pages.text: When you need to give way to cyclists going straight ahead at an Intersection with Blue bicycle lanes, stop at the edge of the Blue bicycle lane and let the cyclists pass before making your right turn.

pages.title: 7.13-25 B
pages.text: If a traffic light has a green arrow, this means you can make the right-hand turn, as cyclists going straight ahead and crossing pedestrians have a red light.

pages.title: 7.13-26 B
pages.text: Even if there is a green turn arrow, you must still ensure that cyclists going straight ahead stop at the red cycle signal.

pages.title: 7.13-27 B
pages.text: Where there is a two-way bicycle lane, road users turning right must not pose a danger or inconvenience to oncoming traffic of cyclists and moped riders.

pages.title: 7.13-28 B
pages.text: When turning right, you must also be aware of oncoming traffic turning left at the Intersection and assess whether they will give way.

pages.title: 7.13-29 B
pages.text: The sign indicates that it is not permitted to turn right at the first Intersection.

pages.title: 7.13-30 B
pages.text: The sign indicates that it is mandatory to turn right at the first Intersection.

pages.title: 7.13-31 B
pages.text: The sign indicates that it is mandatory to follow the direction of the arrow, i.e. turn right at the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.14-1 B
pages.text: Accidents often occur, particularly among young drivers, when turning left at intersections. The other parties involved are typically oncoming traffic, motorbikes and cyclists, whom the driver turning left fails to give way to. Other potential parties involved may include vehicles approaching from the left and right at the Intersection, vehicles overtaking the driver turning left on the left-hand side, and pedestrians crossing the road into which the driver is turning.

pages.title: 7.14-2 BBE
pages.text: When approaching an Intersection and intending to turn left, it is important to assess the situation well in advance and position yourself correctly, as close to the centre of the Roadway as possible. Remember to indicate with your left Blinkers well in advance. Adjust your speed as you approach the Intersection so that you have time to get a good overview of the situation at the Intersection before turning.

pages.title: 7.14-3 BBE
pages.text: If there is no oncoming traffic and the road to the left is clear, you must check your mirror and blind spot just before turning to ensure that you are not overtaken on the left by a vehicle approaching from behind. When turning left, you must not drive so fast that you lose control of the vehicle.

pages.title: 7.14-4 BBE
pages.text: Drivers making a turn must not cause danger or inconvenience for oncoming traffic. This means that whilst turning, you must not force oncoming traffic to slow down, change driving direction or similar.

pages.title: 7.14-5 BBE
pages.text: Nor must you cause danger or inconvenience for oncoming traffic, including cyclists and moped riders, who are continuing straight ahead through the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.14-6 B
pages.text: If there is oncoming traffic at the Intersection that also needs to turn left, you can choose between two ways of making a left turn: the wide left turn and the tight left turn. In the wide left turn, the turning vehicles drive behind one another, which provides a good view of oncoming traffic. However, this can quickly block the Intersection if there are many vehicles needing to turn left.

pages.title: 7.14-7 B
pages.text: If the traffic can agree, it is legal to perform the flat left turn, where drivers pass each other on the left. The flat left turn is the most common form of left turn, but it can also block the view of those turning, which increases the risk of becoming impatient and turning without looking properly.

pages.title: 7.14-8 B
pages.text: With the flat left turn, there is a particular risk of overlooking cyclists and moped riders, as they often do not take up much space in the traffic scene.

pages.title: 7.14-9 BBE
pages.text: When preparing to turn left, it can be risky to focus so much on the distance and speed of oncoming traffic that you forget to check the side road before turning. A pedestrian crossing the Roadway can result in the left-hand turn ending in an accident.

pages.title: 7.14-10 BBE
pages.text: When turning left, do not blindly follow the car in front, which is also turning. It is important to take the time to look around carefully before completing the left turn.

pages.title: 7.14-11 BBE
pages.text: Where there is a two-way Bicycle lane on the left-hand side of the road, you must not cause danger or inconvenience for cyclists approaching from behind when turning.

pages.title: 7.14-12 B
pages.text: When turning left from the middle of a road without a turning lane or median, you must not turn the front wheels to the left before you actually begin the turn.

pages.title: 7.14-13 B
pages.text: If you have a duty to give way to all traffic at a junction and are turning left, you must give way to oncoming traffic continuing straight through the intersection.

pages.title: 7.14-14 B
pages.text: When turning left at a major traffic light-controlled intersection, you should position yourself well in advance as appropriately as possible in the middle of the road and indicate well in advance.

pages.title: 7.14-15 B
pages.text: When approaching an Intersection with multiple turning lanes, choose the lane that best suits your intended route.

pages.title: 7.14-16 B
pages.text: The arrows in the turning lane indicate that it is illegal to turn left at the first Intersection, and you must only indicate a left turn once you have passed the side road where turning left is prohibited.

pages.title: 7.14-17 B
pages.text: When approaching an intersection, you must decide whether to make a wide or a tight left turn, and, if necessary, make eye contact with the oncoming traffic who is also turning left.

pages.title: 7.14-18 B
pages.text: At some intersections, there are marked turning lanes on the roadway.

pages.title: 7.14-19 B
pages.text: The arrows at this Intersection indicate that you should make a wide left turn.

pages.title: 7.14-20 B
pages.text: Arrows at the intersection may also indicate that you should make a slight left turn.

pages.title: 7.14-21 B
pages.text: If you cannot complete the left turn immediately, drive as far forward into the Intersection as possible without encroaching on the oncoming traffic’s lane.

pages.title: 7.14-22 B
pages.text: When stopping at an Intersection and waiting for a clear passage, it is important to keep an eye on the traffic on the road you are about to turn into. At the same time, you must be aware of pedestrians who may be crossing the road, as well as keeping an eye on the Traffic Lights in the left-hand corner of the Intersection and oncoming traffic.

pages.title: 7.14-23 B
pages.text: You must not start your left turn until you can accelerate out of the Intersection. You must avoid starting your left turn if there are pedestrians you need to give way to, or if there is oncoming traffic turning right that is holding back for pedestrians or cyclists.

pages.title: 7.14-24 BBE
pages.text: When the Traffic Light at the left-hand corner of the Intersection changes, you should not simply start turning left blindly. You must first ensure that oncoming traffic is complying with their Duty to stop before completing the left turn.

pages.title: 7.14-25 BBE
pages.text: If the Traffic Light in the left-hand corner shows only amber or red, it acts as a ‘minus green’ signal, indicating which light oncoming traffic has. If the ‘minus green’ signal is not lit, oncoming traffic still has a green light.

pages.title: 7.14-26 BBE
pages.text: If there is a green arrow signal in the left-hand corner of the intersection, this means that oncoming traffic and pedestrians crossing the road you are turning into have a red light. However, you must still ensure that they have fulfilled their duty to stop before you turn.

pages.title: 7.14-27 B
pages.text: When making a left turn, you should position yourself, taking into account other traffic and general conditions, as far to the right as possible on the road you are turning into, and stop signalling.

pages.title: 7.14-28 BBE
pages.text: The sign indicates that it is not permitted to turn left at the Intersection.

pages.title: 7.14-29 BBE
pages.text: The sign indicates that it is illegal to make a U-turn at the Intersection, but turning left is permitted.

pages.title: 7.15-1 B
pages.text: The most common type of accident at roundabouts occurs when drivers already in the roundabout collide with road users entering it. Many accidents also occur at the entrance, where drivers fail to give way to cyclists and moped riders. Other people involved may be pedestrians crossing the road at the exit from the Roundabout.

pages.title: 7.15-2 B
pages.text: The sign warns of a Roundabout up ahead.

pages.title: 7.15-3 BBE
pages.text: When entering a Roundabout, you always have an unconditional duty to give way to all traffic, which is indicated here by a give-way sign and a give way line.

pages.title: 7.15-4 B
pages.text: The ‘Mandatory driving direction’ sign, located inside the Roundabout, indicates that traffic in the Roundabout is one-way.

pages.title: 7.15-5 B
pages.text: If there is no space for traffic signs on the central island of the Roundabout, the sign "Mandatory driving direction in Roundabout" is placed just before the entrance to the Roundabout.

pages.title: 7.15-6 B
pages.text: In larger Roundabouts, there may be lanes with arrow markings indicating which lane to choose, depending on your destination, as you approach the Roundabout.

pages.title: 7.15-7 B
pages.text: The Roundabout may have traffic lights like a junction, which means you must stop in the Roundabout if the signal turns red.

pages.title: 7.15-8 BBE
pages.text: When you are about to exit onto the first side road from a Roundabout, approach the Roundabout in the right-hand lane and indicate right. Inside the Roundabout, stay in the right-hand lane, continue to indicate right and give way to cyclists and moped riders, as you would when turning right. You should exit the Roundabout when it is safe to do so and without causing any hindrance to cyclists and moped riders who are going straight ahead.

pages.title: 7.15-9 BBE
pages.text: When exiting the Roundabout via a road between the first and last slip roads, choose the lane that best suits the traffic. If you are in lane 2 in the Roundabout, move into the right-hand lane at the slip road before the desired exit. You indicate to turn right, check for cyclists and moped riders as you would for a normal right turn, and exit the Roundabout when it can be done without danger or inconvenience to those continuing straight ahead.

pages.title: 7.15-10 BBE
pages.text: At the final exit from a Roundabout, you should position yourself in the left-hand lane before entering and indicate left if necessary, to assist other road users. Inside the Roundabout, keep to the left-hand lane and move safely into the right-hand lane before the desired exit. You should indicate right, check for cyclists and mopeds as you would when turning right, and leave the Roundabout without causing any inconvenience to those continuing straight ahead.

pages.title: 7.15-11 B
pages.text: When approaching a roundabout, it is important to adjust your speed so that you can get a good overview of the situation in the roundabout and, at the same time, signal to road users already in the roundabout that you are giving way.

pages.title: 7.15-12 B
pages.text: You must only enter the Roundabout when you can do so without causing danger or inconvenience to those already in the Roundabout. Many accidents occur because drivers often misjudge the speed of cyclists and moped riders.

pages.title: 7.15-13 BBE
pages.text: Many accidents occur because drivers entering the Roundabout often misjudge the speed of vehicles approaching from the left within the Roundabout.

pages.title: 7.15-14 BBE
pages.text: Many accidents occur in Roundabouts due to excessive speed, where drivers are unable to maintain the correct position because of the high speed.

pages.title: 7.15-15 BBE
pages.text: Particularly in slippery and greasy conditions, you must drive at low speed to avoid skidding when turning into a Roundabout.

pages.title: 7.15-16 B
pages.text: When changing lanes to move into the right-hand lane before exiting the Roundabout, the lane change must be carried out without causing danger for others or unnecessary inconvenience.

pages.title: 7.15-17 BBE
pages.text: When turning right at a Roundabout, you must ensure that you do not cause danger or inconvenience for cyclists and moped riders who are continuing round the Roundabout.

pages.title: 7.15-18 B
pages.text: When turning right out of a Roundabout, you must also be aware of pedestrians crossing the road you are turning onto.

education.title: Module 4: Advanced theory and practical driving on the road

pages.title: Introduction
pages.text:
Module 4: Advanced theory and practical driving on the road.

The instruction in Module 4 is designed to equip you with the skills to adapt your driving in a safe, considerate, energy-efficient and Environmentally friendly manner to changing traffic conditions and applicable traffic regulations in heavy traffic on various types of roads whilst performing all commonly encountered manoeuvres. The aim of the course is also to provide you with sufficient knowledge of specific risks associated with driving to help you become familiar with your own abilities and to develop a safe attitude and behaviour on the road. You must also acquire knowledge of the conditions for applying to take the driving test and obtaining a Driver's license, as well as familiarise yourself with the most important Legal provisions regarding Driver's licenses.

pages.title: 7.4-1 BBE
pages.text: When changing your position on the roadway, either to prepare for a turn or because the number of lanes is reduced, the manoeuvre can often seem surprising, as other Traffic users expect you to stay in your lane. Depending on the conditions, there are two different rules that apply when changing your position: the rule for changing lanes or the merging rule.

pages.title: 7.4-2 B
pages.text: When changing lanes, there must be enough space so that others are not inconvenienced. Vehicles approaching from behind must not be forced to brake. Check the traffic well in advance, indicate well in advance, change lanes calmly and cancel the indicator once the lane change is complete.

pages.title: 7.4-3 B
pages.text: Where the merging rule applies, you must adjust your speed to the traffic in the parallel lane and use a suitable gap to merge. Drivers in the other lane must facilitate the merge by, for example, adjusting their speed and thereby creating space.

pages.title: 7.4-4 BBE
pages.text: On roads where the roadway is divided into lanes by means of road markings, a lane change is made when crossing the lane lines.

pages.title: 7.4-5 BBE
pages.text: Here, the lane is blocked by a stationary vehicle. A lane change must be made at the intersection to drive past the stationary car.

pages.title: 7.4-6 BBE
pages.text: Here, the innermost part of the roadway is also blocked by a stationary vehicle. Even though the roadway is not divided into lanes by lane markings, there are as many lanes as there is room for rows of four-wheeled vehicles. The rule on changing lanes therefore applies when passing the passenger car.

pages.title: 7.4-7 BBE
pages.text: Here, the innermost lane is blocked by Road Construction. Even though there are no marked lane lines, the rule on changing lanes also applies here.

pages.title: 7.4-8 B
pages.text: The warning sign indicates that the road narrows further ahead, but it does not specify whether the lane-change rule or the merging rule applies. It is the roadway markings that determine which rule to use.

pages.title: 7.4-9 BBE
pages.text: Where the number of lanes decreases and the road markings continue through to the narrowing, the lane-change rule must be followed.

pages.title: 7.4-10 B
pages.text: Here, the lane markings continue all the way to the Hatched road markings, so you must follow the rule for changing lanes.

pages.title: 7.4-11 B
pages.text: The arrows here indicate that the lane is about to end, but the arrows do not indicate which rule applies when the lane ends; it is the lane markings that determine this.

pages.title: 7.4-12 B
pages.text: In some cases, an information sign may be erected showing how the lane configuration will be further ahead. It also indicates that drivers must follow the rules for changing lanes, which can be clearly seen from the lane markings on the sign.

pages.title: 7.4-13 BBE
pages.text: Here, the information sign indicates that the left-hand lane ends 200 m further ahead and that the rules for changing lanes must be followed.

pages.title: 7.4-14 B
pages.text: Some acceleration lanes are marked by a wide dotted edge line that runs all the way to the end of the lane. Traffic in the acceleration lane must follow the rules for changing lanes when it crosses the wide edge line. In some cases, the lane to the right of the edge line may be a combined entry and exit lane; in such cases, traffic wishing to move into the exit lane must also follow the rules for changing lanes, without causing danger or unnecessary inconvenience.

pages.title: 7.4-15 B
pages.text: Before changing lanes, you must ensure that this can be done without causing danger or unnecessary inconvenience. Even if the side mirror appears clear, you must check your blind spots by turning your head before changing lanes.

pages.title: 7.4-16 BBE
pages.text: Where the number of lanes is reduced and there are no lane markings, or where the lane markings cease before the narrowing, the merging rule must be followed. Here, you must adjust your speed to match that of the traffic in the adjacent lane and allow sufficient space to merge. Traffic in the adjacent lane must assist the vehicle wishing to merge, for example by adjusting their speed to make room.

pages.title: 7.4-17 B
pages.text: Here the lane markings end, and therefore the merging rule applies as you approach the narrowing.

pages.title: 7.4-18 B
pages.text: Here, the roadway is not divided at all by lane markings; the merging rule applies here too.

pages.title: 7.4-19 BBE
pages.text: In some cases, an information sign may be erected showing how the lanes will be arranged further ahead. The sign also indicates that the merging rule must be followed, as there are no lane markings on the sign.

pages.title: 7.4-20 B
pages.text: The arrow indicates that the left-hand lane ends. It is clear from the information sign and the end of the lane markings that the merge rule applies at the narrowing. Please note that if you change to the right-hand lane before the narrowing, you must follow the rules for changing lanes.

pages.title: 7.4-21 B
pages.text: The information sign regarding the merge rule may also look like this.

pages.title: 7.4-22 BBE
pages.text: Where two roadways merge without the wide broken edge line being carried through, the merging rule also applies.

pages.title: 7.4-23 BBE
