pages.text: It is also illegal to stop or park at an exit from a Bicycle lane that crosses the Roadway, for example onto a side road. Stopping and parking are prohibited 5 metres before and 5 metres after the exit from the Bicycle lane.

pages.title: 7.18-36 BBE
pages.text: It is prohibited to stop and park alongside a stop line if the distance between the vehicle and the stop line is less than 3 metres.

pages.title: 7.18-37 BBE
pages.text: You must not stop or park in a way that obscures Traffic signs or signals.

pages.title: 7.18-38 BBE
pages.text: Stopping and parking are also prohibited on level crossings or other crossings.

pages.title: 7.18-39 BBE
pages.text: It is prohibited to stop and park under bridges, on viaducts and in tunnels.

pages.title: 7.18-40 B
pages.text: When parking the car, you must apply the Parking brake, put the car in gear, remove the ignition key and ensure that the required anti-theft device is activated.

pages.title: 7.18-41 B
pages.text: Before opening the car door, you must always check carefully for traffic approaching from behind, particularly cyclists, moped riders and pedestrians, and wait to open the door until you are sure that it can be done without risk to others.

pages.title: 7.18-42 B
pages.text: When parking alongside a curb on a hill, turn the front wheels fully to the left.

pages.title: 7.18-43 B
pages.text: When parking the car along a curb on a downhill slope, turn the wheels fully to the right.

pages.title: 7.18-44 BBE
pages.text: It is prohibited to stop on a bridge over a Motorway.

pages.title: 7.18-45 BBE
pages.text: On Motorways, it is not permitted to stop or park outside the marked Rest areas. This prohibition also applies to all areas adjacent to the Motorway.

pages.title: 7.18-46 BBE
pages.text: Stopping and parking are also prohibited on Expressways.

pages.title: 7.18-47 BBE
pages.text: It is prohibited to stop and park in a Crawler lane.

pages.title: 7.18-48 BBE
pages.text: It is prohibitet to stop or park immediately before, on, or immediately after a hill with limited visibility.

pages.title: 7.18-49 BBE
pages.text: Stopping and parking are also prohibited just before, on and just after a blind bend.

pages.title: 7.18-50 BBE
pages.text: A solid yellow line on the curb or at the edge of the carriageway emphasises or extends a prohibition on stopping and parking.

pages.title: 7.18-51 BBE
pages.text: At a bus stop, it is not permitted to stop or park in the area marked by a solid yellow side line on both sides of the bus stop sign.

pages.title: 7.18-52 BBE
pages.text: If there is no solid yellow kerb marking at a bus stop, it is not permitted to stop or park within 12 metres before and 12 metres after the bus stop sign.

pages.title: 7.18-53 BBE
pages.text: It is not permitted to stop or park at a marked taxi rank.

pages.title: 7.18-54 BBE
pages.text: If a parking bay is marked with a disabled symbol, this means that it may only be used for stopping and parking by vehicles with a valid permit.

pages.title: 7.18-55 B
pages.text: If you park in a space marked with a disabled symbol without a valid permit or blue parking card, you may be charged double the parking fine.

pages.title: 7.18-56 BBE
pages.text: Where parking is prohibited, stopping for up to 3 minutes is permitted for picking up and dropping off passengers, and loading and unloading is permitted without any time limit.

pages.title: 7.18-57 B
pages.text: The prohibition sign prohibits parking on the roadway. An arrow indicates the direction in which the prohibition applies. An arrow pointing in both directions indicates that the prohibition applies both before and after the sign. The upward-pointing arrow indicates that the prohibition applies from the sign onwards in the driving direction. And the downward-pointing arrow indicates that the prohibition applies from the sign backwards. The prohibition applies until the next Intersection, unless a sign has been erected before the Intersection to lift the prohibition.

pages.title: 7.18-58 B
pages.text: The prohibition sign may have a Supplementary traffic sign limiting the prohibition to apply only on a specific day of the week.

pages.title: 7.18-59 BBE
pages.text: The prohibition sign may be accompanied by a supplementary traffic sign indicating that the prohibition applies only on specific days and at specific times: Black text indicates that the prohibition applies from Monday to Friday. Black text in brackets indicates that the prohibition applies on Saturdays. Red text indicates that the prohibition applies only on Sundays and public holidays.

pages.title: 7.18-60 B
pages.text: The prohibition sign may have supplementary traffic signs indicating that the restrictions vary. Here, parking is prohibited Monday to Friday from 7 am to 6 pm from the sign onwards. During the same period, parking is permitted for one hour from the sign and backwards.

pages.title: 7.18-61 B
pages.text: The prohibition sign prohibits parking on the roadway, but with a supplementary traffic sign, the prohibition may also be extended to include the shoulder.

pages.title: 7.18-62 BBE
pages.text: There are many places where stopping is permitted but parking is prohibited, even if this is not indicated by signs. This applies to places where parking may cause significant inconvenience to other road users, for example if it blocks access to their vehicles or prevents them from driving away.

pages.title: 7.18-63 BBE
pages.text: It is also prohibited to park in a second position.

pages.title: 7.18-64 BBE
pages.text: Parking is not permitted in front of property entrances and exits or in a manner that significantly obstructs access to or from the property.

pages.title: 7.18-65 B
pages.text: If a vehicle is parked in front of the entrance or exit to a property in a manner that significantly impedes access to or from the property, a double parking fine may be imposed.

pages.title: 7.18-66 BBE
pages.text: Parking is prohibited within 30 metres before and after a level crossing.

pages.title: 7.18-67 BBE
pages.text: In play and recreation areas, parking is only permitted within the marked spaces.

pages.title: 7.18-68 BBE
pages.text: The yellow, dotted solid side line on the curb or along the edge of the carriageway marks or extends a no-parking zone.

pages.title: 7.18-69 BBE
pages.text: Parking on the roadway of main roads outside built-up areas is not permitted.

pages.title: 7.18-70 B
pages.text: Outside built-up areas, it is not permitted to stop or park with the whole vehicle in a central reservation.

pages.title: 7.18-71 B
pages.text: Outside built-up areas, it is permitted to stop or park partially in a central reservation, but not with the whole vehicle.

pages.title: 7.18-72 BBE
pages.text: As a general rule, stopping and parking must take place at least 2 metres from tracks found in Port areas or similar locations. However, it is permitted to stop and park closer if you remain with the vehicle and move it immediately when you see or hear a train or rail vehicle approaching.

pages.title: 7.18-73 B
pages.text: Parking bays may be marked with white, unbroken lines or by means of a special surface marking.

pages.title: 7.18-74 BBE
pages.text: When parking in a parking bay, the car must be positioned within the bay’s markings.

pages.title: 7.18-75 B
pages.text: Text or symbols in a parking bay indicate that parking in the bay is reserved for specific types of vehicle.

pages.title: 7.18-76 B
pages.text: The sign indicates that the area is designated for parking.

pages.title: 7.18-77 B
pages.text: The parking symbol may have a supplementary traffic sign indicating restrictions on parking permission.

pages.title: 7.18-78 BBE
pages.text: The parking symbol may have a supplementary traffic sign indicating that the parking area is reserved for specific types of vehicles, such as buses, Trucks and Truck and trailers.

pages.title: 7.18-79 B
pages.text: If the parking sign has a supplementary traffic sign showing a specific vehicle type and the word ‘Permitted’, there are no parking restrictions for passenger cars and vans.

pages.title: 7.18-80 B
pages.text: The "Emergency Bay" sign indicates an area that may be used for emergency stops.

pages.title: 7.18-81 BBE
pages.text: In areas with time-limited parking where there are no parking meters, you must use a Parking disc when parking your car.

pages.title: 7.18-82 B
pages.text: The Parking disc must be placed just inside the windscreen so that it is easily and clearly visible from the outside.

pages.title: 7.18-83 B
pages.text: An electronic parking disc must be affixed to the bottom right-hand corner of the windscreen.

pages.title: 7.18-84 B
pages.text: If you use transparent parking discs that are stuck on, they must be placed in the bottom right-hand corner of the windscreen.

pages.title: 7.18-85 BBE
pages.text: The Parking disc’s hand must be adjusted to the end of the quarter in which parking takes place, and it must not be changed whilst parking is in progress, where the use of a Parking disc is mandatory.

pages.title: 7.18-86 B
pages.text: Signs may indicate that parking is only permitted upon payment of a fee.

pages.title: 7.18-87 BBE
pages.text: When parking in areas where payment is required, you will find pay-and-display machines where the parking rules are indicated.

pages.title: 7.18-88 B
pages.text: The parking ticket must be displayed in the windscreen or in the side window closest to the Sidewalk, in accordance with the rules for the parking disc.

pages.title: 7.18-89 B
pages.text: Some ticket machines do not issue a physical parking ticket. Instead, you pay by credit card by entering your vehicle’s registration number and card details. The parking attendant can then scan the registration number to check whether the parking fee has been paid.

pages.title: 7.18-90 B
pages.text: You can pay for parking via one of the many parking apps available on the market. With parking apps, you can easily pay directly from the app and only for the time you actually use. You can start, extend and end parking sessions from your mobile.

pages.title: 7.18-91 BBE
pages.text: For a breach of the rules on stopping and parking, one fine may be imposed per day, but a new fine may only be imposed 24 hours after the previous one. A maximum of three fines may be imposed for the same offence.

children.title: 7.19  Driving in the dark and the lighting time in general

pages.title: 7.19-1 B
pages.text: Many accidents occur at dusk and in the dark, including single-vehicle accidents and collisions with pedestrians, cyclists, parked cars, animals and objects. It is difficult to judge distance and speed, and lights from oncoming traffic can be dazzling. The risk of hitting road users and obstacles that are difficult to see is therefore high. Your speed must never be so high that you cannot stop within the illuminated area in front of the vehicle.

pages.title: 7.19-2 B
pages.text: All lights and reflectors must be intact and clean, and all lights must be in working order.

pages.title: 7.19-3 B
pages.text: When driving outside the Lighting-up time, motor vehicles must use low-beam headlights (dipped headlights) as driving lights. Alternatively, you may use fog lights or special driving lights.

pages.title: 7.19-4 B
pages.text: If the car has automatic daytime running lights or special daytime running lights, these do not meet the requirements for lighting during the lighting-up time. Therefore, during the lighting-up time, you must use low-beam headlights or high beams.

pages.title: 7.19-5 B
pages.text: When driving with the sun low in the sky behind you, you should use low-beam headlights rather than special daytime running lights to take account of oncoming traffic.

pages.title: 7.19-6 B
pages.text: The lighting-up time is from sunset to sunrise.

pages.title: 7.19-7 B
pages.text: Lighting-up time for headlights must also be observed in rainy weather.

pages.title: 7.19-8 B
pages.text: Lighting-up time for headlights must also be observed in sleet and snow.

pages.title: 7.19-9 B
pages.text: It is also time to switch on your lights in misty and foggy weather. In such conditions, you may consider using your high beams to ensure you are seen from as far away as possible. However, high beams must not be used if the road is sufficiently lit.

pages.title: 7.19-10 B
pages.text: In the dark, high beam headlights are used on unlit roads when, due to speed, the visibility range is insufficient with low-beam headlights.

pages.title: 7.19-11 B
pages.text: Low-beam headlights are used as normal on lit roads in situations where there is a risk of dazzling oncoming traffic.

pages.title: 7.19-12 B
pages.text: When you meet another car on narrow, dark roads and need to dip your headlights, it is important to have adjusted your speed to the shorter visibility range with Low-beam headlights. This means you must reduce your speed to a maximum of 40 km/h before dipping your headlights.

pages.title: 7.19-13 B
pages.text: When you encounter oncoming traffic, you must switch to low-beam headlights approximately 200–300 metres before the encounter.

pages.title: 7.19-14 B
pages.text: When meeting oncoming traffic on a hill, you may get a little closer before switching to dipped headlights, but your speed must be reduced to a maximum of 40 km/h just before the oncoming traffic comes over the hill.

pages.title: 7.19-15 B
pages.text: If oncoming traffic is fitted with marker lights, these indicate that it is a very wide vehicle, and you must therefore adjust your speed and ensure a safe side distance when passing.

pages.title: 7.19-16 B
pages.text: Just before passing oncoming traffic, switch the high beams back on and you may then increase your speed in line with the extra visibility provided by the high beams.

pages.title: 7.19-17 B
pages.text: When encountering a train travelling alongside the road, you must also switch to low-beam headlights if there is a risk of dazzling the train driver.

pages.title: 7.19-18 B
pages.text: When meeting oncoming traffic, such as a cyclist or moped rider, you should dip your headlights 100–150 metres beforehand.

pages.title: 7.19-19 B
pages.text: When you meet oncoming traffic, you should avoid looking directly into their headlights. Instead, you should focus on the right-hand side of the road to keep an eye out for any obstacles. If the oncoming traffic’s headlights are so dazzling that you cannot see anything, you must stop the vehicle immediately.

pages.title: 7.19-20 B
pages.text: When driving with your high beam headlights on and approaching a car ahead, you must switch to low-beam headlights if there is a risk that the high beam headlights will dazzle the driver through their mirrors.

pages.title: 7.19-21 B
pages.text: When driving behind other vehicles in the dark, you must keep a greater distance from the Vehicle in front than in daylight, as it is more difficult to judge your position relative to the Vehicle in front in the dark.

pages.title: 7.19-22 B
pages.text: When overtaking, switch to high beam immediately before passing the Vehicle in front, to ensure the best possible visibility during the manoeuvre.

pages.title: 7.19-23 B
pages.text: The vehicle being overtaken should keep its high beam headlights on to provide the best possible visibility for the overtaking vehicle and switch to low-beam headlights as soon as the overtaking vehicle begins to move back into the right-hand lane after overtaking.

pages.title: 7.19-24 B
pages.text: When stopping your vehicle, you must switch to Position lights.

pages.title: 7.19-25 B
pages.text: If you park on the roadway on an unlit or inadequately lit road, the position lights, tail lights and number plate lights must be switched on.

pages.title: 7.19-26 B
pages.text: When parking at the roadside in a standard car without a Trailer, or on an unlit road in a built-up area, you only need to have the parking lights and rear lights facing the centre of the road switched on.

pages.title: 7.19-27 B
pages.text: During the lighting-up time, fog lights may only be used in fog and during heavy rainfall.

pages.title: 7.19-28 B
pages.text: Rear fog lights may only be used when there is thick fog, and only if they do not cause a nuisance to others.

pages.title: 7.20-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Driving in tunnels requires extra awareness and manoeuvring skills due to their unique design and the specific traffic conditions that arise.

pages.title: 7.20-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: The “Tunnel” warning sign indicates a tunnel up ahead.

pages.title: 7.20-3 BCDCE
pages.text: The length of the tunnel may be indicated on a supplementary traffic sign.

pages.title: 7.20-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: When entering a tunnel, there may be a stop signal which is activated if, for example, an accident has occurred in the tunnel.

pages.title: 7.20-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: If the red stop signal is lit, you must stop at the Stopline.

pages.title: 7.20-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: Some tunnels have a height restriction. If the clearance height is less than 4.3 metres, the maximum permitted height will be indicated by a Prevention sign at the tunnel entrance.

pages.title: 7.20-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: Even though the tunnel is lit, lighting conditions may change, and it takes time for your eyes to adjust to a possible reduction in light levels inside the tunnel, making it easy to overlook any obstacles.

pages.title: 7.20-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: The tunnel may be equipped with Lane signals. A green arrow above the lane indicates that it is open to traffic.

pages.title: 7.20-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: A flashing yellow arrow indicates that you must quickly change to the lane indicated by the arrow.

pages.title: 7.20-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: A red intersection means that the lane must be vacated immediately. In many cases, a red intersection above the right-hand lane is automatically activated if an alarm box in the tunnel is opened.

pages.title: 7.20-11 BCDBECE
pages.text: If there is a red intersection above all lanes, you must not continue driving.

pages.title: 7.20-12 BCDCE
pages.text: If you drive into the tunnel too fast, your eyes may not have time to adjust to the changed lighting conditions. You should therefore adjust your speed as you approach the tunnel, so that your eyes have time to adjust and you can react to any obstacles in the tunnel.

pages.title: 7.20-13 BCDBECE
pages.text: Before entering the tunnel, switch on the car’s low-beam headlights so that the tail lights also come on . . .

pages.title: 7.20-14 BCDBECE
pages.text: … and make sure to remove any sunglasses so that your eyes can adjust more easily and quickly to the changed lighting conditions.

pages.title: 7.20-15 BCDCE
pages.text: In the event of a breakdown, engine failure or similar, there is a risk of a collision with the stationary vehicle, even if it is marked, due to the limited space in the tunnel. In the event of engine failure or other breakdowns, you should, as far as possible, stop at an emergency telephone.

pages.title: 7.20-16 BCDBECE
pages.text: When driving in the tunnel, it is important to keep an eye out for markings indicating emergency lay-bys, escape routes, emergency exits and emergency equipment such as emergency telephones, fire extinguishers, alarm buttons and, where applicable, signage displaying the radio frequency providing information about the tunnel.

pages.title: 7.20-17 BCDCE
pages.text: There may be areas within the tunnel that can be used for emergency stops. These areas are marked with a sign reading “Emergency Bay”.

pages.title: 7.20-18 BCDCE
pages.text: Tunnels are equipped with escape routes and emergency exits at short intervals.

pages.title: 7.20-19 BCDCE
pages.text: The signage for emergency exits and escape routes includes arrows pointing towards the nearest exit.

pages.title: 7.20-20 BCDCE
pages.text: In tunnels, cabinets containing emergency equipment such as alarm buttons, emergency telephones and fire extinguishers are placed at short intervals.

pages.title: 7.20-21 BCDCE
pages.text: These cabinets containing emergency equipment are marked with an illuminated yellow information sign, which may be supplemented by sub-signs such as ‘Fire Extinguisher’ and ‘Emergency Telephone’. A radio frequency may also be indicated, on which information about the tunnel can be heard.

pages.title: 7.20-22 BCDBECE
pages.text: Many tunnels have traffic control with Lane signals, so keep an eye out for changes in the signals. When a yellow arrow is displayed, drivers should look for a suitable opportunity to change lanes …

pages.title: 7.20-23 BCDBECE
pages.text: … When a red Intersection is displayed, the lane must be vacated immediately …

pages.title: 7.20-24 BCDBECE
pages.text: … If there is a red light across all lanes, you must not continue driving. You may want to switch on the car radio and listen to the traffic updates.

pages.title: 7.20-25 BCDBECE
pages.text: When driving through a tunnel, you must maintain a greater safety distance from the vehicle in front than the usual two seconds, so that you have time to react if the vehicle in front brakes or stops.

pages.title: 7.20-26 BCDCE
pages.text: If traffic in the tunnel suddenly slows down or stops, switch on your Hazard warning lights whilst braking. Ensure you maintain a good distance from the vehicle in front so that you are not pushed into the stationary vehicles in the event of a rear-end collision.

pages.title: 7.20-27 BCDCE
pages.text: If you are forced to stop in the tunnel due to traffic conditions, switch off the engine to avoid unnecessary production of carbon monoxide and other harmful exhaust emissions.

pages.title: 7.20-28 BCDBECE
pages.text: If a fire breaks out in your own vehicle or another vehicle, you must immediately leave the car and move towards the nearest exit or escape route.

pages.title: 7.20-29 BCDCE
pages.text: If your engine stalls or you experience any other breakdown, you should try to stop at an emergency telephone. As there are rarely Emergency lanes, you must ensure you switch on your Hazard warning lights.

pages.title: 7.20-30 BCDCE
pages.text: When contacting the Emergency services, it is better to use an emergency telephone in the tunnel rather than a mobile phone, as a red cross often appears automatically over the right-hand lane when an emergency box in the tunnel is opened.

pages.title: 7.20-31 BCDCE
pages.text:
The consortium behind the Øresund Bridge has published a leaflet, ‘Drive safely in the tunnel’, which contains a wealth of useful information and advice on safety in the tunnel.

The leaflet can be downloaded from the Øresund Bridge website: https://www.oresundsbron.com

pages.title: 7.21-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Several major cities are constructing light rail systems, where road users must have enhanced orientation and manoeuvring skills due to the unique design of the light rail systems and the specific traffic structure.

pages.title: 7.21-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Risks associated with driving near light rail include: • Failure to pay attention to Traffic Lights and signs, which may lead to a collision with the light rail. • Lack of focus on the light rail system whilst performing other traffic manoeuvres, which may result in a collision with a light rail train. • The long braking distance of light rail vehicles, which requires other road users to be extra vigilant.

pages.title: 7.21-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: A number of accidents occur on light rail systems: • where road users misunderstand or overlook the red Traffic Light • where pedestrians overlook light rail trains when crossing the tracks • where road users overlook light rail trains whilst manoeuvring their vehicles • where road users misunderstand or misinterpret the specific traffic conditions surrounding the light rail

pages.title: 7.21-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Light rail systems typically operate in specially demarcated areas, such as grassed areas, or on tracks marked with solid side lines or Double solid lines.

pages.title: 7.21-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: The symbol “Light rail vehicle” on a track marked with a solid side line or Double solid line means that the track is reserved exclusively for light rail vehicles.

pages.title: 7.21-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: Bus and light rail signals apply to scheduled buses, light rail vehicles and zero-emission vehicles travelling in specially marked lanes. The lights in the top, middle and bottom openings correspond to red, amber and green lights respectively. The white bar in the bottom aperture may point diagonally upwards to the right or left, corresponding to a green arrow signal to the right or left respectively. Other signage may be in place locally.

pages.title: 7.21-7 BCDBECECE
pages.text: The supplementary traffic sign indicates that there is a light rail line at the intersection of the roads, where light rail vehicles may travel in both directions.

pages.title: 7.21-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: Light rail vehicles must drive in accordance with the conditions, signals and traffic. This means that a light rail vehicle must observe the general and local speed limits applicable both within and outside built-up areas. As a general rule, however, the speed of light rail vehicles must not exceed the speed limit for buses.

pages.title: 7.21-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should adjust your speed when driving near the light rail so that you have time to get used to the changed traffic conditions.

pages.title: 7.21-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should be aware that other road users may be focusing on the Light rail and not on other road users.

pages.title: 7.21-11 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should be aware of the light rail’s route ahead when overtaking or passing a light rail vehicle.

pages.title: 7.21-12 BCDBECE
pages.text: When crossing a light rail track, for example whilst turning, it is important to pay particular attention to any Traffic Lights.

children.title: 8.1.1 Alcohol as a Factor in Accidents and Injuries

pages.title: 8.1.1-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Alcohol, drugs, speeding and failure to wear a seat belt are major risk factors in road traffic.

pages.title: 8.1.1-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Alcohol is responsible for approximately one in six road deaths and many injuries.

pages.title: 8.1.1-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: Driving with alcohol in the blood significantly increases the risk of accidents, particularly for young drivers. Drivers aged 18–24 with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.8–1.2 have a risk of accidents that is 10 times greater than that of 50-year-olds with the same blood alcohol concentration.

pages.title: 8.1.1-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: At a blood alcohol concentration of 0.2, the eye’s ability to focus quickly and adjust from light to dark is impaired.

pages.title: 8.1.1-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: At a blood alcohol concentration of 0.5, the ability to assess situations and perform precise movements simultaneously is impaired. In addition, the field of vision narrows.

pages.title: 8.1.1-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: At a blood alcohol concentration of 0.8, coordination is reduced, and the Reaction time increases.

pages.title: 8.1.1-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: At a blood alcohol concentration of 1.0

pages.title: 8.1.1-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: At a blood alcohol concentration of 1.5

pages.title: 8.1.1-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: At a blood alcohol concentration of 2.0

pages.title: 8.1.1-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: At blood alcohol concentrations above 3.0

pages.title: 8.1.1-11 BCDBECE
pages.text: Blood alcohol concentrations will continue to rise for 30–90 minutes after the last drink has been consumed.

pages.title: 8.1.1-12 BCDBECE
pages.text: Alcohol metabolism only really begins in earnest around 45 minutes after you start drinking.

pages.title: 8.1.1-13 BCDBECE
pages.text: The body’s ability to break down alcohol varies from person to person. The rate at which my body metabolises alcohol depends primarily on weight and gender, but also on factors such as the contents of the stomach, the liver’s ability to metabolise alcohol, muscle mass, etc. As a rule of thumb, it takes a person weighing 60 kg around 1½–2 hours to metabolise one drink.

pages.title: 8.1.1-14 BCDBECE
pages.text: One unit is 12 grams, equivalent to 1.5 cl of pure alcohol. This corresponds to approx. 1 33 cl lager. 1 12 cl glass of wine. 1 8 cl glass of fortified wine. 1 4 cl glass of spirits.

pages.title: 8.1.1-15 BCDBECE
pages.text: A blood alcohol concentration between 0.5 and 0.8 increases the risk of an accident by up to 10 times.

pages.title: 8.1.1-16 BCDBECE
pages.text: A blood alcohol concentration between 0.8 and 1.2 increases the risk of an accident by up to 30 times.

pages.title: 8.1.1-17 BCDBECE
pages.text: A blood alcohol concentration of over 1.2 increases the risk of an accident by up to 200 times

pages.title: 8.1.1-18 BCDBECE
pages.text: Even if you try to hide the fact that you have been drinking alcohol, the police have effective methods for detecting alcohol in both the blood and breath.

pages.title: 8.1.1-19 BCDBECE
pages.text: 18- to 19-year-olds have a much higher risk of accidents when alcohol is in their blood than 35- to 44-year-olds do.

pages.title: 8.1.1-20 BCDBECE
pages.text: The risk of accidents increases on journeys to and from parties when several young people of the same age are gathered in the car.

pages.title: 8.1.1-21 BCDBECE
pages.text: It can be difficult to judge how quickly alcohol is metabolised and when it is safe to drive after drinking. If you have drunk heavily the night before, your blood alcohol concentration may still be too high to, for example, drive to the bakery the next morning.

pages.title: 8.1.1-22 BCDBECE
pages.text: You cannot speed up the Rate at which my body metabolises alcohol, whether through physical activity, sleep, coffee or any other means.

pages.title: 8.1.1-23 BCDBECE
pages.text: Driving under the influence (DUI) involves a blood alcohol concentration above 0.5 per mille or above 0.25 mg per litre of exhaled air and is therefore illegal

pages.title: 8.1.1-24 BCDBECE
pages.text: If you are a group going to a party where alcohol will be served, there are some simple tips you should follow.

pages.title: 8.1.1-25 BCDBECE
pages.text: If you plan to drink, leave the car at home, or agree in advance who will stay sober to drive.

pages.title: 8.1.1-26 BCDBECE
pages.text: Never let others pressure you into driving with alcohol in your blood.

pages.title: 8.1.1-27 BCDBECE
pages.text: As a passenger, you must always ensure that the driver is not driving under the influence. If you are a passenger in a car with a driver under the influence of alcohol, your compensation may be reduced due to your possible negligence.

pages.title: 8.1.1-28 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should take responsibility and take action if anyone tries to drive whilst under the influence of alcohol.

pages.title: 8.1.1-29 BCDBECE
pages.text: First-time holders of a driver's license – whether for a motorbike or a car – will be banned from driving for the first three years if their blood alcohol concentration is between 0.20 and 1.2, which corresponds to 0.10–0.60 mg per litre of breath.

pages.title: 8.1.1-30 BCDBECE
pages.text: If your blood alcohol concentration exceeds 1.2, corresponding to more than 0.60 mg per litre of breath, your Driver's license will be revoked without condition.

pages.title: 8.1.1-31 BCDBECE
pages.text: If your blood alcohol concentration is over 2.0, you will have your Driver's license revoked for 3 years, receive a large fine, risk a prison sentence, and your car may also be confiscated.

pages.title: 8.1.1-32 BCDCE
pages.text: In connection with Driving under the influence (DUI), everyone must complete an ANT course, which covers Alcohol, Drugs and Traffic.

children.title: 8.1.2 Narcotics as a Factor in Accidents and Injuries

pages.title: 8.1.2-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Narcotic substances in the blood significantly increase the risk of accidents. These substances affect the body in different ways. Some have a sedative effect, others a stimulant effect, and some can cause hallucinations, but they all impair the ability to drive.

pages.title: 8.1.2-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: If a person takes different narcotic substances or combines them with alcohol, the effect on the individual can be unpredictable, and the risk of accidents will always be considerably greater.

pages.title: 8.1.2-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: Different types of narcotic substances affect road safety in different ways. Stimulants such as amphetamine, cocaine, ecstasy and designer drugs increase activity levels. You do not feel tired and exhibit increased risk-taking behaviour, which can lead to taking chances and making misjudgements, with a greater risk of road accidents. Some of these substances can also cause hallucinations.

pages.title: 8.1.2-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Depressants lead to reduced alertness, poorer coordination and slower reaction times, which increases the risk of road traffic accidents. The most common depressants include cannabis, opioids such as heroin, morphine and methadone, GHB (also known as ‘fantasy’), sleeping pills, tranquillisers and other strong painkillers.

pages.title: 8.1.2-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: Some substances cause hallucinations, meaning they distort one’s perception of reality, which increases the risk of road traffic accidents. Examples of substances that cause hallucinations include LSD, certain designer drugs, and certain mushrooms and cacti.

pages.title: 8.1.2-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: Narcotic substances in the blood significantly increase the risk of accidents; cannabis increases the risk of accidents by up to three times.

pages.title: 8.1.2-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: Cocaine and heroin increase the risk of accidents by up to 10 times.

pages.title: 8.1.2-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: Amphetamine increases the risk of accidents by up to 30 times.

pages.title: 8.1.2-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: If you take different narcotic substances or mix them with alcohol, the effect on the individual can be unpredictable. A combination of alcohol and other substances can increase the risk of accidents by up to 200 times.

pages.title: 8.1.2-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should not let others pressure you into driving under the influence of drugs, and you should prevent others from driving under the influence of drugs.

pages.title: 8.1.2-11 BCDBECE
pages.text: As a passenger, you should always ensure that the driver is not under the influence of drugs. You should intervene if others are driving under the influence of drugs.

children.title: 8.1.3 Speed as a Factor in Accidents and Injuries

pages.title: 8.1.3-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Speed is a significant factor in accidents and injuries in road traffic accidents involving personal injury.

pages.title: 8.1.3-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Speed is estimated to be a contributing factor in around 25 to 50 per cent of accidents resulting in personal injury.

pages.title: 8.1.3-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: Speed is more often a factor in accidents involving young men than young women. Men aged 18–19 are generally 1.5 times more likely to be involved in an accident than women of the same age. Furthermore, the risk of serious injury is 4.5 times higher for young men than for young women.

pages.title: 8.1.3-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: If you are driving at a speed of over 30 km/h and increase your speed by 10%, the risk of a fatal accident rises by up to 45%.

pages.title: 8.1.3-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: Braking distance increases fourfold when you double your speed.

pages.title: 8.1.3-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: When two cars travelling at 50 km/h and 60 km/h respectively brake at the same time, the car travelling at 60 km/h will still be travelling at 44 km/h once the car travelling at 50 km/h has come to a standstill.

pages.title: 8.1.3-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: The most serious accidents, where speed is a significant factor in both the occurrence of the accident and the extent of the damage, take place in rural areas.

pages.title: 8.1.3-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: The risk of a pedestrian dying in a collision with a car increases significantly, even with small increases in speed. At a speed of 65 km/h, 2 out of 10 pedestrians die; at 75 km/h, 4 out of 10 die; and at 90 km/h, 7 out of 10 die.

pages.title: 8.1.3-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: Speed plays a major role as a factor in accidents and injuries in road traffic accidents involving personal injury. It is often decisive in determining how serious an accident becomes when it is caused by one’s own mistakes or those of other Road users.

pages.title: 8.1.3-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: Many accidents occur, particularly due to high speed, when young people drive to and from parties at the weekend with several peers in the car.

pages.title: 8.1.3-11 BCDBECE
pages.text: It is essential always to observe the speed limits. Driving at extremely high speeds will result in an unconditional driving ban. If you drive at 200 km/h or above, or if you drive over 100 km/h and at the same time exceed the permitted speed by more than 100%, your driving licence will be revoked unconditionally.

pages.title: 8.1.3-12 BCDBECE
pages.text: Exceeding the speed limit by more than 30% results in 1 penalty point on your Driver's license.

pages.title: 8.1.3-13 BCDBECE
pages.text: First-time holders of a driver's license risk a driving ban if they receive 2 penalty points on their license within the first 3 years of the probationary period.

pages.title: 8.1.3-14 BCDBECE
pages.text: First-time holders of a driver's license will be banned from driving if they exceed the speed limit by more than 60%.

pages.title: 8.1.3-15 BCDBECE
pages.text: First-time holders of a driver's license lose their right to drive if they drive at 160 km/h or more on the Motorway.

pages.title: 8.1.3-16 BCDCE
pages.text: Most typical accidents, where speed plays a decisive role in the risk of accidents and injuries, can easily be avoided by following this simple advice: Observe the speed limits.

pages.title: 8.1.3-17 BCDCE
pages.text: Reduce your speed if conditions do not allow you to drive at the maximum permitted speed.

pages.title: 8.1.3-18 BCDCE
pages.text: Never let others influence you into breaking the speed limit.

pages.title: 8.1.3-19 BCDCE
pages.text: Alert the driver if the speed limit is being exceeded.

children.title: 8.1.4 Neglecting to use Safety Belts as a Factor in Injuries

pages.title: 8.1.4-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Every year, there are many accidents resulting in fatalities and serious injuries that could have been avoided if those involved had worn a seat belt.

pages.title: 8.1.4-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Approximately one in four road traffic fatalities could have been prevented by the use of a seat belt, which corresponds to around 100 people a year.

pages.title: 8.1.4-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: The risk of being killed is 5–10 times greater if you are thrown from the car than if you remain inside it.

pages.title: 8.1.4-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Wearing a seat belt almost doubles the chance of surviving an accident for front-seat passengers and increases the chances of survival by around 25% for those in the back seat.

pages.title: 8.1.4-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: For example, if you weigh 75 kg and crash into a wall at 50 km/h, you need to be able to withstand a force of approximately 1.5 tonnes to remain in the car.

pages.title: 8.1.4-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: Even at speeds of 10 km/h, you cannot withstand the impact without a seat belt.

pages.title: 8.1.4-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: Many accidents occur when driving at low speeds, where the seat belt still plays a crucial role. It can be the difference between escaping unharmed or sustaining serious injuries.

pages.title: 8.1.4-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: Drivers aged 18–24 who are involved in accidents use their seat belts less often than more experienced drivers who are also involved in accidents.

pages.title: 8.1.4-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: The risk of accidents increases on journeys to and from parties at the weekend, when there are many young people of the same age in the car. On these journeys, there is a greater tendency not to wear a Seat belt.

pages.title: 8.1.4-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: Almost all common injuries caused by not wearing a seat belt can be prevented by following some simple advice.

pages.title: 8.1.4-11 BCDBECE
pages.text: Always wear a seat belt – even on short journeys, . .

pages.title: 8.1.4-12 BCDBECE
pages.text: Never let others persuade you to drive without a seat belt, . . .

pages.title: 8.1.4-13 BCDBECE
pages.text: Make sure everyone in the car wears a seat belt, . . .

pages.title: 8.1.4-14 BCDBECE
pages.text: Do not carry more passengers than there are seat belts for.

pages.title: 8.2.1-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Inattention is the cause of around one third of all accidents. Distracting activities are carried out for approximately one third of the time spent driving. Around two thirds of the causes of inattention stem from things inside the car, often conditions that the driver can control themselves.

pages.title: 8.2.1-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: Lack of attention, misunderstandings and incorrect judgements often contribute significantly to most road traffic accidents.

pages.title: 8.2.1-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: A safe attitude and behaviour on the road are best achieved through an understanding of one’s own limitations and a healthy scepticism towards what one immediately perceives in traffic. This attitude is reinforced by developing a driving style that compensates for one’s own limitations and ensures a good safety margin during all manoeuvres.

pages.title: 8.2.1-4 BCDBECE
pages.text: Distraction occurs when the driver does something that takes their attention away from driving. Typical everyday activities such as looking for items in the glove compartment, using a sat-nav, eating and drinking, or talking to a passenger divert the driver’s attention from the traffic. Other distractions include operating the radio, GPS and smartphones whilst driving. This equipment should be operated by a passenger or when the car is stationary.

pages.title: 8.2.1-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: Other passengers, particularly noisy children, but also animals, can be distracting.

pages.title: 8.2.1-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: An unbalanced state of mind caused by strong excitement, grief, worry or similar can significantly distract attention.

pages.title: 8.2.1-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: You must always be aware of the traffic ahead, to the sides and behind you, whilst anticipating how the traffic may develop in the coming seconds.

pages.title: 8.2.1-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should avoid engaging in distracting activities and refrain from unnecessary actions that may divert your attention from the traffic. If necessary, you should pull over to the side of the road.

pages.title: 8.2.2-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should be patient and help other road users, even when they make mistakes.

pages.title: 8.2.2-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should help road users who are having difficulty finding their way – for example, by letting them change lanes or move position at an Intersection – even if they are responsible for the situation.

pages.title: 8.2.2-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should give large vehicles and trucks and trailers plenty of space when they are manoeuvring, such as when turning or reversing – even if they are at fault.

pages.title: 8.2.2-4 BCDCE
pages.text: You should keep an extra safe distance from vehicles in front that appear uncertain or inexperienced.

pages.title: 8.2.2-5 BCDBECE
pages.text: It is important to drive at low speed near Road Construction, especially when road workers are on or near the road, and to ensure you keep a safe distance from them.

pages.title: 8.2.2-6 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should ensure that the road is clear of emergency vehicles in the most practical way possible in the situation, or follow the instructions given.

pages.title: 8.2.2-7 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should refrain from using your lights or horn to signal to a driver who, for example, is a little slow to pull away at a traffic light-controlled intersection.

pages.title: 8.2.2-8 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should avoid using lights and the horn to signal to drivers who are pulling in front of you and reducing the Safety distance, unless it is necessary to prevent a dangerous situation.

pages.title: 8.2.2-9 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should avoid using abusive language, gestures or signalling towards other road users.

pages.title: 8.2.2-10 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should always be alert and prepared, for example by moving your foot to the brake if a situation seems unpredictable or unsafe.

pages.title: 8.2.2-11 BCDBECE
pages.text: Cooperating with others on the road can help to improve road safety.

pages.title: 8.2.3-1 BCDBECE
pages.text: Critically assessing one’s own strengths and weaknesses as a driver can help to gain a better understanding of one’s driving skills.

pages.title: 8.2.3-2 BCDBECE
pages.text: One should adapt one’s driving and take particular account of the vehicle’s design, equipment, state of maintenance, load, and road and weather conditions.

pages.title: 8.2.3-3 BCDBECE
pages.text: You should take responsibility and the necessary precautions in traffic and cooperate with other road users in a manner appropriate to your own driving skills.

pages.title: 10.1.2-1 B
pages.text:
You adjust yourself for a driving test by completing and signing an approved application form and submitting it to Citizen Services.

The application must be accompanied by:

- A personal identification number certificate or similar documentation of your personal identification number.

- A baptism or birth certificate and, for married persons, also a marriage certificate or other proof of surname.

- A clear photograph (portrait without headwear) measuring 35 x 45 mm and without stamps.

- The medical certificate must be submitted to the local authority using the Danish Road Safety and Transport Agency’s digital solution.

You must also complete a traffic-related first aid course if you are applying for a Driver's license for the first time. The course must last at least 8 hours.

pages.title: 10.1.2-2 B
pages.text: The driving instructor must confirm with their signature on the application form that you have received instruction in accordance with the curriculum, including that the initial practical instruction took place at a closed training ground.

pages.title: 10.1.2-3 B
pages.text:
Driver's licenses are issued by the Danish Road Safety and Transport Agency upon passing the driving test.

A Category B driver's license entitles the holder to drive:

- Passenger cars and vans with a maximum permitted gross vehicle weight (GVW) not exceeding 3,500 kg. The passenger car must be designed to carry no more than 8 passengers in addition to the driver.

- A car with a Trailer attached with a maximum Permitted gross vehicle weight of 750 kg.

- A car with a Trailer attached with a maximum Permitted gross vehicle weight exceeding 750 kg, provided that the combined Permitted gross vehicle weight of the car and Trailer does not exceed 3,500 kg.

- Three-wheeled motorcycles, three-wheeled cars, tractors, motorised equipment, and small and large mopeds.

pages.title: 10.1.2-4 B
pages.text: The driving test is taken before a Driving examinor from the Danish Road Safety and Transport Agency or, for those called up for service in the Armed Forces and the Emergency Services, before special driving examiners.

children.title: 10.2 Requirements for the theoretical exam and the practical test

pages.title: 10.2-1 B
pages.text: The driving test is divided into a theory test and a practical test. You must pass the theory test before taking the practical test. For the theory test, you must bring the Driver's license application, duly completed and signed by the driving instructor or instructors who have completed your training. In addition to the application, you must bring the completed and signed module plan, as well as any previously issued Driver's licenses (e.g. for a motorcycle), or special identification such as a passport or other suitable form of identification, along with photo ID.

pages.title: 10.2-2 B
pages.text: Before the test, participants are briefed on the conduct and conditions of the test, including how to complete the tick-box form, and it is emphasised that the use of aids is not permitted. During the test, only invigilators and candidates are permitted access to the test room.

pages.title: 10.2-3 B
pages.text: The test is marked in accordance with the Danish Road Safety and Transport Agency’s marking guidelines, and up to five incorrect answers will result in the standard car test being marked as passed. The result of the test is announced immediately after the test has finished. Candidates who have failed must be informed of which topics in the syllabus they answered incorrectly.

pages.title: 10.2-4 B
pages.text: You must pass the theory test before you can sit the practical test. For the practical test, you must bring the Driver's license application, duly completed and signed by the driving instructor or instructors who have completed your training. There may be a requirement for any supporting documents to be attached to the application. In addition to the application, you must bring the completed and signed module plan and any previously issued Driver's licenses, e.g. for a motorcycle. If you do not hold a previously issued credit card-style Driver's license, you must bring a valid passport or an original birth, name or baptism certificate, as well as photo ID.

pages.title: 10.2-5 B
pages.text: During the practical driving test, you must be able to inspect the vehicle and assess whether it meets safety requirements without the use of tools. This includes being able to explain how the inspection is carried out.

pages.title: 10.2-6 B
pages.text: The driving test normally lasts 30–35 minutes, of which at least 25 minutes must be set aside for assessing the candidate’s practical skills. During the test, at least two of the following manoeuvres must always be included: • Reversing straight ahead or reversing around the corner to the right whilst remaining in the correct lane. • Performing a three-point turn. Reversing may only be required to be performed with some precision • Parking the vehicle and leaving a parallel or perpendicular parking space, by reversing or driving forwards, on level, uphill or downhill roads. • Brake accurately. The test may be extended if necessary and may be terminated if your driving ability is very poor.

pages.title: 10.2-7 B
pages.text: The driving test is conducted with the Driving examinor sitting next to you in an approved driving school vehicle, which you must provide yourself. The driving instructor, or their representative, may, with your and the Driving examinor’s consent, observe the test from the back seat of the car. During the test, you are considered to be the driver of the car, with the resulting responsibilities and obligations.

pages.title: 10.2-8 B
pages.text: You must drive in accordance with the instructions regarding the route and manoeuvres given by the driving examinor. The instructions must be given clearly and in good time so that you can perceive and understand them and have time to prepare for and carry out the instructed manoeuvre. The driving examinor must not force you into abnormal traffic situations. The driving examinor must intervene verbally or by using the vehicle’s controls if necessary for safety reasons or to avoid a collision.

pages.title: 10.2-9 B
pages.text: As part of the test centre’s quality assurance of the practical test, a further Driving examinor may, after prior consultation with the driving instructor, be present during the practical test.

pages.title: 10.2-10 B
pages.text: A few minor errors cannot in themselves result in the test being marked as a fail, as your driving must be assessed as a whole. The result of the test must be communicated immediately after the test has ended. If you have failed, you must be informed which skill requirements in the curriculum have not been satisfactorily met.

children.title: 10.3 Certain Legal Rules for Driving Licenses

pages.title: 10.3-1 B
pages.text: Driver's licenses for ordinary cars are issued with a validity period of 15 years at a time, However, in special cases, e.g. due to illness, they may be issued with a shorter validity period and subject to specific conditions. Once the validity period has expired, the driver's license can be renewed by contacting the local authority.

pages.title: 10.3-2 B
pages.text: You must carry your Driver's license with you whilst driving and show it to the police on request. If your Driver's license is damaged or lost, you must contact Citizen Services to have a new one issued.

pages.title: 10.3-3 B
pages.text: You can download a digital version of your Danish driver's license. It serves as both a valid driver's license and proof of identity, which means you do not need to carry your physical driver's license with you when driving in Denmark.

pages.title: 10.3-4 B
pages.text: If the police have reason to believe that you no longer meet the conditions for holding a Driver's license, they may revoke it or summon you to a driving test.

pages.title: 10.3-5 B
pages.text: If your Driver's license has been revoked, it can normally only be reissued after you have passed a re-examination. If the re-examination is to be taken by a first-time applicant, special driving lessons must be completed beforehand. The special driving lessons must be taken with an approved driving instructor and must comprise at least 8 theory lessons and 8 practical driving lessons.

pages.title: 10.3-6 B
pages.text: If your driving licence has been revoked as a result of Driving under the influence (DUI), drug-driving or driving under the influence of illness, etc., you must complete a course on alcohol and traffic, known as an ANT course. In addition, you must pass a driving test.

pages.title: 10.3-7 B
pages.text: First-time applicants for a motorcycle or small car driver's license who have not held their first driver's license for three years will, in the event of certain breaches of the requirements of the Road Traffic Act, be subject to a driving ban or a revoked driver’s license.

pages.title: 10.3-8 B
pages.text: If you break the road traffic rules, this may result in a fine, a driving ban, or a conditional or suspended driver's license.

pages.title: 10.3-9 B
pages.text: Under this system, every time you commit a dangerous traffic offence, you will receive both a fine and one or more penalty points. If you accumulate three penalty points within three years, your Driver's license will be suspended, and you will be required to sit a theory and practical test, which you must pass in order to retain your Driver's license.

pages.title: 10.3-10 B
pages.text: If your first Driver's license was issued less than three years ago, you will be banned from driving after receiving two penalty points within three years.

pages.title: 10.3-11 B
pages.text: The offences that result in a penalty point are: - If you exceed the speed limit by more than 30%. - If you fail to maintain a safe safety distance from the Vehicle in front. - If you drive through a red light. - If you fail to give way.

pages.title: 10.3-12 B
pages.text: - If you breach the rules on overtaking and the ban on overtaking. - If you cross a solid line whilst overtaking. - If you overtake in front of or within a Crosswalk. - If you accelerate whilst a vehicle is overtaking from behind.

pages.title: 10.3-13 B
pages.text: - If you drive against the direction of traffic. - If you drive illegally in the Emergency lane on a Motorway. - If you drive recklessly, weaving in and out of traffic or overtaking in heavy traffic. - If you breach the requirements on turning, reversing, starting off and changing lanes.

pages.title: 10.3-14 B
pages.text: - If you drive on the left-hand side of a traffic island. - If you race or compete on the road. - If you drive over a railway track when a signal to stop has been given. - If children and young people under the age of 15 for whom you are responsible do not use the fitted seatbelts.

pages.title: 10.3-15 B
pages.text: In addition to a fine, you will also receive a penalty point on your Driver's license if you use a hand-held mobile phone whilst driving.

pages.title: 10.3-16 B
pages.text: If, after smoking cannabis, you drive with a low concentration of THC in your blood, namely between 0.001 and 0.003 mg/kg, you will receive a penalty point on your Driver's license. At higher concentrations, you will face a conditional or revoked driver's license.

pages.title: 10.3-17 B
pages.text: Certain types of traffic offences are defined as “reckless driving”; reckless driving carries harsher penalties and consequences.

pages.title: 10.3-18 B
pages.text: Reckless driving is: Negligent manslaughter or causing serious bodily harm under aggravating circumstances Driving in a manner that poses an imminent danger to life or limb Particularly reckless driving Speeding by more than 100% when driving at over 100 km/h Driving under the influence (DUI) with a blood alcohol concentration exceeding 2.0

pages.title: 10.3-19 B
pages.text: There are stricter penalties for reckless driving

pages.title: 10.3-20 B
pages.text: The consequence of reckless driving is that the police can immediately revoke the Driver's license; the police may also confiscate the vehicle, even if it is borrowed, hired or leased!

education.title: Module 5: Final theory and practical driving module

pages.title: Introduction
pages.text:
Module 5: Final theory and practical driving module.

The teaching in Module 5 is designed to enhance your ability to independently plan and organise your driving with a view to developing your skills in risk awareness, understanding your own limitations, and energy-efficient and Environmentally friendly driving. You must also complete training at a driving skills centre and acquire sufficient knowledge of the basic physical principles of driving to help you understand the importance of adapting your speed, steering and braking to the conditions.

pages.title: 9.1.1-1 B
pages.text: Road grip is caused by the friction between the tyres and the road. Engine power, braking power and steering depend on road grip, which is crucial for every manoeuvre.

pages.title: 9.1.1-2 B
pages.text: Road grip is significantly reduced in wet and slippery conditions, particularly on snow, sand and slippery roads in general. Therefore, the accelerator, clutch, brakes and steering wheel must be used with great care, and speed must be kept suitably low. Road grip can be improved by using winter tyres when driving on snow-covered roads.

pages.title: 9.1.2-1 B
pages.text: A particularly heavy load at the rear of the vehicle increases the pressure on the rear wheels, whilst the pressure on the front wheels is reduced. This can reduce the front wheels’ Road grip to such an extent that it significantly impairs steering ability and the ability to utilise engine power in front-wheel-drive vehicles.

pages.title: 9.1.2-2 B
pages.text: Choosing the wrong type of tyre can have a significant impact on road grip. Worn tyre tread reduces road grip in wet conditions. When driving in heavy rain or through puddles, there is a risk of aquaplaning even with new tyres or at relatively low speeds.

pages.title: 9.1.2-3 B
pages.text: Both too high and too low tyre pressure result in poor contact between the tyre and the roadway, reducing road grip and altering the car’s steering characteristics.

children.title: 9.2 Speed, centrifugal force, braking distance and utilisation of road grip

pages.title: 9.2.1-1 B
pages.text: When a car starts moving, kinetic energy is generated, which allows it to continue moving for a while even after the connection between the engine and the wheels has been cut off. The relationship between speed and kinetic energy means that doubling the speed results in a fourfold increase in kinetic energy.

pages.title: 9.2.1-2 B
pages.text: Kinetic energy is converted into heat in the brakes during braking. In a collision, however, the kinetic energy is converted into damage to both the person and the vehicle. The damage is significantly worse the higher the speed.

pages.title: 9.2.2-1 B
pages.text: A car driving through a bend or performing an evasive manoeuvre is affected by centrifugal force, which will attempt to ‘pull’ the car out of the bend.

pages.title: 9.2.2-2 B
pages.text: There is a relationship between speed and centrifugal force, whereby doubling the speed results in a fourfold increase in centrifugal force.

pages.title: 9.2.2-3 B
pages.text: When driving through bends, halving the bend radius will double the centrifugal force.

pages.title: 9.2.2-4 B
pages.text: These conditions are particularly important when driving vehicles with high construction profiles, such as a van or a passenger car with a roof box. If you drive too fast through bends in such vehicles, the risk of overturning increases significantly.

pages.title: 9.2.3-1 B
pages.text: Braking can reduce the distance the car can travel under its own momentum, but doubling the speed results in a fourfold increase in braking distance when braking with the same force.

pages.title: 9.2.3-2 B
pages.text: The braking distance is the distance the car travels from the moment braking begins until the car comes to a standstill. The braking distance depends, among other things, on how hard you press the Brake pedal. At a speed of, for example, 60 km/h on a flat, dry road, the Braking distance is: - approx. 50 m with very gentle braking, - approx. 30 m with fairly heavy braking, and - approx. 20 m with very hard braking.

pages.title: 9.2.3-3 B
pages.text: The braking distance will almost double with relatively small increases in speed, for example: - from approx. 30 to 40 km/h, - from approx. 60 to 80 km/h, and - from approx. 80 to 100 km/h.

pages.title: 9.2.3-4 B
pages.text: The braking distance also depends on road grip (or road conditions). To maintain, for example, a shorter braking distance of approx. 35 m at 80 km/h on a level, dry road without locking the wheels, you must reduce your speed to: - 60 km/h on wet tarmac or gravel, - 40 km/h on compacted snow, and - 30 km/h on icy roads. The braking distance will also be increased when driving downhill.

pages.title: 9.2.3-5 B
pages.text: At 30 km/h, the braking distance using the Service brake must not exceed approx. 5.5 metres for a Passenger car and 7 metres for a van weighing up to 3,500 kg. With the Emergency brake, it must be up to 11 metres for a Passenger car and 14 metres for a van. If the Parking brake is used, the Braking distance at the same speed must not exceed 20 metres.

pages.title: 9.2.3-6 B
pages.text: The stopping distance for a vehicle depends not only on the braking distance but also on the driver’s Reaction time and the distance the vehicle travels before the driver reacts. There may be various factors whilst driving that distract the driver, resulting in a longer Reaction time than normal.

pages.title: 9.2.4-1 B
pages.text: In cars without ABS, on slippery roads you should brake with light pressure and control the pedal yourself so that the wheels are just kept in rotation – otherwise the Braking distance will be longer. In cars with ABS, press the pedal all the way down and hold it there for maximum effect. Sharp turns of the steering wheel, heavy braking or acceleration when cornering on a slippery road can cause the car to lose control. If one pair of wheels is on a slippery road and the other on a dry road, the car may pull to one side, even with ABS.

pages.title: 9.2.4-2 B
pages.text: When braking with ABS brakes, the system ensures that the wheels continue to rotate and do not lock. During the regulation of braking force, strong vibrations may occur in the Brake pedal. This is completely normal and indicates that the ABS system is working. Despite the vibrations, you should continue to apply pressure to the brake pedal for as long as you wish to brake.

pages.title: 9.2.4-3 B
pages.text: Most new cars are equipped with Electronic Stability Control (ESC), also known as Electronic Stability Programme (ESP), which helps to prevent skidding or Overturning. This system can reduce the risk of skidding when cornering, during evasive manoeuvres, or if the car has veered off the shoulder and the driver attempts to steer it back onto the road with a sudden movement of the steering wheel.

pages.title: 9.2.4-4 B
pages.text: When entering a bend without an electronic stability programme, high speed, combined with the driver braking and turning the steering wheel at the same time, can easily cause the vehicle to skid.

pages.title: 9.2.4-5 B
pages.text: Cars with Electronic Stability Control are fitted with sensors that detect the car’s movements in all directions.

pages.title: 9.2.4-6 B
pages.text: When the system detects that a skid is imminent, one or more wheels are braked for a short or longer period to correct the car’s trajectory.

pages.title: 9.2.4-7 B
pages.text: At the driving skills centre, exercises such as the following are carried out: - Braking on dry and wet roads - Slalom - Double evasive manoeuvre - Combined braking and evasive manoeuvre - Driving through bends - Driving over and back over a high kerb The aim is to learn how to react correctly to sudden obstacles by steering around them or combining braking and steering, as well as to experience how much speed needs to be reduced on slippery roads

pages.title: 9.2.4-8 B
pages.text: In the braking exercise on a normal dry road, you must drive at approx. 60 km/h and, upon reaching a marker, brake with firm and sustained pressure on the Brake pedal so that the braking distance is as short as possible.

pages.title: 9.2.4-9 B
pages.text: On a slippery road, gradually increasing your speed up to approx. 50 km/h, you must brake over the shortest possible distance. Adjust your speed so that you can judge for yourself how fast you need to be driving to maintain a Braking distance of approx. 20 m. Then set off on the slippery road without wheel spin or skidding.

children.title: 9.3 Obstacles on the road and slalom

pages.title: 9.3.1-1 B
pages.text: At approx. 50 km/h on a normal dry road, drive a slalom course between cones placed 15–20 m apart. The impact on the car must be as small as possible, and steering must be carried out in such a way that the car settles between each turn.

pages.title: 9.3.2-1 B
pages.text: On a normal dry road, at 50–60 km/h, perform a double evasive manoeuvre without braking to avoid colliding with a marked obstacle; make a quick lane change to pass the obstacle and then quickly return to the original lane once the obstacle has been passed.

pages.title: 9.3.2-2 B
pages.text: On a slippery road, a rapid lane change is made to pass the obstacle at an appropriate high speed, but you must judge for yourself to what speed you need to reduce in order to complete the manoeuvre safely.

pages.title: 9.3.3-1 B
pages.text: In the combined braking and evasive manoeuvre on a normal dry road, drive at 70 km/h and brake before an obstacle that is so close that stopping is not possible; steer past the obstacle without making excessive steering movements and bring the car to a stop.

pages.title: 9.3.3-2 B
pages.text: On a slippery road, brake before a marked obstacle that is so close that stopping alone is not possible; steer past the obstacle without making excessive steering movements and bring the car to a stop. In this exercise, you must judge for yourself to what speed you need to reduce in order to complete the exercise safely.

pages.title: 9.4.1-1 B
pages.text: When driving through a slippery curved road, you must experience the importance of speed when negotiating curved roads of varying radii. The curved road is driven both on the inside and outside of the road, at a speed appropriate to the road surface friction, and you must learn to react correctly to any front-wheel or rear-wheel skidding.

children.title: 9.5 Maintaining control after driving onto a high verge

pages.title: 9.5.1-1 B
pages.text: On a normal dry road, drive over a high kerb on the right-hand side at gradually increasing speeds, then brake gently whilst steering the car straight ahead along the kerb, and only steer back over the kerb and thus back onto the road when the speed is low enough to do so without risk. If conditions are permitted, the exercise can also be carried out on the left-hand side of the road.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: Road markings improve road safety by helping traffic to position itself correctly and manoeuvre safely.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: Road markings is a collective term for the longitudinal markings on the roadway and consists of kerb lines, lane lines, warning lines, stop lines and stop areas.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: The kerb lines demarcate the part of the roadway intended for use by cars, motorcycles and large mopeds.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: The narrow kerb line is a warning sign, as it indicates that there is normally no room for pedestrians and cyclists, who are therefore forced to use the same part of the Roadway as cars and motorcycles.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: The wide edge line indicates that there is space to the right of the line for pedestrians, cyclists and moped riders.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: The wide edge line may also demarcate special lanes reserved for specific types of vehicles, in this case a Bicycle lane.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: Here, a Bus lane.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: However, this specific lane may be reserved for other specific types of vehicles.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: The wide kerb line must be present to demarcate other special lanes, such as a turning lane here.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: These special lanes may also be a combination of Bicycle lane, Bus lane and turning lane.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: Edge lines may be crossed where they are broken; however, the solid edge line may also be crossed when turning onto or off the road.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: If the solid edge line does not demarcate a special lane, it may be crossed when stopping or parking.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: If the solid line does not demarcate a specific lane, it may also be crossed when overtaking on the right of a vehicle turning left.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: If you are driving slowly it is permitted to cross the edge line to help someone pass you. You may only do so while the other vehicle is overtaking you.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: Lane markings are short lines with long gaps between them.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: On roadways without markings, e.g. lane lines, there are as many lanes as there is space for rows of four-wheeled vehicles alongside one another.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: The lane markings here divide the roadway into 3 lanes.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: Here, the roadway is divided into two lanes, one very wide and one relatively narrow.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: The warning lines are long dashes with short gaps.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: On narrow, winding roads, or on roads with many junctions, the warning line may be used as a centre line. In these cases, the warning line is used along the entire length of the road.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: The warning line is used as a warning of a stop line.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: It is permitted to cross a warning line if this can be done without danger or unnecessary inconvenience to others. When crossing, particular care must be taken.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: The stop line is a narrow unbroken line, which may be a single line or part of a double line.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: The solid line marks the separation between carriageways and must not be crossed or driven over by vehicles, not even when turning, turning at an Intersection, entering a property or similar. If the line is part of a double line, the lines separate opposing directions of traffic, and in this case vehicles must only follow the nearest line.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: However, it is permitted to cross the centre line where it is interrupted.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: The single stop line is used to divide the roadway into waiting bays and lanes at traffic light-controlled intersections. Here, too, it is prohibited to cross or overshoot the stop line.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: It may be tempting to cross the stop line when overtaking a slow-moving vehicle, but this is prohibited.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: It is only permitted to cross the stop line during Road Construction, when passing a stationary or parked vehicle, and in similar special conditions. When crossing the line, Traffic must exercise particular caution.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: Hatched road markings are used to direct traffic into specific lanes and consist of either a completely white or a hatched area. If the lane marking is hatched, it is usually bordered by a narrow line. Motor vehicles must pass the lane marking on the side where the hatching points forwards. It is not permitted to drive, stop or park on a hatched road marking.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: However, where the hatched road markings are marked by a dotted line, it is permitted to cross the hatched road markings from the side where the line is dotted.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text:
Road signs are categorised as follows:

• Give way signs
• Warning signs
• Prohibition signs
• Signs giving orders
• Information signs

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: Give-way signs are erected immediately at the point where or from which the specified give-way rule applies. However, advance warning signs may be erected, in which case the distance is indicated on a Supplementary traffic sign.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: Warning signs are triangular with the apex pointing upwards, a red border and a white central panel with a black symbol indicating the nature of the danger. Outside built-up areas, warning signs are normally placed between 150 and 250 metres before the danger spot. If they are placed at a different distance, this is indicated on a Supplementary traffic sign. In built-up areas, the signs may be placed at a shorter distance from the danger spot without any indication of distance.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: Prohibition signs are white and round with a red border and are normally erected immediately at the point where or from which the prohibition applies. Signs erected at some distance from the point are fitted with a Supplementary traffic sign indicating the distance.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: Mandatory signs are round, blue signs with a white symbol indicating the nature of the requirement. Mandatory signs are placed immediately at the location where or from which the requirement applies.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: Information signs are square and are placed either at the location, close to the relevant area, or at the start of the stretch of road to which the sign’s content relates. Signs erected at a distance may be provided with a distance indication directly on the sign or on a Supplementary traffic sign. Certain information signs may indicate prohibitions, mandatory requirements or special rules that apply at the location or to the stretch of road.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text:
Variable traffic signs can be illuminated or be made up of slats which can be switched on and off as needed.

On the illuminated boards, the background color may be black with red border and red and white symbols or white background with red border and red and black symbols.

Illuminated boards hold as much authority as regular traffic signs.

pages.title: 7.0 Road Markings and Traffic Signs
pages.text: Traffic islands, traffic lights and similar installations must be passed on the right, unless the road is one-way or otherwise indicated by road markings or signage.
